Exciton superfluidity in two-dimensional bilayers at zero and high magnetic fields

Sankar Das Sarma Affiliation: Condensed Matter Theory Center and Joint Quantum Institute, Department of Physics, University of Maryland, College Park, Maryland 20742, USA    Yang-Zhi Chou Affiliation: Condensed Matter Theory Center and Joint Quantum Institute, Department of Physics, University of Maryland, College Park, Maryland 20742, USA
October 15, 2026
Abstract

We study how interlayer exciton superfluidity evolves with layer separation in two-dimensional bilayers, connecting the electron–hole system at zero magnetic field with the quantum Hall system at total filling factor νT=1\nu_{T}=1. A particle–hole transformation relates their order parameters, although the kinetic energy is quenched in the quantum Hall regime. Hartree–Fock theory with the unscreened Coulomb interaction predicts coherence at every finite separation, with an energy scale that decreases inversely with separation at large distances. We examine how screening, correlations, and spatial instabilities modify this prediction. At zero field, we solve the linearized gap equation with the full momentum and frequency dependence of the interaction screened within the random-phase approximation, without an imposed cutoff. The apparent plasmon enhancement of pairing in the ladder approximation is largely cancelled by the second-order crossed-rung correction. Static screening determines the leading pairing exponent in the controlled high-density limit at fixed separation. At large separation, the pairing scale falls exponentially with squared separation while the instability persists; extending this conclusion to fixed density assumes Fermi-liquid layers and higher-order dynamical contributions that are subleading to the static pairing interaction. At high field, we obtain an analytic uniform Hartree–Fock saddle point in the lowest Landau level that remains coherent at every finite separation. Within Hartree–Fock theory, its finite-wave-vector collective-mode instability favors a density-modulated coherent state, an excitonic supersolid. This distinguishes loss of spatial uniformity from loss of coherence. We conjecture that the quantum Hall bilayer evolves continuously from strong interlayer coherence to weak pairing of composite fermions, with a scale far below the mean-field prediction at large separation. Such suppression could in principle produce an apparent experimental critical separation at finite temperature without a ground-state quantum phase transition. The comparison separates the existence, energy scale, and spatial stability of interlayer coherence.

I Introduction

An electron in one two-dimensional layer and a hole in a parallel layer attract each other, and at low temperature the resulting interlayer excitons can condense into a state with spontaneous coherence between the layers. Because the electron and the hole are in different layers the exciton cannot recombine, and the condensate is a superfluid that carries equal and opposite currents in the two layers [1, 2]. It is the bilayer form of the excitonic instability of a semimetal [3]. The subject has two standard settings. The first is the balanced electron-hole bilayer at zero magnetic field, realized in semiconductor and atomic double layers [4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. The second is the quantum Hall bilayer at total filling factor νT=1\nu_{T}=1, in which each layer has a half-filled lowest Landau level and a particle-hole transformation of one layer turns the electron-electron bilayer into an electron-hole bilayer [9, 10]. It is in the second setting that the phenomenon was first observed and has been studied in the most detail.

The two settings are usually treated separately, with different languages: pairing and the Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) instability in one, the pseudospin ferromagnet in the other. They are one problem. After a particle-hole transformation of one layer the Hamiltonian is the same apart from the kinetic energy and one-body terms, the broken symmetry is the same, the layer separation dd is the experimental tuning parameter in both, and the density enters through one further parameter, rsr_{s} at zero field and the filling factor in a field. Here rsr_{s} is the dimensionless Coulomb interaction parameter, defined as the mean interparticle spacing in units of the effective Bohr radius. In both, the analytic predictions for the dependence on dd come from mean-field theory, the Hartree-Fock (HF) approximation, and its extensions: the theory of Ref. [11] and the Eliashberg theory with dynamical screening [12] at zero field, and the theory of the coherent state and of its collective mode at νT=1\nu_{T}=1 [13, 14, 15]. And in both, mean-field theory gives coherence at every separation, with a scale that decays only as 1/d1/d. The questions are then the same too. Does the coherence at every dd survive beyond mean-field theory? What is the true dependence of its scale on dd? Is the evolution from small to large dd a transition or a crossover? And what is the relation of the coherent state to the states of broken translation symmetry that appear on the way?

This paper treats both settings and compares them. The two parts are of unequal length, because the problems are unequal in what can be done. At zero field there are small parameters, and the theory can be carried beyond mean field in two limits. At νT=1\nu_{T}=1 the kinetic energy is quenched, there is no small parameter, and nothing is known in a controlled way beyond HF theory; what can be done there is to state that theory completely and to say exactly what it does and does not establish.

Three questions that are often run together must be kept apart, and their separation organizes the paper. The first is the existence of an interlayer-coherent solution. The second is the magnitude of its energy scale. The third is its stability against competing states.

At zero field, screening qualitatively changes the unscreened mean-field scale, and the crossed-rung diagram largely cancels the enhancement obtained from dynamical screening in the ladder approximation. We analyze the resulting scale in two limits: small rsr_{s} and large layer separation. Competing crystalline phases at low density lie outside our scope. At νT=1\nu_{T}=1, the uniform Hartree-Fock coherence scale is known in closed form, although its reliability at large separation remains unresolved. Within Hartree-Fock theory, the uniform state develops a finite-wave-vector instability beyond d/ℓ≃1.175d/\ell\simeq 1.175 (with ℓ\ell being the magnetic length) toward a density-modulated state that retains interlayer coherence.

The difficulties in the subject arise where an answer to one of these questions is inferred from another: a large scale from the existence of the solution, or a loss of coherence from an instability of the uniform state. The results below are arranged so that each is assigned to the question it answers.

Zero field. Whether the Coulomb interaction alone can produce a pairing instability of a metal at a useful temperature is an old question. For a single electron layer or a three-dimensional electron gas the bare interaction is repulsive, and ss-wave pairing requires the dynamically screened interaction to be less repulsive at low frequency than at high frequency, the difference being supplied by the plasmon [16, 17, 18, 19]. A recent analysis of this problem [20] emphasized that the standard Eliashberg route to a quantitative TcT_{c} is uncontrolled there. Migdal’s theorem [21, 22], which justifies dropping vertex corrections for phonons because the Debye energy is much smaller than the Fermi energy, has no analog when the boson is the plasmon of the same electrons, because the plasmon energy is comparable to the Fermi energy. The calculated TcT_{c} then depends on a frequency cutoff that the theory cannot fix, and for cutoffs small enough to make the neglect of vertex corrections plausible the ss-wave instability disappears [20]. A small parameter of the Migdal type can be restored in an all-electron bilayer by a large ratio of the layer masses [23].

The electron-hole bilayer is the natural system in which to revisit the question, because one essential ingredient is reversed. Electrons in one layer and holes in the other attract, so the bare interaction in the pairing channel is attractive at every wave vector [1, 2, 3]. Interlayer pairing, the condensation of interlayer excitons, is therefore present already at the HF level [11], and screening can only reduce it. The role of dynamical screening was studied within Eliashberg theory in Ref. [12], which found a finite TcT_{c} over the range of density and separation studied, well below the unscreened HF value and above the statically screened one. Related questions arose earlier for graphene double layers, where static screening was argued to suppress the gap to unobservable values [24] and dynamical screening was found to restore much of it [25, 26]. A comparison of the energies of the exciton gas and of the electron-hole plasma found the outcome to depend strongly on how the screening of the attraction is treated [27]. Quantum Monte Carlo calculations [28, 29] and experiments on semiconductor and atomic double layers [4, 5, 6, 7, 8] provide further motivation.

In the zero-field part of this paper we carry the program of Ref. [20] over to the bilayer. The plasmon of the single layer is replaced by the two plasmons of the double layer, superconductivity by interlayer superfluidity, and the ratio of the plasmon energy to the Fermi energy by a ratio involving the binding energy EBE_{B} of the interlayer exciton. We ask three questions. What does the dynamically screened interaction look like, and where is it attractive? What transition temperature does it give when the equations are solved without ad hoc cutoffs? In which limits, if any, is the result controlled? The bilayer allows the third question to be answered. At large separation the plasmon energy that matters for interlayer pairing becomes small compared with the Fermi energy, so one can test whether that is what a theorem of the Migdal type requires.

High field. The purpose of the high-field part of this paper is to set out in closed form, and in one place, what HF theory does and does not establish about the separation dependence of interlayer coherence in the problem projected onto the lowest Landau level (LLL). Most of the ingredients are known: the collective mode and its finite-wave-vector softening [13, 14, 30], the interlayer exchange integral and the stiffness [15, 31], the closed form of that integral in the closely related graphene double-layer problem [32], and the density-wave states of unrestricted HF [33, 34, 35]. What we add is the explicit HF amplitude scale TcHF​(d)T_{c}^{\rm HF}(d) and a clear statement of the logical content of these results. The result is simple but consequential. The interlayer exchange field is positive at every finite d/ℓd/\ell, where ℓ\ell is the magnetic length, and hence the T=0T=0 HF state is coherent at every finite d/ℓd/\ell. The HF coherence scale has a 1/d1/d tail. There is no zero-temperature critical separation in the projected LLL HF theory.

There is a separate finite-wave-vector instability. The uniform coherent state develops a roton minimum which collapses at d/ℓ≃1.175d/\ell\simeq 1.175 in the zero-width model. This instability has been widely identified, on heuristic grounds, with the disappearance of the (111)(111) state and the loss of interlayer coherence at d/ℓ∼1d/\ell\sim 1 [14, 31]. Within HF theory this identification is incorrect: the softening by itself does not imply a loss of coherence. A finite-qq roton collapse destabilizes spatial uniformity. It does not set the interlayer exchange field to zero. The ensuing HF phase has coexisting interlayer coherence and layer-density modulation [34, 31]. It is an excitonic supersolid.

Our main results are the following.

(i) Within the random-phase approximation (RPA) the screened interlayer interaction W12​(q,i​ν)W_{12}(q,i\nu) is attractive at every qq and every Matsubara frequency ν\nu, and its magnitude increases monotonically with |ν||\nu| from the statically screened value at ν=0\nu=0, approaching the magnitude of the bare, unscreened interaction as |ν|→∞|\nu|\to\infty. On the real axis it is repulsive in the region between the acoustic and the optical plasmon (Sec. IV).

(ii) Within the ladder approximation, the leading gap function is nodeless in momentum and Matsubara frequency. The linearized gap equation is ultraviolet convergent and can be solved without an imposed cutoff. The bare interaction transfers only wave vectors q≲1/dq\lesssim 1/d, which confines pairing to within ℏ​vF/d\hbar v_{F}/d of the Fermi surface and supplies an intrinsic cutoff (Secs. V and VII).

(iii) For d≫aBd\gg a_{B} the pairing in the ladder approximation is dominated by a wedge-shaped region of frequency and momentum, in which ν\nu exceeds the plasmon frequency ω+​(q)\omega_{+}(q) at the transferred wave vector and the interaction is therefore unscreened. In this region ν≫vF​q\nu\gg v_{F}q. Virtual transitions through this region give a plasmon-induced coupling λpl\lambda_{\rm pl} that we obtain in closed form. It decays only as d−1/2d^{-1/2}, whereas the static coupling decays as d−2d^{-2} (Sec. VI). The numerical solution confirms the analytic theory (Sec. VII).

(iv) The plasmon-induced coupling does not survive the leading vertex correction. In the wedge the carriers are slow compared with the plasmons, the opposite of Migdal’s limit, and the crossed rung, which is of the same order in the screened interaction as λpl\lambda_{\rm pl}, cancels it. We evaluate the crossed rung with the full dynamically screened interaction. The sum λnet\lambda_{\rm net} of the plasmon-induced and crossed terms is a small fraction of λpl\lambda_{\rm pl} at every separation examined. We obtain its limiting forms exactly, C3​(d)​rs3C_{3}(d)\,r_{s}^{3} for rs→0r_{s}\to 0 at fixed dd and Jw​g​rs4​(aB/d)7/2J_{w}\sqrt{g}\,r_{s}^{4}(a_{B}/d)^{7/2} for d→∞d\to\infty at fixed rsr_{s}, and the numerical results reproduce both (Appendix F). The cancellation is exact at every order for carriers with linearized dispersion coupled to Gaussian density fluctuations, static carriers being the adiabatic limit; the remainder is an effect of the curvature of the Fermi surface, which we compute at second order (Sec. VIII).

(v) The theory is controlled in two limits. For rs→0r_{s}\to 0 at fixed dd the leading exponent of TcT_{c} is −1/λs-1/\lambda_{s}; this is leading-order perturbation theory in the statically screened interaction. For large dd at any rsr_{s} in the liquid phase we argue that it is −(m∗/m)/λs-(m^{*}/m)/\lambda_{s}; this rests on the cancellation just described, which is established at second order and in the linearized limit, and on Fermi-liquid theory. In both limits the answer is that of static screening, not that of the dynamically screened ladder, which at large dd overestimates TcT_{c} by a factor that grows as exp⁡(const×d2)\exp({\rm const}\times d^{2}) (Sec. IX).

(vi) At νT=1\nu_{T}=1 the uniform HF theory of the LLL is analytic at every d/ℓd/\ell. The interlayer exchange field XDX_{D} is positive at every finite separation, so the uniform HF saddle at T=0T=0 is interlayer coherent at every finite separation. The quasiparticle splitting is ΔHF=XD\Delta_{\rm HF}=X_{D}, the mean-field amplitude scale is kB​TcHF=XD/4k_{B}T_{c}^{\rm HF}=X_{D}/4, and XD→e2/ϵ​dX_{D}\to e^{2}/\epsilon d at large dd. The velocity of the collective mode and the phase stiffness follow in closed form from the same integral, and the dispersion of the mode from its Bessel transform (Sec. XI).

(vii) The softening of the collective mode at d/ℓ≃1.175d/\ell\simeq 1.175 is an instability of the uniform state toward a coherent density wave, which within HF is an excitonic supersolid. It is not a loss of interlayer coherence, and the common identification of the two is not supported by the HF theory on which it rests (Secs. XI.4 and XI.5).

(viii) The two problems have the same mean-field structure and the same 1/d1/d tail. At zero field the tail is replaced by a Gaussian decay in the two controlled limits, conditionally for d→∞d\to\infty, once the response of the layers is included. This is a precedent for one element of our expectation at νT=1\nu_{T}=1, the failure of the HF tail. The other element, a crossover from strong to weak coupling with no transition, is not derived in either problem. The expectation is stated as a conjecture, and the zero-field result is not evidence for it (Sec. XII).

Scope. The paper is a theory of mean-field coherence and of the weak-pairing side of the problem, in both settings. It is not a review of the experiments, of the quantum Monte Carlo and exact-diagonalization work, or of other filling factors, and the strongly paired regime at zero field enters only through the discussion of the crossovers in Appendix E. We distinguish throughout between statements of different kinds: a theorem within a stated approximation, an exact identity, a result in a controlled limit, a result that is conditional on a stated assumption, the output of an approximation with no estimate of its error, and a conjecture. Table 6 in Sec. XII assigns each of the main results to one of them.

Organization. Section II sets out what the two problems have in common and fixes the notation. Sections III–X contain the zero-field theory: the model, the screened interaction, the ladder theory and its analytic and numerical solution, the vertex corrections, and the controlled limits. Section XI contains the theory at νT=1\nu_{T}=1. Section XII compares the two, and Sec. XIII concludes. Appendices A–D contain the polarization function of a layer, the exciton binding energy, the solution of the unscreened gap equation, and the numerical details of the zero-field theory. Appendix E gives the complete set of pairing-channel diagrams through second order in the bare and in the screened interaction, states which of them our results contain, derives the two controlled limits diagram by diagram, and discusses the two crossovers to Bose condensation of excitons and the relation to the renormalization group. Appendix F contains the asymptotic evaluation of λnet\lambda_{\rm net}. Appendices G–M contain the response functions, the finite-temperature theory, the quantitative scales, and the derivations for νT=1\nu_{T}=1.

II One problem in two settings

II.1 Hamiltonian and symmetry

Both systems consist of two parallel two-dimensional layers a distance dd apart, with a background dielectric constant ϵ\epsilon, Coulomb interactions, and no tunneling between the layers. Carriers in the same layer interact through Vq=2​π​e2/ϵ​qV_{q}=2\pi e^{2}/\epsilon q, and carriers in different layers through an interaction of magnitude Uq=Vq​e−q​dU_{q}=V_{q}e^{-qd}. Without tunneling the number of carriers is conserved in each layer separately, and the Hamiltonian is invariant under independent changes of phase in the two layers. The exciton condensate, in which an electron of one layer is coherent with a hole of the other, breaks the relative U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry and leaves the total one intact. This is the order of both problems. At zero field it appears as the pair amplitude of an electron and a hole, the gap function of Sec. V. At νT=1\nu_{T}=1 it appears as the interlayer coherence ⟨cm​T†​cm​B⟩\langle c^{\dagger}_{mT}c_{mB}\rangle of Sec. XI between the two layers, labeled TT and BB, at guiding center mm; this is the in-plane component of the layer pseudospin.

At zero field the layers contain electrons and holes with kinetic energy ℏ2​k2/2​m\hbar^{2}k^{2}/2m, and the interlayer interaction is attractive [Eq. (2)]. At νT=1\nu_{T}=1 both layers contain electrons, each layer has a half-filled lowest Landau level, and the interlayer interaction is repulsive [Eq. (46)]. A particle-hole transformation of one layer within the lowest Landau level turns the electrons of that layer at filling 1/21/2 into holes at filling 1/21/2 and reverses the sign of the interlayer interaction, apart from one-body terms [9]. In these variables the νT=1\nu_{T}=1 bilayer is a balanced electron-hole bilayer with an attractive interlayer interaction and no kinetic energy, and the Halperin (111)(111) state [36] is its exciton condensate. This is the sense in which the two problems are one.

II.2 Parameters

At zero field the model has two dimensionless parameters, the density parameter rsr_{s} and the separation d/aBd/a_{B}, where aBa_{B} is the Bohr radius (Sec. III); the combinations that appear most often are kF​dk_{F}d and the ratio EB/EFE_{B}/E_{F} of the exciton binding energy to the Fermi energy. At νT=1\nu_{T}=1, in the lowest Landau level and for layers of zero thickness, the only parameter is d/ℓd/\ell. The two sets are related. A spin-polarized layer at filling 1/21/2 has the density n=1/4​π​ℓ2n=1/4\pi\ell^{2}, and a spin-polarized Fermi gas of that density at zero field would have kF=(4​π​n)1/2=1/ℓk_{F}=(4\pi n)^{1/2}=1/\ell. In the notation of Sec. III with g=1g=1,

dℓ=kF​d,rs=2​ℓaB=2​κLL,κLL≡e2/ϵ​ℓℏ​ωc=ℓaB,\frac{d}{\ell}=k_{F}d,\quad r_{s}=\frac{2\ell}{a_{B}}=2\kappa_{\rm LL},\quad\kappa_{\rm LL}\equiv\frac{e^{2}/\epsilon\ell}{\hbar\omega_{c}}=\frac{\ell}{a_{B}}, (1)

where ωc\omega_{c} is the cyclotron frequency and κLL\kappa_{\rm LL} is the parameter of Landau-level mixing. The separation in units of the magnetic length is thus the same quantity as kF​dk_{F}d at zero field: the layer separation measured against the distance between the carriers.

Projection onto the lowest Landau level is the limit κLL→0\kappa_{\rm LL}\to 0, that is, rs→0r_{s}\to 0 at fixed kF​dk_{F}d. At zero field this is a limit of weak coupling, in which the interaction energy is small compared with the kinetic energy. In a strong field it is not, because the kinetic energy has been removed from the problem altogether and the Coulomb energy e2/ϵ​ℓe^{2}/\epsilon\ell is the only scale. This is the essential difference between the two problems. It is the reason the zero-field theory has controlled limits (Sec. IX), while at νT=1\nu_{T}=1 the only exact statement is the one at d=0d=0.

II.3 Mean-field theory and the diagrams

In both problems the mean-field theory is the HF approximation with the bare Coulomb interaction, and in both the term that produces the coherence is the same diagram: the exchange self-energy with one interlayer interaction line. It is Fig. 5(a), with the screened line replaced by the bare one, at zero field, and Fig. 14(b) at νT=1\nu_{T}=1. What differs is the set of states on which it acts. At zero field the carriers have a Fermi surface. The exchange self-energy is then anomalous, it satisfies a gap equation whose kernel contains the Cooper logarithm, multiplied for the unscreened interaction by the logarithm of the interaction itself, and the resulting scale is exponentially small, exp(−const/α)\exp(-{\rm const}/\sqrt{\alpha}) [Eq. (21)]. In the lowest Landau level all single-particle states are degenerate. There is no logarithm, the self-consistency condition is algebraic, and the gap is the exchange integral itself [Eq. (54)].

The corrections to mean-field theory are organized in the same way in the two problems. At zero field the particle-hole bubbles of each layer screen the interaction; their sum to all orders is the RPA of Sec. IV. The leading vertex correction is the crossed rung of Sec. VIII, and the complete set of diagrams through second order is given in Appendix E. At νT=1\nu_{T}=1 the bubble within the filled pseudospin band vanishes, and the corrections come from particle-hole pairs between the filled and the empty pseudospin band [Figs. 14(c) and 14(d)]. Their ladder sum is the time-dependent HF (TDHF) theory of the collective mode (Sec. XI.4), and their contribution to the self-energy is what uniform HF theory leaves out.

II.4 The common questions

Four questions are asked of both problems. (1) Does mean-field theory give interlayer coherence at every separation? (2) How does the scale of the coherence depend on dd at large separation, and does the mean-field answer survive the corrections? (3) Is the evolution from small to large dd a phase transition or a crossover from strong to weak coupling? (4) What is the relation of the coherent state to the states of broken translation symmetry? These questions distinguish the existence of a coherent solution from its energy scale and stability. In particular, an instability of the uniform state need not imply a loss of interlayer coherence. Table 1 lists the correspondence between the two problems and the answers obtained in Secs. III–XI; they are compared in Sec. XII.

II.5 Conventions

At zero field TcT_{c} denotes the mean-field temperature at which the pairing instability occurs. In two dimensions the transition is of Kosterlitz-Thouless type [37], with a transition temperature that approaches the mean-field one in the weak-coupling regime of interest there. At νT=1\nu_{T}=1 the corresponding mean-field quantity is written TcHFT_{c}^{\rm HF}. It is an amplitude scale, and it is far above the temperature of the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition (Appendix H). The two are therefore kept apart in the notation.

Each part uses its natural units, aBa_{B} and EFE_{F} or Ry{\rm Ry} at zero field and ℓ\ell and EC=e2/ϵ​ℓE_{\rm C}=e^{2}/\epsilon\ell at νT=1\nu_{T}=1. Several symbols need care. ECE_{\rm C} is the Coulomb unit of the high-field problem, while Ec=ℏ2/m​d2E_{c}=\hbar^{2}/md^{2} is the curvature energy of the zero-field problem. The letter ν\nu without a subscript is a Matsubara frequency in the zero-field sections; in Sec. XI and its appendices it is a filling factor, in νT\nu_{T} and in the ν=1\nu=1 ferromagnet of a single layer. Δ\Delta, also written ΔHF\Delta_{\rm HF}, is the HF quasiparticle splitting at νT=1\nu_{T}=1; at zero field Δ⁡(ξ)\Delta(\xi) is the gap function and 𝚫\bm{\Delta} in Sec. VIII is a momentum transfer. PP is the pseudospin polarization in Sec. XI and the dimensionless polarization function of a layer in the zero-field sections. The zero-field theory is written for spin degeneracy gg, with numerical results for g=2g=2, whereas the νT=1\nu_{T}=1 bilayer is spin polarized. The layers are labeled 1 and 2 at zero field and TT and BB at νT=1\nu_{T}=1. The cyclotron frequency ωc\omega_{c} appears only in Eq. (1); elsewhere ωc\omega_{c} is a frequency cutoff. The quantities δ=d/ℓ\delta=d/\ell and Q=q​ℓQ=q\ell, the function F⁡(δ)F(\delta), and the kernels of Sec. XI.4 are defined in Sec. XI and have these meanings only there and in Appendices G–M.

III Zero magnetic field: model and scales

We consider electrons of mass mm and density nn in layer 1 and holes of the same mass and density in layer 2, separated by a distance dd, with a background dielectric constant ϵ\epsilon and no interlayer tunneling,

H=\displaystyle H={} ∑l​𝐤​σξ𝐤​ψl​𝐤​σ†​ψl​𝐤​σ+12​A​∑l,𝐪Vq:ρl​(𝐪)​ρl​(−𝐪):\displaystyle\sum_{l\mathbf{k}\sigma}\xi_{\mathbf{k}}\,\psi^{\dagger}_{l\mathbf{k}\sigma}\psi_{l\mathbf{k}\sigma}+\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{l,\mathbf{q}}V_{q}:\!\rho_{l}(\mathbf{q})\rho_{l}(-\mathbf{q})\!:
−1A∑𝐪Uqρ1(𝐪)ρ2(−𝐪),\displaystyle-\frac{1}{A}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}U_{q}\,\rho_{1}(\mathbf{q})\rho_{2}(-\mathbf{q}), (2)

with ψl=1​𝐤​σ\psi_{l=1\mathbf{k}\sigma} (ψl=2​𝐤​σ\psi_{l=2\mathbf{k}\sigma}) being the annihilation operator of the electron in layer 1 (hole in layer 2) carrying momentum 𝐤\mathbf{k} and spin σ\sigma, ξ𝐤=ℏ2​k2/2​m−EF\xi_{\mathbf{k}}=\hbar^{2}k^{2}/2m-E_{F}, ρl​(𝐪)=∑𝐤​σψl​𝐤​σ†​ψl​𝐤+𝐪​σ\rho_{l}(\mathbf{q})=\sum_{\mathbf{k}\sigma}\psi^{\dagger}_{l\mathbf{k}\sigma}\psi_{l\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}\sigma}, and

Vq=2​π​e2ϵ​q,Uq=Vq​e−q​d.V_{q}=\frac{2\pi e^{2}}{\epsilon q},\qquad U_{q}=V_{q}\,e^{-qd}. (3)

Each layer has spin degeneracy gg. All formulas are given for general gg; numerical results are for g=2g=2, and the spinless model of Ref. [12] is recovered by setting g=1g=1. The interlayer attraction is independent of spin, so pairing of an electron with a hole of either spin is degenerate and we consider one spin pair.

The model has two dimensionless parameters, rsr_{s} and d/aBd/a_{B}, with aB=ϵ​ℏ2/m​e2a_{B}=\epsilon\hbar^{2}/me^{2} and π​rs2​aB2​n=1\pi r_{s}^{2}a_{B}^{2}n=1. Table 2 collects the derived quantities. The total density of states of a layer is N0=g​m/2​π​ℏ2N_{0}=gm/2\pi\hbar^{2}, and that of one spin species, which enters the pairing problem, is N0/gN_{0}/g. We use

N0​Vq=c​kFq,c=g​α,α=e2ϵ​ℏ​vF=g​rs2,N_{0}V_{q}=\frac{c\,k_{F}}{q},\qquad c=g\alpha,\qquad\alpha=\frac{e^{2}}{\epsilon\hbar v_{F}}=\frac{\sqrt{g}\,r_{s}}{2}, (4)

so that α\alpha is the fine-structure constant of the layer.

III.1 The interlayer exciton

An isolated electron-hole pair is bound at every dd. The binding energy EBE_{B} follows from the relative-motion problem with reduced mass m/2m/2 and potential −e2/ϵr2+d2-e^{2}/\epsilon\sqrt{r^{2}+d^{2}}, which we solve numerically (Appendix B). The result, Fig. 1(a), interpolates between EB=2​RyE_{B}=2\,{\rm Ry} at d=0d=0 and

EB≃e2ϵ​d​[1−2​aB/d](d≫aB),E_{B}\simeq\frac{e^{2}}{\epsilon d}\Bigl[1-\sqrt{2a_{B}/d}\,\Bigr]\qquad(d\gg a_{B}), (5)

where the correction is the zero-point energy of the in-plane oscillation. The approach to Ed=e2/ϵ​dE_{d}=e^{2}/\epsilon d is slow: EB/Ed=0.33E_{B}/E_{d}=0.33, 0.570.57, and 0.740.74 at d/aB=1d/a_{B}=1, 55, and 2020.

The ratio EB/EFE_{B}/E_{F} separates the regime of tightly bound excitons from that of weakly paired Fermi liquids [38, 39]. The zero-field theory of this paper concerns the second regime, EB≲EFE_{B}\lesssim E_{F}, where the Fermi surfaces exist and the pairing is of the BCS type. The linearized gap equation at fixed chemical potential is not valid on the other side, where the chemical potential is pulled below the band edge. Figure 1(b) shows the regimes in the (rs,d/aB)(r_{s},d/a_{B}) plane together with three other lines that will emerge below: kF​d=1k_{F}d=1, ℏ​Ω∗=EF\hbar\Omega_{*}=E_{F}, and the line on which the static and the plasmon-induced couplings are equal.

IV Zero magnetic field: Dynamically screened interlayer interaction

IV.1 Random-phase approximation

In the RPA the screened interaction is the 2×22\times 2 matrix W^=[1−V^​Π]−1​V^\hat{W}=[1-\hat{V}\Pi]^{-1}\hat{V} in the layer index, with V^11=V^22=Vq\hat{V}_{11}=\hat{V}_{22}=V_{q}, V^12=−Uq\hat{V}_{12}=-U_{q}, and Π⁡(q,ω)\Pi(q,\omega) the noninteracting polarization of one layer [40], given in Appendix A. The matrix is diagonal in the channels in which the two number densities oscillate out of phase and in phase. Because the carriers have opposite charge, the first is a charge oscillation with interaction Vq+UqV_{q}+U_{q} and the second is charge neutral with interaction Vq−UqV_{q}-U_{q}. With

ε±​(q,ω)=1−(Vq±Uq)​Π​(q,ω),\varepsilon_{\pm}(q,\omega)=1-(V_{q}\pm U_{q})\Pi(q,\omega), (6)

the intralayer and interlayer interactions are

W11\displaystyle W_{11} =12​[Vq+Uqε++Vq−Uqε−],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{V_{q}+U_{q}}{\varepsilon_{+}}+\frac{V_{q}-U_{q}}{\varepsilon_{-}}\right], (7)
W12\displaystyle W_{12} =12​[Vq−Uqε−−Vq+Uqε+]=−Uqε+​ε−.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{V_{q}-U_{q}}{\varepsilon_{-}}-\frac{V_{q}+U_{q}}{\varepsilon_{+}}\right]=-\frac{U_{q}}{\varepsilon_{+}\varepsilon_{-}}. (8)

A negative W12W_{12} is attractive.

IV.2 Collective modes

The zeros of ε±\varepsilon_{\pm} give the two plasmons of the double layer [41, 42]. With the high-frequency form of the polarization, valid for ω≫vF​q\omega\gg v_{F}q,

ω±2​(q)=2​π​n​e2ϵ​m​q​(1±e−q​d),\omega_{\pm}^{2}(q)=\frac{2\pi ne^{2}}{\epsilon m}\,q\,\bigl(1\pm e^{-qd}\bigr), (9)

so that the charge mode is optical, ω+∝q\omega_{+}\propto\sqrt{q}, and the neutral mode is acoustic. For the optical mode the condition ω≫vF​q\omega\gg v_{F}q holds at long wavelength for any dd. For the acoustic mode it requires 𝒢≫1\mathcal{G}\gg 1, and Eq. (9) then gives v−≃vF​𝒢/2v_{-}\simeq v_{F}\sqrt{\mathcal{G}/2}. At arbitrary separation the RPA velocity of the acoustic mode is

v−vF=1+𝒢1+2​𝒢,𝒢=g​daB,\frac{v_{-}}{v_{F}}=\frac{1+\mathcal{G}}{\sqrt{1+2\mathcal{G}}},\qquad\mathcal{G}=\frac{g\,d}{a_{B}}, (10)

which exceeds vFv_{F} for every dd, so the mode is undamped at long wavelength. Figure 2 shows the dispersions.

The plasmon energy at the wave vector q=1/dq=1/d that characterizes the interlayer interaction will play a central role. We define it from Eq. (9) at q=1/dq=1/d with the factor 1+e−q​d1+e^{-qd} replaced by its long-wavelength value 2,

ℏ​Ω∗≡(4​π​n​e2​ℏ2ϵ​m​d)1/2=2​g​EF​Ed.\hbar\Omega_{*}\equiv\Bigl(\frac{4\pi ne^{2}\hbar^{2}}{\epsilon md}\Bigr)^{1/2}=\sqrt{2g\,E_{F}E_{d}}. (11)

For g=2g=2 this is 2​EF​Ed2\sqrt{E_{F}E_{d}}. It is a characteristic scale, not a cutoff: ω+​(q)\omega_{+}(q) vanishes as q→0q\to 0, and the relevant comparison at each wave vector is with the local frequency ω+​(q)\omega_{+}(q). The plasmon energy relevant to interlayer pairing is thus proportional to the geometric mean of the Fermi energy and EdE_{d}, the exciton binding energy at large separation. This is the sense in which EB/EFE_{B}/E_{F} replaces the ratio ℏ​ωp/EF\hbar\omega_{p}/E_{F} of the single-layer problem.

IV.3 Real frequencies

Figure 3 shows the real and imaginary parts of W12​(q,ω+i​0)W_{12}(q,\omega+i0). The structure follows from Eq. (8). Outside the particle-hole continuum ε±\varepsilon_{\pm} are real. Above both plasmons they are positive and the interaction is attractive, tending to −Uq-U_{q}. Between the plasmons ε+<0<ε−\varepsilon_{+}<0<\varepsilon_{-} and the interaction is repulsive. Between the acoustic plasmon and the continuum both are negative and it is attractive again. At ω=0\omega=0 it is attractive at every qq. The repulsive band continues into the continuum, where the imaginary part is of the same size as the real part. The imaginary part has both signs: the charge mode contributes Im​W12>0{\rm Im}\,W_{12}>0 and the neutral mode Im​W12<0{\rm Im}\,W_{12}<0.

The fraction of the (q,ω)(q,\omega) plane in which the interaction is repulsive grows with rsr_{s} as the optical plasmon moves up. In the low-energy window q<2​kFq<2k_{F}, ℏ​ω<EF\hbar\omega<E_{F} it is between 6% and 16% for 0.5≤rs≤100.5\leq r_{s}\leq 10 and 0.25≤d/aB≤50.25\leq d/a_{B}\leq 5, and it decreases with dd. This is the counterpart of Fig. 1 and Fig. 5 of Ref. [20], where the bare interaction is repulsive and the plasmon produces an attractive region.

IV.4 Imaginary frequencies

The pairing problem at TcT_{c} involves the interaction at Matsubara frequencies. There the polarization is real and negative, Π⁡(q,i​ν)=−N0​P​(q,ν)\Pi(q,i\nu)=-N_{0}P(q,\nu) with 0<P≤10<P\leq 1 decreasing in |ν||\nu| (Appendix A), so that ε±​(q,i​ν)=1+(Vq±Uq)​N0​P≥1\varepsilon_{\pm}(q,i\nu)=1+(V_{q}\pm U_{q})N_{0}P\geq 1 and

−Uq≤W12​(q,i​ν)=−Uqε+​(q,i​ν)​ε−​(q,i​ν)<0.-U_{q}\leq W_{12}(q,i\nu)=-\frac{U_{q}}{\varepsilon_{+}(q,i\nu)\,\varepsilon_{-}(q,i\nu)}<0. (12)

Within the RPA the interlayer interaction on the imaginary axis is attractive at every wave vector and frequency, and its magnitude increases monotonically with |ν||\nu| from the statically screened value to the bare value. Screening cannot turn the attraction into a repulsion. The repulsive region on the real axis and Eq. (12) are reconciled by the spectral representation

W12​(q,i​ν)=−Uq+2π​∫0∞d​ω​ω​Im​W12​(q,ω)ω2+ν2,W_{12}(q,i\nu)=-U_{q}+\frac{2}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\infty}d\omega\,\frac{\omega\,{\rm Im}\,W_{12}(q,\omega)}{\omega^{2}+\nu^{2}}, (13)

in which the positive spectral weight of the charge mode screens and the negative weight of the neutral mode antiscreens, the net being a reduction of the attraction.

Two limits of Eq. (12) organize everything that follows. For ν≪vF​q\nu\ll v_{F}q the screening is static. For ν≫vF​q\nu\gg v_{F}q the polarization takes its high-frequency form N0​P=n​q2/m​ν2N_{0}P=nq^{2}/m\nu^{2}, which is fixed by the ff-sum rule, and

W12​(q,i​ν)≃−Uq​ν4[ν2+ω+2​(q)]​[ν2+ω−2​(q)](ν≫vF​q).W_{12}(q,i\nu)\simeq\frac{-U_{q}\,\nu^{4}}{[\nu^{2}+\omega_{+}^{2}(q)][\nu^{2}+\omega_{-}^{2}(q)]}\quad(\nu\gg v_{F}q). (14)

The interaction is unscreened for ν\nu above the plasmon frequencies. Since ω+∝q\omega_{+}\propto\sqrt{q} vanishes at long wavelength, at any nonzero ν\nu there is a range of small qq in which the full 1/q1/q attraction survives. Figure 4 illustrates this.

Interpolating between the two limits gives a two-pole plasmon-pole approximation, the bilayer version of the one used in Ref. [20]: in each channel 1/ε±​(q,i​ν)=1−Ω±2/(ν2+ω~±2)1/\varepsilon_{\pm}(q,i\nu)=1-\Omega_{\pm}^{2}/(\nu^{2}+\tilde{\omega}_{\pm}^{2}), with Ω±2=(Vq±Uq)​n​q2/m\Omega_{\pm}^{2}=(V_{q}\pm U_{q})nq^{2}/m fixed by the ff-sum rule and ω~±2=Ω±2/[1−1/ε±​(q,0)]\tilde{\omega}_{\pm}^{2}=\Omega_{\pm}^{2}/[1-1/\varepsilon_{\pm}(q,0)] by the static limit. It is exact in both limits and is compared with the RPA in Fig. 4(b).

V Zero magnetic field: Pairing theory

V.1 Linearized gap equation

With the anomalous Green function ℱ⁡(𝐩,i​ω)=−⟨ψ1,−𝐩​ψ2,𝐩⟩\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{p},i\omega)=-\langle\psi_{1,-\mathbf{p}}\psi_{2,\mathbf{p}}\rangle and the anomalous self-energy ϕ\phi, the linearized equation that determines TcT_{c} is [Fig. 5(a)]

ϕ(𝐤,iωn)=−T∑m∫d2​p(2​π)2\displaystyle\phi(\mathbf{k},i\omega_{n})=-T\sum_{m}\!\int\!\!\frac{d^{2}p}{(2\pi)^{2}}\, W12​(𝐤−𝐩,i​ωn−i​ωm)\displaystyle W_{12}(\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{p},i\omega_{n}-i\omega_{m})
×ϕ⁡(𝐩,i​ωm)ωm2+ξp2.\displaystyle\times\frac{\phi(\mathbf{p},i\omega_{m})}{\omega_{m}^{2}+\xi_{p}^{2}}. (15)

For ss-wave pairing only the angular average of the interaction enters,

K⁡(k,p,ν)=N0​∫02​πd​θ2​π​W12​(|𝐤−𝐩|,i​ν),K(k,p;\nu)=N_{0}\!\int_{0}^{2\pi}\!\frac{d\theta}{2\pi}\,W_{12}\bigl(|\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{p}|,i\nu\bigr), (16)

and with energies in units of EFE_{F} Eq. (15) becomes

ϕ(k,ωn)=−Tg∑m∫dξpK⁡(k,p,ωn−ωm)ωm2+ξp2ϕ(p,ωm).\phi(k,\omega_{n})=-\frac{T}{g}\sum_{m}\int d\xi_{p}\,\frac{K(k,p;\omega_{n}-\omega_{m})}{\omega_{m}^{2}+\xi_{p}^{2}}\,\phi(p,\omega_{m}). (17)

The factor 1/g1/g appears because the pairing equation involves the density of states per spin, N0/gN_{0}/g, whereas N0=g​m/(2​π​ℏ2)N_{0}=gm/(2\pi\hbar^{2}) includes the spin degeneracy gg. TcT_{c} is the temperature at which the largest eigenvalue η⁡(T)\eta(T) of the kernel reaches unity. We consider three versions: the unscreened interaction, W12→−UqW_{12}\to-U_{q}, which is the linearized HF theory without the normal exchange self-energy that Ref. [11] includes (Appendix E); the statically screened interaction W12​(q,0)W_{12}(q,0); and the dynamically screened interaction W12​(q,i​ν)W_{12}(q,i\nu). In the first two the gap is independent of frequency and the Matsubara sum gives tanh⁡(ξp/2​T)/2​ξp\tanh(\xi_{p}/2T)/2\xi_{p}.

By Eq. (12), −K>0-K>0 for all arguments. The kernel of Eq. (17) is therefore positive, the eigenfunction is nodeless, and η⁡(T)\eta(T) increases without bound as T→0T\to 0 because of the logarithm at the Fermi surface, indicating a pairing instability for arbitrarily weak attraction. Within the RPA there is a pairing instability at every rsr_{s} and dd, in agreement with Ref. [12]. This is the essential difference from the single layer, where the kernel is repulsive and the instability depends on a delicate balance and on a cutoff [20].

V.2 Normal self-energy and vertex

Equation (15) contains bare propagators and bare vertices. Eliashberg theory as usually applied, and as applied to this problem in Ref. [12], dresses the propagators with the normal self-energy Σ=−𝒢​W11\Sigma=-\mathcal{G}\,W_{11} (where 𝒢\mathcal{G} denotes the dressed normal-state one-particle Green function), in particular with the factor Z=1−∂Σ/∂(i​ω)Z=1-\partial\Sigma/\partial(i\omega) (the Eliashberg renormalization factor, with quasiparticle weight Z−1Z^{-1}), and keeps the vertices bare. For phonons this is justified by Migdal’s theorem. Here it is not, and the self-energy and the vertex are tied together by the Ward identity for the density vertex Λ\Lambda [43]. At q=0q=0 and frequency transfer ν\nu the identity is

Λ⁡(𝐩,i​ω+i​ν,i​ω)=1−Σ⁡(𝐩,i​ω+i​ν)−Σ⁡(𝐩,i​ω)i​ν,\Lambda(\mathbf{p};i\omega+i\nu,i\omega)=1-\frac{\Sigma(\mathbf{p},i\omega+i\nu)-\Sigma(\mathbf{p},i\omega)}{i\nu}, (18)

which is equivalent to 𝒢⁡(i​ω+i​ν)​Λ​𝒢​(i​ω)=[𝒢⁡(i​ω)−𝒢⁡(i​ω+i​ν)]/i​ν\mathcal{G}(i\omega+i\nu)\,\Lambda\,\mathcal{G}(i\omega)=[\mathcal{G}(i\omega)-\mathcal{G}(i\omega+i\nu)]/i\nu, the relation that the bare propagators satisfy with Λ=1\Lambda=1. When the self-energy is linear in frequency over the interval, the right-hand side of Eq. (18) is 1−∂Σ/∂(i​ω)=Z1-\partial\Sigma/\partial(i\omega)=Z, and a propagator near the Fermi surface is 𝒢=Z−1/(i​ω−ξp∗)\mathcal{G}=Z^{-1}/(i\omega-\xi^{*}_{p}). In the process of Fig. 5(b) each of the two lines then contributes two vertices and the propagator of the virtual state between them, Z×Z−1×ZZ\times Z^{-1}\times Z, to the effective interaction between low-energy pairs, and the pair propagator that follows carries Z−2Z^{-2}. The quasiparticle weights cancel, and the only renormalization that remains is that of the density of states of the low-energy pair. The self-energy and vertex corrections must therefore be treated consistently with the Ward identity. Retaining ZZ while leaving the density vertex bare (Λ=1\Lambda=1) instead produces a factor Z−4Z^{-4} in this limit.

The cancellation with vertex corrections and the Z−4Z^{-4} factor without them are both estimates based on counting powers of ZZ. Both assume a self-energy that is linear in frequency over the full range of virtual states and independent of momentum. The first condition requires ℏ​Ω∗≪EF\hbar\Omega_{*}\ll E_{F} and therefore large dd. In the opposite limit, virtual states at frequencies so high that the propagator and the vertex have both returned to their bare values, omitting Λ\Lambda makes no error, and the factor Z−2Z^{-2} of the low-energy pair propagator is then a genuine reduction of the coupling and not an artifact. Where a given rsr_{s} and dd lies between these limits depends on the frequency and momentum dependence of Σ\Sigma and of Λ\Lambda, which the identity at q=0q=0 does not determine and which we have not computed [44]. The estimates are therefore not bounds. At general rsr_{s} and dd the Ward identity therefore does not make the dressed ladder equal to the bare one, and we do not claim that it does.

We use bare propagators and bare vertices in Eq. (15) for a different reason: this is the complete theory at first order in the screened interaction (Appendix E). The self-energy and the vertex corrections enter together at the next order, and including one without the other is not an improvement. We call this the ladder approximation. It is the bilayer counterpart of the theory of Ref. [20]. The remaining term of second order in the interlayer interaction, the crossed rung of Fig. 5(c), is the subject of Sec. VIII.

V.3 Numerical method

Equation (17) is solved as an eigenvalue problem in the two variables ξp\xi_{p} and ωm\omega_{m}. The kernel K⁡(k,p,ν)K(k,p;\nu) has a logarithmic singularity at p=kp=k for ν≠0\nu\neq 0, a consequence of the unscreened 1/q1/q interaction at small qq, and the factor 1/(ωm2+ξp2)1/(\omega_{m}^{2}+\xi_{p}^{2}) varies on the scale of the temperature, so both variables must be resolved over many decades. The momentum variable is divided into cells that are geometric in |ξp||\xi_{p}| between 10−13​EF10^{-13}E_{F} and 63​EF63\,E_{F}. The kernel is averaged over each cell, which integrates its singularity, and 1/(ωm2+ξp2)1/(\omega_{m}^{2}+\xi_{p}^{2}) is integrated over each cell in closed form. The angular integral in Eq. (16) uses a substitution that resolves the forward direction. The Matsubara frequencies up to 105​EF10^{5}E_{F} are grouped into blocks of geometrically increasing size, with the kernel averaged over each block. The discretization errors are of second order in the logarithmic cell size and are removed by Richardson extrapolation in both variables. No momentum or frequency cutoff is imposed. Details and tests, including the reproduction of the BCS result for a model kernel to 0.2%0.2\%, are given in Appendix D.

VI Zero magnetic field: Analytic results at large separation

For kF​d≫1k_{F}d\gg 1 the bare interaction transfers only q≲1/d≪kFq\lesssim 1/d\ll k_{F}. Near the Fermi surface |𝐤−𝐩|2≃(ξk−ξp)2/ℏ2​vF2+kF2​θ2|\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{p}|^{2}\simeq(\xi_{k}-\xi_{p})^{2}/\hbar^{2}v_{F}^{2}+k_{F}^{2}\theta^{2}, the kernel depends only on ξk−ξp\xi_{k}-\xi_{p}, and three results follow.

VI.1 Unscreened interaction

For W12=−UqW_{12}=-U_{q} the angular average is a modified Bessel function,

−Kg=A​K0​(|ξk−ξp|​dℏ​vF),A=cπ​g=απ.-\frac{K}{g}=A\,K_{0}\!\Bigl(\frac{|\xi_{k}-\xi_{p}|\,d}{\hbar v_{F}}\Bigr),\qquad A=\frac{c}{\pi g}=\frac{\alpha}{\pi}. (19)

It is logarithmic for |ξk−ξp|≪ℏ​vF/d|\xi_{k}-\xi_{p}|\ll\hbar v_{F}/d and exponentially small beyond. The interaction cannot scatter a pair further than ℏ​vF/d\hbar v_{F}/d from the Fermi surface, which is the intrinsic cutoff of the problem. With K0​(z)≃ln⁡(2​e−γ/z)K_{0}(z)\simeq\ln(2e^{-\gamma}/z) the gap equation becomes

Δ⁡(ξ)=A​∫0Ωbd​ξ′ξ′​tanh⁡ξ′2​T​ln⁡Ωbmax⁡(ξ,ξ′)​Δ​(ξ′),\Delta(\xi)=A\!\int_{0}^{\Omega_{b}}\!\frac{d\xi^{\prime}}{\xi^{\prime}}\tanh\frac{\xi^{\prime}}{2T}\,\ln\frac{\Omega_{b}}{\max(\xi,\xi^{\prime})}\,\Delta(\xi^{\prime}), (20)

with Ωb=2​e−γ​ℏ​vF/d\Omega_{b}=2e^{-\gamma}\hbar v_{F}/d. The logarithm of the kernel multiplies the BCS logarithm, and the instability condition is A​ln⁡(Ωb/T)∼1\sqrt{A}\,\ln(\Omega_{b}/T)\sim 1 in place of λ​ln⁡(Ω/T)=1\lambda\ln(\Omega/T)=1. Equation (20) has the same form as the gap equation of color superconductivity with unscreened magnetic gluons [45]. It is solved in Appendix C, with the result

kB​Tc(0)=4π​κ0​ℏ​vFd​exp⁡[−π2​A],A=απ,k_{B}T_{c}^{(0)}=\frac{4}{\pi}\,\kappa_{0}\,\frac{\hbar v_{F}}{d}\,\exp\!\Bigl[-\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{A}}\Bigr],\qquad A=\frac{\alpha}{\pi}, (21)

where κ0→1\kappa_{0}\to 1 for α→0\alpha\to 0. The unscreened HF transition temperature thus decays only as 1/d1/d, and its dependence on the coupling is exp(−const/rs)\exp(-{\rm const}/\sqrt{r_{s}}). The numerical solution confirms the 1/d1/d law to one part in 10310^{3} for kF​dk_{F}d between 5 and 500 and gives κ0=1.26\kappa_{0}=1.26, 1.421.42, 1.701.70, 1.971.97, and 2.452.45 for rs=0.5r_{s}=0.5, 1, 2, 3, and 5.

VI.2 Static screening

For kF​d≫1k_{F}d\gg 1 the statically screened interaction depends on qq only through y=q​dy=qd, and its Fermi-surface average, the BCS coupling constant, is

λs\displaystyle\lambda_{s} ≡N0g​⟨|W12​(q,0)|⟩FS=𝒮⁡(𝒢)π​g​kF​d,\displaystyle\equiv\frac{N_{0}}{g}\bigl\langle|W_{12}(q,0)|\bigr\rangle_{\rm FS}=\frac{\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{G})}{\pi g\,k_{F}d}, (22)
𝒮⁡(𝒢)\displaystyle\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{G}) =∫0∞d​y​𝒢​y​e−y[y+𝒢⁡(1+e−y)]​[y+𝒢⁡(1−e−y)],\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\!dy\,\frac{\mathcal{G}\,y\,e^{-y}}{[y+\mathcal{G}(1+e^{-y})][y+\mathcal{G}(1-e^{-y})]},

where 𝒢=g​d/aB\mathcal{G}=gd/a_{B} is the capacitive parameter (not the Green function). The function 𝒮\mathcal{S} has a maximum of 0.250.25 at 𝒢≃0.8\mathcal{G}\simeq 0.8 and falls as π2/8​𝒢\pi^{2}/8\mathcal{G} for 𝒢≫1\mathcal{G}\gg 1, so that

λs≃π16​g3/2​rs​(aBd)2(d≫aB).\lambda_{s}\simeq\frac{\pi}{16\,g^{3/2}}\,r_{s}\Bigl(\frac{a_{B}}{d}\Bigr)^{2}\qquad(d\gg a_{B}). (23)

Both plasmon channels screen statically: the charge channel removes the long-range part and the neutral channel adds the factor aB/da_{B}/d. The transition temperature Tc(s)∝exp(−1/λs)T_{c}^{(s)}\propto\exp(-1/\lambda_{s}) is exponentially small in d2d^{2}. For g=2g=2 and rs=2r_{s}=2, Eq. (22) gives 1/λs=551/\lambda_{s}=55 at d=2​aBd=2a_{B} and 245245 at d=5​aBd=5a_{B}; the full Fermi-surface average of the static interaction, which is used in Table 4, gives 4949 and 234234.

VI.3 Dynamic screening: the plasmon-induced coupling

The dynamically screened kernel is shown in Fig. 6 as a function of the two variables on which it depends near the Fermi surface. It takes the small static value λs\lambda_{s} when ν≲|ξp|\nu\lesssim|\xi_{p}|, which is the region reached by on-shell scattering. In the wedge

|ξp|≲ℏ2​ν22​c​EF(ν<Ω∗),|ξp|≲ℏ​vFd(ν>Ω∗),|\xi_{p}|\lesssim\frac{\hbar^{2}\nu^{2}}{2c\,E_{F}}\quad(\nu<\Omega_{*}),\quad|\xi_{p}|\lesssim\frac{\hbar v_{F}}{d}\quad(\nu>\Omega_{*}), (24)

it is larger by orders of magnitude, because there Eq. (14) applies with ν>ω+​(q)\nu>\omega_{+}(q) and the interaction is unscreened. The first boundary is the condition ν=ω+​(q)\nu=\omega_{+}(q) at q=|ξp|/ℏ​vFq=|\xi_{p}|/\hbar v_{F}, and the second is the range of the bare interaction.

We use a two-step theory. First, we eliminate virtual states in the wedge to second order in the kernel to obtain an effective low-energy pairing coupling. We then solve the resulting BCS gap equation to determine TcT_{c}. States in the wedge are far off the energy shell, ν≫|ξp|\nu\gg|\xi_{p}|, and their pair propagator is 1/ν21/\nu^{2} with no logarithm. They contribute through the second-order process of Fig. 5(b): a pair at the Fermi surface is scattered into the wedge and back. Eliminating the wedge to second order in the kernel gives an effective coupling in the low-energy sector,

λeff\displaystyle\lambda_{\rm eff} =λs+λpl,\displaystyle=\lambda_{s}+\lambda_{\rm pl}, (25)
λpl\displaystyle\lambda_{\rm pl} =1g2​∫d​ξ​∫0∞d​νπ​K​(ξ,ν)2−K​(ξ,0)2ν2+ξ2,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{g^{2}}\int\!d\xi\!\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\frac{d\nu}{\pi}\,\frac{K(\xi;\nu)^{2}-K(\xi;0)^{2}}{\nu^{2}+\xi^{2}}, (26)

where K⁡(ξ,ν)=K⁡(kF,p,ν)K(\xi;\nu)=K(k_{F},p;\nu) at ξp=ξ\xi_{p}=\xi. The subtraction removes the iteration of the static kernel, which is part of the BCS logarithm. The sign of λpl\lambda_{\rm pl} is positive whatever the sign of KK: the gap function at high frequency is −K-K times the low-energy pair amplitude, and it feeds back with a second factor of −K-K. This is the mechanism of plasmon-induced pairing in the repulsive single-layer problem. Here it adds to an interaction that is already attractive.

In the wedge, with y=q​dy=qd and w=ν/Ω∗w=\nu/\Omega_{*}, Eq. (14) becomes W12=−Uqs(y;w)/e−yW_{12}=-U_{q}\,s(y;w)/e^{-y} with

s⁡(y,w)=e−y[1+y⁡(1+e−y)2​w2]​[1+y⁡(1−e−y)2​w2],s(y;w)=\frac{e^{-y}}{\bigl[1+\frac{y(1+e^{-y})}{2w^{2}}\bigr]\bigl[1+\frac{y(1-e^{-y})}{2w^{2}}\bigr]}, (27)

and K=−(c/π)​k​(η,w)K=-(c/\pi)\,k(\eta;w) with k⁡(η,w)=∫η∞d​y​s​(y,w)/y2−η2k(\eta;w)=\int_{\eta}^{\infty}dy\,s(y;w)/\sqrt{y^{2}-\eta^{2}} and η=|ξ|​d/ℏ​vF\eta=|\xi|d/\hbar v_{F}. Equation (26) then reduces to a pure number times c​ℏ​Ω∗/EFc\,\hbar\Omega_{*}/E_{F}:

λpl\displaystyle\lambda_{\rm pl} =𝒥π3​g​α​ℏ​Ω∗EF=𝒥2​π3​rs​EdEF=𝒥​g2​π3​rs2​aBd,\displaystyle=\frac{\mathcal{J}}{\pi^{3}g}\,\alpha\,\frac{\hbar\Omega_{*}}{E_{F}}=\frac{\mathcal{J}}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi^{3}}\;r_{s}\sqrt{\frac{E_{d}}{E_{F}}}=\frac{\mathcal{J}\sqrt{g}}{2\pi^{3}}\;r_{s}^{2}\sqrt{\frac{a_{B}}{d}}, (28)
𝒥\displaystyle\mathcal{J} =∫0∞d​ww2​∫0∞d​η​k​(η,w)2=4.777.\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\frac{dw}{w^{2}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\!d\eta\;k(\eta;w)^{2}=4.777.

Numerically λpl=0.109​rs​Ed/EF\lambda_{\rm pl}=0.109\,r_{s}\sqrt{E_{d}/E_{F}}, which for g=2g=2 is 0.109​rs2​aB/d0.109\,r_{s}^{2}\sqrt{a_{B}/d}. Equation (28) is the central analytic result of the ladder theory. It holds for 𝒢≫1\mathcal{G}\gg 1 and kF​d≫1k_{F}d\gg 1; the direct numerical evaluation of Eq. (26) with the full RPA kernel approaches it from above and is within 3% of it at d=5​aBd=5a_{B} and within 0.2% at d=20​aBd=20a_{B} for rs=1r_{s}=1 and 2.

The plasmon-induced coupling is the product of the Coulomb coupling α\alpha and the ratio of the plasmon energy at q=1/dq=1/d to the Fermi energy. It decays as d−1/2d^{-1/2}, against d−2d^{-2} for λs\lambda_{s}. The two are equal at

d×aB=(π48​𝒥​g2)2/3rs−2/3≃0.74rs−2/3(g=2),\frac{d_{\times}}{a_{B}}=\Bigl(\frac{\pi^{4}}{8\mathcal{J}g^{2}}\Bigr)^{2/3}r_{s}^{-2/3}\simeq 0.74\,r_{s}^{-2/3}\quad(g=2), (29)

and beyond d×d_{\times} the plasmon-induced coupling dominates.

The low-energy sector that remains after the elimination is a BCS problem with coupling λeff\lambda_{\rm eff}. Its logarithm is cut off at ℏ​vF/d\hbar v_{F}/d: by Eq. (24) a state at energy ξ\xi couples only to the part of the wedge with ν>ω+​(|ξ|/ℏ​vF)\nu>\omega_{+}(|\xi|/\hbar v_{F}), so the effective coupling falls off for |ξ|≳ℏ​vF/d|\xi|\gtrsim\hbar v_{F}/d, as the static one does. Hence

kB​Tc≃C​ℏ​vFd​exp⁡[−1λs+λpl],k_{B}T_{c}\simeq C\,\frac{\hbar v_{F}}{d}\,\exp\!\Bigl[-\frac{1}{\lambda_{s}+\lambda_{\rm pl}}\Bigr], (30)

with CC of order unity. The elimination also gives the eigenvalue away from TcT_{c}. The wedge enters at second order, so in the eigenvalue equation its contribution carries a factor 1/η1/\eta, and

η2=(λs​η+λpl)​ln⁡C​ℏ​vFkB​T​d.\eta^{2}=\bigl(\lambda_{s}\,\eta+\lambda_{\rm pl}\bigr)\ln\frac{C\hbar v_{F}}{k_{B}T\,d}. (31)

For λpl=0\lambda_{\rm pl}=0 this is the BCS line η=λs​ln⁡(1/T)\eta=\lambda_{s}\ln(1/T). When the plasmon-induced term dominates, η\eta grows as the square root of the logarithm. Equation (31) reduces to Eq. (30) at η=1\eta=1, and it provides a test of the theory that does not involve the exponentially small TcT_{c} itself.

Terms of third and higher order in the kernel, in which the virtual pair scatters within the wedge before it returns, all have the same sign and raise TcT_{c}. The third-order term is smaller than λpl\lambda_{\rm pl} by a factor of order ℏ​Ω∗/EF\hbar\Omega_{*}/E_{F}. In the exponent it is to be compared with λpl2\lambda_{\rm pl}^{2}, so it changes ln⁡Tc\ln T_{c} by an amount of order (ℏ​Ω∗/EF)/λpl∼1/α(\hbar\Omega_{*}/E_{F})/\lambda_{\rm pl}\sim 1/\alpha, which does not depend on dd. It belongs to the prefactor: CC is a function of rsr_{s} and is not universal. At large dd,

ln⁡kB​Tc​dℏ​vF≃−2​π3𝒥​g​1rs2​daB=−9.2rs2​daB(g=2).\ln\frac{k_{B}T_{c}\,d}{\hbar v_{F}}\simeq-\frac{2\pi^{3}}{\mathcal{J}\sqrt{g}}\,\frac{1}{r_{s}^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{d}{a_{B}}}=-\frac{9.2}{r_{s}^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{d}{a_{B}}}\quad(g=2). (32)

The dynamically screened TcT_{c} is a stretched exponential in dd. It lies between the power law of the unscreened theory and the Gaussian of the statically screened one, and it is far closer to the former.

VII Zero magnetic field: Numerical results within ladder approximation

VII.1 Transition temperature

All results in this section are for the ladder approximation, Eq. (17). Figure 7 shows the mean-field TcT_{c} from its full solution for the three interactions, and Table 3 lists representative values. The ordering Tc(s)<Tc<Tc(0)T_{c}^{(s)}<T_{c}<T_{c}^{(0)} is a direct consequence of Eq. (12), since the three kernels are ordered pointwise. The separations between them are very large. At rs=2r_{s}=2 and d=5​aBd=5a_{B}, for example, the unscreened, dynamically screened, and statically screened transition temperatures are 10−0.910^{-0.9}, 10−2.810^{-2.8}, and 10−10210^{-102} in units of EF/kBE_{F}/k_{B}. Within the ladder approximation, static screening is not an approximation to dynamic screening in any part of the parameter space we have examined.

The unscreened result follows the 1/d1/d law of Eq. (21). The dynamically screened result decays faster than any power but much more slowly than an exponential in d2d^{2}. Figure 8(a) tests Eq. (30). It shows ln⁡(ℏ​vF/kB​Tc​d)\ln(\hbar v_{F}/k_{B}T_{c}d) from the full numerical solution against 1/(λs+λpl)1/(\lambda_{s}+\lambda_{\rm pl}), with the two couplings computed independently from Eqs. (22) and (26). All points with EB<EFE_{B}<E_{F}, for rsr_{s} between 0.25 and 3 and for exponents between 3 and 135, lie on the line of unit slope to within an additive constant: ln⁡C\ln C is between −1.6-1.6 and +6.6+6.6, while the exponent varies by a factor of more than forty. For the points with 1/(λs+λpl)>101/(\lambda_{s}+\lambda_{\rm pl})>10 the numerical exponent and the two-step estimate differ by at most 13%. The test rests on the 31 points at which TcT_{c} is computed directly, which reach exponents up to 23 and have ln⁡C\ln C between −1.6-1.6 and +0.2+0.2. The points at larger exponents are extrapolated with the variable of Eq. (31) (Appendix D); the slope and the intercept of the extrapolation are taken from the numerical η⁡(T)\eta(T) and not from the theory, but these points assume the linearity that Fig. 8(b) shows over the computed range, and they are a weaker test. The constant is not universal. At fixed rsr_{s} it tends to a limit at large dd: for rs=2r_{s}=2, ln⁡C\ln C is −1.29-1.29, −1.34-1.34, and −1.37-1.37 at d/aB=20d/a_{B}=20, 30, and 50. It increases as rsr_{s} decreases, as expected from the third-order term discussed in Sec. VI.3.

Figure 8(b) tests Eq. (31). The combination η2/(λs​η+λpl)\eta^{2}/(\lambda_{s}\eta+\lambda_{\rm pl}) formed from the numerical eigenvalue is a linear function of ln⁡(1/T)\ln(1/T) below kB​T≈3×10−3​EFk_{B}T\approx 3\times 10^{-3}E_{F}, both above and below TcT_{c}, with a slope between 0.97 and 1.08, and between 1.04 and 1.06 at the lowest temperatures. The excess over unity decreases slowly with decreasing temperature and is the signature of the third-order term.

The dependence on rsr_{s} at fixed dd is shown in Fig. 9. Tc/EFT_{c}/E_{F} increases rapidly with rsr_{s}, as exp(−const/rs2)\exp(-{\rm const}/r_{s}^{2}) at large dd according to Eq. (32), until EBE_{B} becomes comparable to EFE_{F}, where the mean-field TcT_{c} at fixed chemical potential ceases to be meaningful.

VII.2 Eigenvalue and gap function

Figure 10(a) shows the eigenvalue η⁡(T)\eta(T) for the three interactions. For static screening it is a straight line in ln⁡(1/T)\ln(1/T) with slope λs\lambda_{s}, the BCS form. For the unscreened interaction it is quadratic, the signature of Eq. (20). For dynamic screening it follows Eq. (31): it rises steeply at temperatures comparable to the plasmon energy, where the wedge is populated directly, and then grows as the square root of the logarithm.

The gap function at TcT_{c}, Fig. 10(b), is nodeless. It rises with frequency from its low-frequency value to a plateau that is larger by a factor of 7 to 10 in the examples shown, and the rise takes place at frequencies somewhat below Ω∗\Omega_{*}, where the wedge opens. The plateau is the amplitude in the wedge that mediates λpl\lambda_{\rm pl}. In the repulsive single-layer problem the corresponding gap function changes sign at the plasmon scale [16, 20]; here it does not.

VII.3 Frequency cutoff

In the single-layer problem the calculated TcT_{c} depends strongly on the Matsubara cutoff ωc\omega_{c}, and no value of ωc\omega_{c} can be justified [20]. Figure 11 shows the corresponding dependence here, obtained by restricting both frequencies in Eq. (17) to |ω|<ωc|\omega|<\omega_{c}, for rs=1r_{s}=1 and d=2​aBd=2a_{B}. TcT_{c} rises by many orders of magnitude as ωc\omega_{c} is raised through Ω∗\Omega_{*} and the wedge is included, and it then converges to the cutoff-free value as 1/ωc1/\omega_{c}. It is lower than that value by a factor of 2.3 at ℏ​ωc=10​EF≈7​ℏ​Ω∗\hbar\omega_{c}=10\,E_{F}\approx 7\hbar\Omega_{*} and by 8% at 100​EF100\,E_{F}. The whole dependence is reproduced by the two-step theory with the frequency integral of Eq. (26) cut off at ωc\omega_{c}, which confirms that the effect of dynamic screening in the ladder is the coupling λpl\lambda_{\rm pl} and nothing else.

The convergence is the difference from the single layer. There the coupling keeps growing with ωc\omega_{c}, and it competes with a static repulsion of the same size. Here the range of the interlayer interaction limits the wedge to |ξ|≲ℏ​vF/d|\xi|\lesssim\hbar v_{F}/d, the contribution of frequencies above Ω∗\Omega_{*} falls as 1/ν21/\nu^{2}, and the static term has the same sign. The slow convergence nevertheless shows how much of the result comes from frequencies well above Ω∗\Omega_{*}, where the interaction is the bare one.

The two-pole plasmon-pole approximation of Sec. IV reproduces the RPA result for log10⁡Tc\log_{10}T_{c} to within 0.15 at the points where we have compared them (Table 3), as expected from the fact that it is exact in the wedge. It gives the lower value in each case.

VIII Zero magnetic field: Vertex corrections and the crossed rung

The results of Secs. VI and VII are those of the ladder approximation. The large enhancement of TcT_{c} over the statically screened value comes from one term, λpl\lambda_{\rm pl}, which is of second order in the screened interaction. At that order the irreducible vertex has another term that contains only the interlayer interaction, the crossed rung of Fig. 5(c). A theorem of the Migdal type would make it negligible. We show here that it is not negligible, that it can be computed, and that it cancels λpl\lambda_{\rm pl}.

VIII.1 Why Migdal’s theorem does not apply

Migdal’s argument requires the boson to be slow, ω≪vF​q\omega\ll v_{F}q at the wave vectors that matter. The vertex correction is then of order ωD/EF\omega_{D}/E_{F} [21]. In the bilayer the wave vectors that matter are q≲1/dq\lesssim 1/d, and both collective modes are fast there:

Ω∗vF/d=𝒢,v−vF≃𝒢/2,𝒢=g​daB.\frac{\Omega_{*}}{v_{F}/d}=\sqrt{\mathcal{G}},\qquad\frac{v_{-}}{v_{F}}\simeq\sqrt{\mathcal{G}/2},\qquad\mathcal{G}=\frac{g\,d}{a_{B}}. (33)

The wedge of Eq. (24), from which the whole of λpl\lambda_{\rm pl} comes, is by its definition the region ν>ω+​(q)≫vF​q\nu>\omega_{+}(q)\gg v_{F}q. The smallness of the plasmon energy compared with the Fermi energy, ℏ​Ω∗/EF=(2​g​Ed/EF)1/2≪1\hbar\Omega_{*}/E_{F}=(2gE_{d}/E_{F})^{1/2}\ll 1 at large dd, does not help: Migdal’s parameter is the ratio of the boson velocity to the Fermi velocity, and it is large. The same is true of the plasmon of a single layer [20].

A bilayer in which Migdal’s theorem does hold. The criterion is made explicit by comparison with the all-electron bilayer with unequal layer masses of Ref. [23]. There the electrons of a light layer, of mass m1m_{1}, are paired by the exchange of the acoustic plasmon of a heavy layer, of mass m2m_{2}, and the Coulomb interaction is purely repulsive. At small separation and comparable densities the velocity of that plasmon is of order ℏ​kF/(m1​m2)1/2\hbar k_{F}/(m_{1}m_{2})^{1/2}, which is below the Fermi velocity of the light layer by a factor of order (m1/m2)1/2(m_{1}/m_{2})^{1/2}. For m2/m1≫1m_{2}/m_{1}\gg 1 the boson is therefore slow for the carriers that pair. The heavy layer plays the part of the ions and its acoustic plasmon that of the acoustic phonon, Migdal’s theorem holds with the mass ratio as its small parameter, and Eliashberg theory is controlled although no part of the interaction is attractive. As the mass ratio approaches unity the control is lost and the result depends on a frequency cutoff [23]. The equal-mass electron-hole bilayer is at the opposite end of the same axis. By Eqs. (10) and (33) both modes are faster than both carriers of the pair at every separation, there is no mass ratio to make them slow, and the theorem that applies is the adiabatic one of Sec. VIII.3. The two problems are complementary. In one, the retardation of a slow mode produces an attraction from a repulsion, and the ladder is controlled. In the other, the mode is fast, retardation is ineffective, and the ladder overestimates the pairing. In an electron-hole bilayer with a large mass ratio and small separation, the acoustic mode can be slower than the light carrier but faster than the heavy carrier. Since an interlayer pair contains both carriers, neither limit discussed above directly applies. Whether the dynamical enhancement of pairing survives vertex corrections in this regime remains unresolved by the present analysis. At sufficiently large dd, the acoustic mode is faster than both carriers for any finite mass ratio.

VIII.2 Second-order vertex at the Fermi surface

Consider an electron at 𝐤\mathbf{k} and a hole at −𝐤-\mathbf{k} scattered to 𝐤′\mathbf{k}^{\prime} and −𝐤′-\mathbf{k}^{\prime}, all at the Fermi surface and at zero frequency, with 𝚫=𝐤′−𝐤\bm{\Delta}=\mathbf{k}^{\prime}-\mathbf{k}. To second order in W12W_{12} the amplitude is

Γ(2)=\displaystyle\Gamma^{(2)}={} ∫d​ν2​π​∫d2​q(2​π)2​W12​(𝐪,i​ν)​W12​(𝚫−𝐪,i​ν)\displaystyle\int\!\frac{d\nu}{2\pi}\!\int\!\frac{d^{2}q}{(2\pi)^{2}}\,W_{12}(\mathbf{q},i\nu)\,W_{12}(\bm{\Delta}-\mathbf{q},i\nu)
×[Blad+Bcr],\displaystyle\times\bigl[B_{\rm lad}+B_{\rm cr}\bigr], (34)

where BladB_{\rm lad} and BcrB_{\rm cr} denote the electron–hole propagator factors for the second-order ladder and crossed-rung diagrams, respectively. The first term is the second iteration of the ladder. The electron is at 𝐤+𝐪\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q} with frequency ν\nu and the hole at −𝐤−𝐪-\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{q} with frequency −ν-\nu, so that 𝒢e​𝒢h=1/(ν2+ξ12)\mathcal{G}_{e}\mathcal{G}_{h}=1/(\nu^{2}+\xi_{1}^{2}) with ξ1=ξ𝐤+𝐪\xi_{1}=\xi_{\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}}. The second term is the crossed rung. The electron is again at 𝐤+𝐪\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}, but the hole absorbs the two momentum transfers in the opposite order: it is at 𝐪−𝐤′\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{k}^{\prime} and it carries the frequency +ν+\nu. With ξ2=ξ𝐤′−𝐪\xi_{2}=\xi_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}-\mathbf{q}} the product is 1/[(i​ν−ξ1)​(i​ν−ξ2)]1/[(i\nu-\xi_{1})(i\nu-\xi_{2})]. The interaction factors are symmetric under 𝐪→𝚫−𝐪\mathbf{q}\to\bm{\Delta}-\mathbf{q}, which exchanges ξ1\xi_{1} and ξ2\xi_{2}. After symmetrization

Blad\displaystyle B_{\rm lad} =12​[1ν2+ξ12+1ν2+ξ22],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\Bigl[\frac{1}{\nu^{2}+\xi_{1}^{2}}+\frac{1}{\nu^{2}+\xi_{2}^{2}}\Bigr],
Bcr\displaystyle B_{\rm cr} =ξ1​ξ2−ν2(ν2+ξ12)​(ν2+ξ22),\displaystyle=\frac{\xi_{1}\xi_{2}-\nu^{2}}{(\nu^{2}+\xi_{1}^{2})(\nu^{2}+\xi_{2}^{2})},
Blad+Bcr\displaystyle B_{\rm lad}+B_{\rm cr} =(ξ1+ξ2)22​(ν2+ξ12)​(ν2+ξ22).\displaystyle=\frac{(\xi_{1}+\xi_{2})^{2}}{2(\nu^{2}+\xi_{1}^{2})(\nu^{2}+\xi_{2}^{2})}. (35)

This is an identity. For a parabolic band

ξ1+ξ2=ℏ2m​𝐪⋅(𝐪−𝚫).\xi_{1}+\xi_{2}=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{m}\,\mathbf{q}\cdot(\mathbf{q}-\bm{\Delta}). (36)

The terms of first order in 𝐪\mathbf{q} have cancelled. The electron and the hole of a pair move in opposite directions, so for scattering at small angle a momentum transfer that raises the energy of one lowers the energy of the other by the same amount, ξ2=−ξ1\xi_{2}=-\xi_{1}, and then Bcr=−BladB_{\rm cr}=-B_{\rm lad} at every frequency. What is left is the curvature of the dispersion.

As in Eq. (26) we separate the product of the static interactions and define, for X=ladX={\rm lad}, cr,

λX=\displaystyle\lambda_{X}={} N0g⟨∫d​ν2​π∫d2​q(2​π)2[W12(𝐪,iν)W12(𝚫−𝐪,iν)\displaystyle\frac{N_{0}}{g}\Bigl\langle\int\!\frac{d\nu}{2\pi}\!\int\!\frac{d^{2}q}{(2\pi)^{2}}\bigl[W_{12}(\mathbf{q},i\nu)W_{12}(\bm{\Delta}-\mathbf{q},i\nu)
−W12(𝐪,0)W12(𝚫−𝐪,0)]BX⟩𝐤′,\displaystyle-W_{12}(\mathbf{q},0)W_{12}(\bm{\Delta}-\mathbf{q},0)\bigr]B_{X}\Bigr\rangle_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}, (37)

where the average is over the direction of 𝐤′\mathbf{k}^{\prime}. The ladder term is the plasmon-induced coupling, λlad=λpl\lambda_{\rm lad}=\lambda_{\rm pl}. The crossed term λcr\lambda_{\rm cr} is an addition to the pairing interaction between the low-energy states, of the same order, and the effective coupling of the low-energy sector becomes

λeff=λs+λnet+λGMB,λnet=λpl+λcr.\lambda_{\rm eff}=\lambda_{s}+\lambda_{\rm net}+\lambda_{\rm GMB},\qquad\lambda_{\rm net}=\lambda_{\rm pl}+\lambda_{\rm cr}. (38)

The last term is the crossed rung with the two static interactions,

λGMB=−N0g⟨∫d2​q(2​π)2\displaystyle\lambda_{\rm GMB}=-\frac{N_{0}}{g}\Bigl\langle\int\!\frac{d^{2}q}{(2\pi)^{2}}\, W12​(𝐪,0)​W12​(𝚫−𝐪,0)\displaystyle W_{12}(\mathbf{q},0)W_{12}(\bm{\Delta}-\mathbf{q},0)
×θ⁡(−ξ1​ξ2)|ξ1−ξ2|⟩𝐤′,\displaystyle\times\frac{\theta(-\xi_{1}\xi_{2})}{|\xi_{1}-\xi_{2}|}\Bigr\rangle_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}, (39)

the analog of the induced interaction of Gor’kov and Melik-Barkhudarov [46]. It is repulsive and of order λs2​ln⁡kF​d\lambda_{s}^{2}\ln k_{F}d.

In the wedge ν≫|ξ1,2|\nu\gg|\xi_{1,2}|, so Blad≃1/ν2B_{\rm lad}\simeq 1/\nu^{2} and, by Eqs. (35) and (36), Blad+Bcr≃(ξ1+ξ2)2/2​ν4B_{\rm lad}+B_{\rm cr}\simeq(\xi_{1}+\xi_{2})^{2}/2\nu^{4}. The cancellation leaves a fraction (ℏ2​q2/m​ℏ​ν)2(\hbar^{2}q^{2}/m\hbar\nu)^{2}, which at q∼1/dq\sim 1/d and ν∼Ω∗\nu\sim\Omega_{*} is 1/[𝒢​(kF​d)2]1/[\mathcal{G}(k_{F}d)^{2}]. We denote by λw\lambda_{w} the residual contribution of the wedge to λnet\lambda_{\mathrm{net}} after the partial cancellation between the ladder and crossed-rung diagrams. It is of order λpl/[𝒢​(kF​d)2]\lambda_{\mathrm{pl}}/[\mathcal{G}(k_{F}d)^{2}], with a coefficient evaluated in Appendix F:

λw=Jw​g​rs4​(aBd)7/2,Jw=3.441×10−4,\lambda_{w}=J_{w}\,\sqrt{g}\,r_{s}^{4}\Bigl(\frac{a_{B}}{d}\Bigr)^{7/2},\qquad J_{w}=3.441\times 10^{-4}, (40)

to be compared with λpl∝d−1/2\lambda_{\rm pl}\propto d^{-1/2} and λs∝d−2\lambda_{s}\propto d^{-2}. The wedge is not the only contribution to λnet\lambda_{\rm net}. At frequencies and energies of the order of the curvature energy ℏ2/m​d2\hbar^{2}/md^{2} the factor Blad+BcrB_{\rm lad}+B_{\rm cr} is not small, and the screened interaction differs from its static value by the term linear in |ν|/vF​q|\nu|/v_{F}q that comes from the particle-hole continuum. This region gives the leading term of λnet\lambda_{\rm net} at small rsr_{s}, which can be obtained in closed form (Appendix F):

λnet\displaystyle\lambda_{\rm net} →C3(d)rs3(rs→0),\displaystyle\to C_{3}(d)\,r_{s}^{3}\qquad(r_{s}\to 0),
C3\displaystyle C_{3} →7​π​ζ​(3)256​g5/2(aBd)5(d≫aB),\displaystyle\to\frac{7\pi\zeta(3)}{256\,g^{5/2}}\Bigl(\frac{a_{B}}{d}\Bigr)^{5}\qquad(d\gg a_{B}), (41)

with C3​(d)C_{3}(d) given for every dd by Eq. (93). The integrand of λnet\lambda_{\rm net} is nonnegative, so the two contributions add. The second is of lower order in rsr_{s} and falls off faster with dd, so that Eq. (41) is the limit of λnet\lambda_{\rm net} for rs→0r_{s}\to 0 at fixed dd and Eq. (40) its limit for d→∞d\to\infty at fixed rsr_{s}.

We have evaluated Eqs. (37) and (39) with the full RPA interaction by direct four-dimensional quadrature (Appendix D). The ladder term reproduces the independently computed λpl\lambda_{\rm pl} of Eq. (26) to better than 0.5%0.5\%. The results are shown in Fig. 12 and Table 4. The crossed rung is negative and nearly equal in magnitude to λpl\lambda_{\rm pl} at every separation, including kF​d<1k_{F}d<1, because the wedge is by construction the region in which the carriers are slow. The net coupling is at most 8% of λpl\lambda_{\rm pl} in the range examined, at most 1.2% for kF​d>2k_{F}d>2 and 0.25% for kF​d>5k_{F}d>5, and it falls off with dd approximately as d−4d^{-4}: between d=8​aBd=8a_{B} and 20​aB20a_{B} the local exponent is between −4.0-4.0 and −4.2-4.2 for the values of rsr_{s} in Fig. 12. This is between the powers 7/27/2 and 55 of Eqs. (40) and (41). The dependence on rsr_{s} at fixed dd is likewise between rs3r_{s}^{3} and rs4r_{s}^{4}: the local exponent is between 3.3 and 3.9 for d≥5​aBd\geq 5a_{B} and 0.25≤rs≤30.25\leq r_{s}\leq 3, and decreases toward 3 as rsr_{s} decreases. Both limits are reproduced by the numerical results with no adjustable quantity [Appendix F and Fig. 22]. In additional calculations for rsr_{s} down to 1/321/32 the ratio λnet/C3​rs3\lambda_{\rm net}/C_{3}r_{s}^{3} tends to 1 linearly in rsr_{s}, and its extrapolation to rs=0r_{s}=0 is within 1.3% of 1 at every separation examined. In calculations for dd up to 320​aB320\,a_{B} at rs=1r_{s}=1 the ratio (λnet−C3​rs3)/λw(\lambda_{\rm net}-C_{3}r_{s}^{3})/\lambda_{w} decreases to 1.012 and extrapolates to 1.001 at d=∞d=\infty. For d≥5​aBd\geq 5a_{B} the computed values are described by λnet≃C3​(d)​rs3+C4​(d)​rs4\lambda_{\rm net}\simeq C_{3}(d)r_{s}^{3}+C_{4}(d)r_{s}^{4}, where C4C_{4} depends on rsr_{s} by at most 12% for 0.25≤rs≤30.25\leq r_{s}\leq 3 and approaches Jw​g​(aB/d)7/2J_{w}\sqrt{g}\,(a_{B}/d)^{7/2} from above. For kF​d≳2k_{F}d\gtrsim 2 the net coupling is small compared with λs\lambda_{s}, and it is partly offset by λGMB\lambda_{\rm GMB}.

VIII.3 The adiabatic limit and the cancellation beyond second order

The cancellation is not special to second order. Its origin can be identified exactly in two limits, and we state separately what these limits prove and what they do not.

Static sources. In the wedge the energies of the carriers change by much less than ℏ​ν\hbar\nu during the process, so the carriers act as static sources for the density fluctuations of the two layers, which in the RPA are Gaussian. For an electron and a hole held at in-plane separation 𝐫\mathbf{r} and coupled linearly to a Gaussian field, the pair propagator in imaginary time is known exactly. Apart from the self-energy factors of each charge,

P⁡(τ)\displaystyle P(\tau) ∝exp[−1ℏ∫0τ∫0τdτ1dτ2W12(𝐫,τ1−τ2)]\displaystyle\propto\exp\Bigl[-\frac{1}{\hbar}\int_{0}^{\tau}\!\!\int_{0}^{\tau}\!d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}\,W_{12}(\mathbf{r},\tau_{1}-\tau_{2})\Bigr]
=exp[−1ℏ∫d​ν2​πW12(𝐫,iν)2−2​cos⁡ν​τν2].\displaystyle=\exp\Bigl[-\frac{1}{\hbar}\int\!\frac{d\nu}{2\pi}\,W_{12}(\mathbf{r},i\nu)\,\frac{2-2\cos\nu\tau}{\nu^{2}}\Bigr]. (42)

The exponent is linear in the interaction. At long times it is −τW12(𝐫,0)/ℏ-\tau\,W_{12}(\mathbf{r},0)/\hbar plus terms that grow more slowly than τ\tau. The interaction energy of the two sources is the statically screened interaction. The slower terms contain the dynamical part of the interaction. Those from the plasmons tend to a constant. Those from the particle-hole continuum grow logarithmically and change the pair amplitude by a power law. Neither contributes to the energy. A ladder built from the same interaction contains at second order a term linear in τ\tau and proportional to ∫d​ν​W122/ν2\int d\nu\,W_{12}^{2}/\nu^{2}, which is λpl\lambda_{\rm pl}. The crossed diagram removes it. The static-source approximation applies to finite-mass carriers in the wedge, where ν≫vF​q\nu\gg v_{F}q; it does not require taking m→∞m\to\infty. At fixed density and layer separation, the literal infinite-mass limit gives EB/EF→∞E_{B}/E_{F}\to\infty and lies outside the weak-pairing regime considered here.

Carriers with linear dispersion. The result does not require the sources to be at rest. For a fermion with linearized dispersion, ξ𝐤+𝐪=ℏ​𝐯⋅𝐪\xi_{\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}}=\hbar\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{q}, the propagator in an arbitrary potential that depends on space and time is known in closed form, and its average over a Gaussian field is again the exponential of a form bilinear in the sources [47, 48, 49]. For an electron and a hole on opposite patches of the Fermi surface the ladder and all crossed diagrams, with any number of interlayer lines, then sum to an exponential whose exponent is of first order in W12W_{12}. In this limit the logarithmic renormalization of the interaction in the Cooper channel is cancelled by the crossed channel, and the coupling does not flow. This is a statement about the interaction and not about correlation functions: the pair susceptibility remains singular, and it is a power law of the energy, as in a one-dimensional system of counterpropagating fermions [49]. Equation (35) with ξ2=−ξ1\xi_{2}=-\xi_{1} is the second-order instance: Bcr=−BladB_{\rm cr}=-B_{\rm lad} at every frequency.

What follows, and what does not. The distinction between the irreducible vertex and the full amplitude matters here. In the linearized limit the crossed diagram, which belongs to the irreducible vertex II of Eq. (71), does not vanish: it equals minus the iteration of the first-order rung, which is reducible. What vanishes, at every order and every frequency, is their sum, that is, the contribution of second and higher order to the effective interaction between low-energy pairs. A pairing instability at a finite temperature therefore requires what the linearization omits, the curvature of the dispersion, and every term of second and higher order in W12W_{12} in that effective interaction is proportional to it. At second order we have evaluated these terms without approximation: they are λnet\lambda_{\rm net} and λGMB\lambda_{\rm GMB}. We have not evaluated the curvature terms of third and higher order. The exact cancellations for static sources and for carriers with linearized dispersion, both assuming Gaussian density fluctuations, suggest that the higher-order curvature terms are also suppressed. We proceed on this expectation, which remains unverified beyond second order for carriers with quadratic dispersion. Three points limit what the solvable limits establish. (i) They concern the pair propagator for prescribed kinematics, not the irreducible vertex of the full problem with curvature. (ii) They assume Gaussian density fluctuations, which is the RPA. In an interacting Fermi liquid the higher cumulants of the density are suppressed at q≪kFq\ll k_{F} by the cancellation of fermion loops [49], which is the regime relevant at large dd, but we have not shown this for arbitrary rsr_{s}. (iii) The criterion for slow carriers is local in qq. The plasmon is gapless, and what is required is ν≳ω+​(q)≫vF​q\nu\gtrsim\omega_{+}(q)\gg v_{F}q at each wave vector. Since ω+​(q)/vF​q\omega_{+}(q)/v_{F}q is of order 𝒢\sqrt{\mathcal{G}} at q=1/dq=1/d and increases as q→0q\to 0, the criterion is met uniformly at large dd.

We refer to the statement that carriers slow compared with the modes of the medium interact through its static response as the adiabatic theorem. It is the opposite of Migdal’s limit. Migdal’s theorem states that the vertex corrections are negligible when the boson is slow. Here the boson is fast, the vertex corrections are of order unity, and in the solvable limits their sum is known: the dynamical part of the interaction drops out of the pairing. For carriers with curvature the cancellation is incomplete at second order by the amounts given in Eqs. (40) and (41). The intralayer vertex and self-energy corrections of Sec. V.2, which cancel in the same region by the Ward identity, are part of the same structure.

VIII.4 Consequences

With the crossed rung included the effective coupling is λs+λnet+λGMB\lambda_{s}+\lambda_{\rm net}+\lambda_{\rm GMB}, which for kF​d≳2k_{F}d\gtrsim 2 differs little from λs\lambda_{s} (Table 4). To the accuracy of the exponent the transition temperature is then that of the statically screened theory, and the ladder overestimates it by a factor exp⁡[1/λs−1/(λs+λpl)]\exp[1/\lambda_{s}-1/(\lambda_{s}+\lambda_{\rm pl})]. At rs=1r_{s}=1 and d=2​aBd=2a_{B}, this factor is ∼1040\sim 10^{40}: the ladder estimate exceeds the statically screened estimate by about 40 orders of magnitude, to exponential accuracy.

Two remarks are in order. First, the identity of Eq. (35) applies without change to the particle-particle channel of a single layer, where the plasmon-induced attraction of the ladder arises from the same second-order process through the region ν≫vF​q\nu\gg v_{F}q. This suggests that a large part of that attraction is removed by the crossed diagram there too. At kF​d=0.18k_{F}d=0.18, where the interlayer interaction is close to that of a single layer, we find that the crossed rung removes 93%93\% of λpl\lambda_{\rm pl}. This is in line with the conclusion of Ref. [20] that the Eliashberg treatment of the plasmon mechanism is not reliable. It does not show that a single layer has no pairing instability. In the single layer the momentum transfers are not confined to small angles, we have not computed the remainder for that case, and other routes to pairing are not addressed by this argument. Second, the unscreened HF theory is not affected by this argument in the same way, because it has no small parameter at all: the adiabatic limit selects the statically screened interaction, not the bare one.

IX What is controlled at zero field

This section states the conclusions; the derivations, diagram by diagram, are in Appendix E.
