It is natural to expect the theory to be exact in two limits: at small rsr_{s} for every dd, because the interaction is weak, and at large dd for every rsr_{s}, by an argument of the Migdal type, because the exciton binding energy is then small compared with the Fermi energy. Both limits are controlled, the first as a rigorous statement about the leading exponent and the second under an assumption that we state. In neither is the result that of the dynamically screened ladder.

IX.1 Small rsr_{s}

At fixed d/aB>0d/a_{B}>0 and rs→0r_{s}\to 0 one has kF​d→∞k_{F}d\to\infty, so Eq. (22) applies: λs=g​rs​aB​𝒮​(g​d/aB)/(2​π​g​d)\lambda_{s}=\sqrt{g}\,r_{s}a_{B}\,\mathcal{S}(gd/a_{B})/(2\pi g\,d) is of first order in rsr_{s}. All other terms are of higher order, and

limrs→0λs​ln⁡EFkB​Tc=1(d/aB​fixed).\lim_{r_{s}\to 0}\ \lambda_{s}\,\ln\frac{E_{F}}{k_{B}T_{c}}=1\qquad(d/a_{B}\ \text{fixed}). (43)

Four qualifications apply.

First, only the leading exponent is exact, and the corrections to ln⁡Tc\ln T_{c} are not bounded. They grow as ln⁡(1/rs)\ln(1/r_{s}), which is small compared with 1/λs∝1/rs1/\lambda_{s}\propto 1/r_{s} but is not a constant. Two sources are identified in Appendix E. The static crossed rung replaces the energy scale ℏ​vF/d\hbar v_{F}/d of the prefactor by ℏ2/m​d2\hbar^{2}/md^{2}, which is 2​EF/(kF​d)2∝rs2​EF2E_{F}/(k_{F}d)^{2}\propto r_{s}^{2}E_{F}. And the intralayer terms are of relative order α​ln⁡(1/α)\alpha\ln(1/\alpha), as in the effective mass of the two-dimensional electron gas at high density [50], which changes ln⁡Tc\ln T_{c} by an amount of order ln⁡(1/α)\ln(1/\alpha). The prefactor of TcT_{c} is therefore a power of rsr_{s} times a function of d/aBd/a_{B}, and its determination requires the other terms of second order: λGMB\lambda_{\rm GMB}, the intralayer vertex and self-energy corrections, and the corrections to the polarization that the Ward identity requires together with them. The net dynamical interlayer term is not among them. It changes ln⁡Tc\ln T_{c} by λnet/λs2→R⁡(d)​rs\lambda_{\rm net}/\lambda_{s}^{2}\to R(d)\,r_{s}, which vanishes with rsr_{s} [Eq. (95)]; R=1.56R=1.56 at d=aBd=a_{B} and 0.560.56 at d=5​aBd=5a_{B}. The situation is that of the weakly interacting Fermi gas, where the induced interaction changes the prefactor of the BCS TcT_{c} [46].

Second, the ladder reproduces the leading weak-coupling exponent at fixed d/aBd/a_{B} because λpl/λs∝rs→0\lambda_{\mathrm{pl}}/\lambda_{s}\propto r_{s}\to 0. However, this does not ensure an accurate TcT_{c}. Even when λpl≪λs\lambda_{\mathrm{pl}}\ll\lambda_{s}, the ladder enhances the transition temperature relative to the statically screened estimate by the factor exp⁡[1/λs−1/(λs+λpl)]≃exp⁡(λpl/λs2).\exp[1/\lambda_{s}-1/(\lambda_{s}+\lambda_{\rm pl})]\simeq\exp(\lambda_{\mathrm{pl}}/\lambda_{s}^{2}). Since λs∝rs\lambda_{s}\propto r_{s} and λpl∝rs2\lambda_{\mathrm{pl}}\propto r_{s}^{2}, this factor approaches a constant as rs→0r_{s}\to 0, but that constant can be enormous. For g=2g=2, the full expression gives an exponent of about 980 at d=2​aBd=2a_{B}; its large-separation asymptote is 22.6​(d/aB)7/222.6(d/a_{B})^{7/2}. Moreover, reaching λpl≪λs\lambda_{\mathrm{pl}}\ll\lambda_{s} requires rs≪0.64​(aB/d)3/2r_{s}\ll 0.64(a_{B}/d)^{3/2} at large separation. The crossed rung is needed to remove this spurious dynamical enhancement. At rs=1r_{s}=1 and d=2​aBd=2a_{B}, where λpl\lambda_{\rm pl} exceeds λs\lambda_{s} and this expansion does not apply, the difference of the exponents is 1/λs−1/(λs+λpl)=931/\lambda_{s}-1/(\lambda_{s}+\lambda_{\rm pl})=93. For any fixed rsr_{s}, however small, the second-order term of the ladder exceeds the first-order one beyond d×d_{\times} of Eq. (29), and along any path on which dd grows faster than rs−2/3r_{s}^{-2/3} the ladder has the wrong exponent. A second-order term that overtakes the first-order term is the sign that a contribution of the same order has been left out, and Sec. VIII identifies it. With the crossed rung, λnet/λs\lambda_{\rm net}/\lambda_{s} is the sum of a term proportional to rs3​(aB/d)3/2r_{s}^{3}(a_{B}/d)^{3/2} and one proportional to rs2​(aB/d)3r_{s}^{2}(a_{B}/d)^{3} at large dd, by Eqs. (40) and (41), and it vanishes whether rs→0r_{s}\to 0 or d→∞d\to\infty. The quantity that the ladder gives as λpl/λs2\lambda_{\rm pl}/\lambda_{s}^{2}, a constant at small rsr_{s}, becomes λnet/λs2=R⁡(d)​rs\lambda_{\rm net}/\lambda_{s}^{2}=R(d)\,r_{s}. The ladder approximation alone reproduces the leading weak-coupling exponent in Eq. (43) at fixed d/aBd/a_{B}. Including the crossed rung is necessary to make this conclusion uniform in increasing separation, including paths on which d/aBd/a_{B} grows faster than rs−2/3r_{s}^{-2/3}.

Third, Eq. (22) requires kF​d≫1k_{F}d\gg 1, and the form λs∝rs\lambda_{s}\propto r_{s} is not uniform as d→0d\to 0. For kF​d≲1k_{F}d\lesssim 1 the coupling is the full Fermi-surface average of the static interaction, which at d=0d=0 is (α/π)​ln⁡(2/g​α)(\alpha/\pi)\ln(2/g\alpha) and so behaves as rs​ln⁡(1/rs)r_{s}\ln(1/r_{s}). Equation (43) is expected to hold there with this average for λs\lambda_{s}, but along paths on which kF​dk_{F}d does not become large the small-angle expressions of this paper do not apply.

Finally, the controlled weak-coupling regime yields an unobservably small pairing scale. At rs=0.25r_{s}=0.25 and d=aBd=a_{B}, 1/λs=1631/\lambda_{s}=163, giving a leading exponential factor e−1/λs∼10−71e^{-1/\lambda_{s}}\sim 10^{-71} in TcT_{c}. This limit therefore serves primarily as a controlled benchmark for assessing the pairing theory.

IX.2 Large dd

Consider now d→∞d\to\infty at fixed rsr_{s}, in the liquid phase. Then kF​d≫1k_{F}d\gg 1, 𝒢≫1\mathcal{G}\gg 1, and EB≃Ed≪EFE_{B}\simeq E_{d}\ll E_{F}.

It is not Migdal’s theorem. By Eq. (33) the plasmons are fast, and Eliashberg theory, which keeps the ladder and drops the vertex corrections, is not justified. It retains λpl\lambda_{\rm pl}, which the full theory does not contain. Dressing the propagators with ZZ while keeping the vertices bare (Sec. V.2) reduces λpl\lambda_{\rm pl} but does not remove it.

The control comes from the large energy denominators of the plasmons. All interlayer momentum transfers are q≲1/d≪kFq\lesssim 1/d\ll k_{F}, the carriers are slow compared with both plasmons, and by the argument of Sec. VIII the pairing interaction is the static one. Because q≪kFq\ll k_{F} it can be written in terms of Fermi-liquid quantities. The statically screened interlayer interaction is −Uq/{[1+(Vq+Uq)χ][1+(Vq−Uq)χ]}-U_{q}/\{[1+(V_{q}+U_{q})\chi][1+(V_{q}-U_{q})\chi]\} with χ=∂n/∂μ\chi=\partial n/\partial\mu the exact proper compressibility of a layer, and the quasiparticles couple to it through the static density vertex, which by the Ward identity is χ/N∗\chi/N^{*} in units of the inverse quasiparticle weight, with N∗=g​m∗/2​π​ℏ2N^{*}=gm^{*}/2\pi\hbar^{2} and m∗m^{*} being the quasiparticle effective mass of an isolated layer [43]. For (Vq±Uq)​|χ|≫1(V_{q}\pm U_{q})|\chi|\gg 1, which holds for d≫aBd\gg a_{B}, the compressibility cancels,

W12qp​(q)=−1N∗2​UqVq2−Uq2=−1N∗2​ϵ​q4​π​e2​sinh⁡q​d,W_{12}^{\rm qp}(q)=-\frac{1}{N^{*2}}\,\frac{U_{q}}{V_{q}^{2}-U_{q}^{2}}=-\frac{1}{N^{*2}}\,\frac{\epsilon\,q}{4\pi e^{2}\sinh qd}, (44)

which is the interaction of two quasiparticles through the geometric capacitance of the double layer. It does not depend on the sign of the compressibility. Averaging over the Fermi surface with the quasiparticle density of states gives λ=(m/m∗)​λs\lambda=(m/m^{*})\lambda_{s} with λs\lambda_{s} from Eq. (23), and

ln⁡Tc=−m∗m​16​g3/2π​rs​(daB)2​[1+o⁡(1)].\ln T_{c}=-\frac{m^{*}}{m}\,\frac{16\,g^{3/2}}{\pi\,r_{s}}\Bigl(\frac{d}{a_{B}}\Bigr)^{2}\bigl[1+o(1)\bigr]. (45)

The corrections that have been computed, to 𝒮⁡(𝒢)\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{G}), to the Fermi-surface average, and from the terms of second order, are of relative order aB/da_{B}/d and 1/kF​d1/k_{F}d or smaller. For the terms that have not been computed the assumption stated next gives only that their relative contribution vanishes as d→∞d\to\infty, without a rate. Equation (45) rests on two assumptions. The first is that each layer is a Fermi liquid. The second is that the cancellation of the dynamical terms, which is exact in the linearized limit at every order and which we have verified with curvature at second order, holds for the curvature terms of higher order as well. Precisely, the assumption is that the sum δ​λ\delta\lambda of all contributions to the pair coupling that are not contained in the static quasiparticle interaction satisfies δ​λ/[(m/m∗)​λs]→0\delta\lambda/[(m/m^{*})\lambda_{s}]\to 0 as d→∞d\to\infty. A contribution proportional to d−2d^{-2} would not change the form of the result but would change its coefficient, and is excluded by this assumption and not by anything we have proven. At second order the assumption can be checked, because the remainder is known: for d→∞d\to\infty the net dynamical term is λw\lambda_{w} of Eq. (40), which changes ln⁡Tc\ln T_{c} by λw/λs2=0.101​rs2​(d/aB)1/2\lambda_{w}/\lambda_{s}^{2}=0.101\,r_{s}^{2}(d/a_{B})^{1/2} for g=2g=2 [Eq. (102)]. This increases with dd, but it is smaller than the leading term by the factor λw/λs∝rs3​(aB/d)3/2\lambda_{w}/\lambda_{s}\propto r_{s}^{3}(a_{B}/d)^{3/2}. We consider the second assumption very likely to be correct at higher order as well, but we have not proven it, and Eq. (45) should be read with that qualification. If it holds, the large-dd limit is controlled at any rsr_{s}, as anticipated. The conditions are kF​d≫1k_{F}d\gg 1 and d≫aBd\gg a_{B}. Since Ed/EF=g​rs2​aB/2​dE_{d}/E_{F}=gr_{s}^{2}a_{B}/2d, the condition EB≪EFE_{B}\ll E_{F} implies both of them when rs≳1r_{s}\gtrsim 1, and in this sense the ratio of the exciton binding energy to the Fermi energy is the control parameter. But the mechanism is the adiabatic one and not Migdal’s, and the theory it selects is static screening and not Eliashberg theory. The transition temperature in the controlled regime decreases as a Gaussian in dd, Eq. (45), and not as the stretched exponential of Eq. (32). Figure 13 shows the parameters.

IX.3 Between the limits

For rs≳1r_{s}\gtrsim 1 and d≲rs​aBd\lesssim r_{s}a_{B}, which includes the experimental systems, kF​d≲1k_{F}d\lesssim 1 and no parameter is small. The crossed rung still removes most of the plasmon-induced coupling there (Table 4), but the remainder is no longer negligible, the couplings are not small, the intralayer vertex corrections are of order μ≈0.28\mu\approx 0.28 to 0.390.39, and EBE_{B} is comparable to EFE_{F} or larger, so that the problem approaches that of bound pairs. The numbers in Fig. 7 are then the output of a definite approximation, the RPA ladder, with no estimate of its error. The analysis of Sec. VIII indicates the sign of the error: both corrections we have computed lower the coupling. What survives is qualitative. Within the RPA the interaction on the imaginary axis is attractive throughout, so the ladder has an instability at every rsr_{s} and dd; this does not fix the sign of the complete irreducible vertex at intermediate coupling. Within the ladder the unscreened and the statically screened results bracket the dynamically screened one. No such bound holds for the full problem: with the two corrections we have computed the effective coupling is already below λs\lambda_{s} at some points of Table 4, because λGMB\lambda_{\rm GMB} is negative. And the true result is expected to lie much closer to the statically screened theory than the ladder suggests.

Table 5 summarizes the comparison with phonons and with the single-layer plasmon problem.

X Discussion of the zero-field theory

Relation to earlier work. The existence of the instability at all dd within the RPA, and the ordering of the three theories, agree with Ref. [12]. That work describes the decay of TcT_{c} with dd as exponential over the range of separations it covers. Our Eq. (32) gives the asymptotic form of the ladder result as a stretched exponential, exp⁡(−const​d)\exp(-{\rm const}\sqrt{d}), which cannot be distinguished from an exponential over a short range. Reference [12] includes the normal self-energy without the vertex correction, which reduces the plasmon-induced coupling relative to the ladder with bare propagators (Sec. V.2). A quantitative comparison of the two calculations would require the frequency dependence of the self-energy and must allow for the different spin degeneracy, and we do not attempt it. The analyses of graphene double layers [25, 26] reached the same qualitative conclusion about dynamic against static screening. All of these calculations, like our Secs. VI and VII, solve a gap equation with one screened interaction line, and the large enhancement over static screening that they find is the term λpl\lambda_{\rm pl}. Section VIII shows that at second order this term belongs to the ladder approximation and not to the problem: the crossed rung, which is of the same order, cancels it. The earlier conclusion that static screening suppresses the transition temperature to very small values at large separation [24] is, by this analysis, the correct one in the regime where the pairing is weak. Reference [27] compared the ground-state energies of the exciton gas and of the electron-hole plasma with the electron-hole attraction taken as unscreened, statically screened, or dynamically screened in a plasmon-pole form, and concluded that the phase diagram is very sensitive to this choice and, in the dynamical case, to the energy at which the screening is evaluated. The present analysis removes that ambiguity at the two ends. On the weak-pairing side the relevant energy is far below the plasmon energies and the screening is static. On the Bose side the pairs are neutral and the attraction is unscreened (Appendix E). This is consistent with the finding of Ref. [27] that the exciton gas has the lower energy at very low density in every approximation. The onset density for superfluidity found in mean-field theory when the screening is computed self-consistently in the paired state [51], and in quantum Monte Carlo calculations [29], concerns the strongly paired side and is outside the scope of the linearized theory.

Magnitudes. The temperatures in the regime where the theory is controlled are extremely small. In the ladder approximation Tc≈10−9​EFT_{c}\approx 10^{-9}E_{F} at rs=1r_{s}=1, d=5​aBd=5a_{B} (Table 3), and with the crossed rung the exponent there is −1/λs≈−490-1/\lambda_{s}\approx-490. The examples we have computed suggest that observable transition temperatures require EBE_{B} comparable to EFE_{F} or larger, where the weak-pairing theory does not apply and the relevant description approaches that of a Bose gas of dipoles; the crossover itself has not been calculated here. The interlayer coherence observed in the experiments is in that range of parameters.

Limitations. The results are for the ideal model. (a) Any mismatch of the two Fermi contours, from a density imbalance or from different anisotropies of the two bands, cuts off the logarithm and removes the instability once it exceeds the gap. A difference of the isotropic masses alone does not: at equal densities the two Fermi circles coincide whatever the masses, and the logarithm survives with vFv_{F} replaced by the mean of the two Fermi velocities. (b) Disorder that is not identical in the two layers breaks pairs [1]. Both effects eliminate the exponentially small gaps of the controlled regime. (c) We assumed a Fermi liquid in each layer. At large rsr_{s} the layers, or the excitons, may crystallize [28, 52, 53], and the argument does not apply. (d) The sign property, Eq. (12), is a property of the RPA. It relies on Π⁡(q,i​ν)≤0\Pi(q,i\nu)\leq 0, which the exact proper polarization need not satisfy at rs≳2r_{s}\gtrsim 2, where the compressibility of a layer is negative. Equation (45) does not depend on it. (e) The crossed rung was evaluated between states at the Fermi surface and at zero frequency, which is what determines the exponent of a weak-coupling TcT_{c}. We have not solved a gap equation with the crossed rung in the kernel, and for kF​d≲1k_{F}d\lesssim 1 and rs≳2r_{s}\gtrsim 2, where the couplings are not small, the two-step estimate of Eq. (38) is only indicative. (f) We took equal masses. The cancellation of Eq. (35) does not depend on this: to first order in 𝐪\mathbf{q} it requires only that the hole energy be odd under 𝐪→−𝐪\mathbf{q}\to-\mathbf{q} at fixed 𝐤\mathbf{k}, which holds for any dispersion.

Open problems. The dynamical terms of third order with curvature have not been evaluated; their calculation would test the assumption on which Eq. (45) rests. The prefactor of TcT_{c} in both limits requires the remaining terms of second order, the static crossed rung beyond its logarithm and the intralayer terms; its energy scale is ℏ2/m​d2\hbar^{2}/md^{2} (Appendix E). The coefficient C4​(d)C_{4}(d) of the next term of λnet\lambda_{\rm net} is known only numerically (Appendix F). The intermediate regime requires a method that does not rely on a small parameter. A solution of the gap equation with the crossed rung included in the kernel at all frequencies would give the corrected TcT_{c} at kF​d≲1k_{F}d\lesssim 1.

XI High magnetic field: the νT=1\nu_{T}=1 quantum Hall bilayer

We now turn to the same problem in a strong magnetic field. By the particle-hole transformation of Sec. II, and apart from one-body terms, the quantum Hall bilayer at total filling factor one is the electron-hole bilayer of the preceding sections with the kinetic energy removed and the interaction projected onto the lowest Landau level, which brings in its form factor and the guiding-center algebra; by Eq. (1) d/ℓd/\ell takes the place of kF​dk_{F}d. The controlled limits of Sec. IX are then not available. In exchange the mean-field theory, which at zero field requires the numerical solution of a gap equation, becomes analytic.

The νT=1\nu_{T}=1 bilayer quantum Hall state is the simplest realization of spontaneous interlayer coherence in a two-component electron system. Two half-filled layers form the Halperin (111)(111) state [36], an incompressible integer quantum Hall state with a neutral interlayer phase mode. In the pseudospin representation the layer index is a spin-1/21/2 label and the ground state is an easy-plane quantum Hall ferromagnet [13, 14, 54, 15]. In the electron-hole representation it is an exciton superfluid. The experimental development includes the original transport observation of the bilayer quantum Hall state at νT=1\nu_{T}=1 and of its disappearance at large layer separation [55], the resonantly enhanced zero-bias tunneling peak [56], the measured linearly dispersing collective mode [57], quantized Hall drag [58, 59], counterflow transport [60, 61], activated transport in the separate layers [62], and exciton transport and perfect Coulomb drag [63, 64]. These experiments establish the charged and neutral responses of the coherent bilayer; broad accounts are given in Refs. [9, 10].

Everything derived in this section and in Appendices G–M is a Hartree-Fock statement, apart from the exact result at d=0d=0 and the finite-sphere data of Appendix M. Nothing is known in a controlled way beyond HF in this problem. Our own expectations for the real system are collected, and labeled as such, in Sec. XII.3.

XI.1 Hamiltonian and uniform Hartree-Fock saddle

The LLL-projected bilayer Hamiltonian is

H=12​A​∑𝒒∑α​βVα​β​(q):ρα​(−𝒒)​ρβ​(𝒒):,H=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\bm{q}}\sum_{\alpha\beta}V_{\alpha\beta}(q):\rho_{\alpha}(-\bm{q})\rho_{\beta}(\bm{q}):, (46)

where α,β=T,B\alpha,\beta=T,B and

VT​T​(q)=2​π​e2ϵ​q,VT​B​(q)=2​π​e2ϵ​q​e−q​d.V_{TT}(q)=\frac{2\pi e^{2}}{\epsilon q},\qquad V_{TB}(q)=\frac{2\pi e^{2}}{\epsilon q}e^{-qd}. (47)

These are VqV_{q} and UqU_{q} of Eq. (3); the layers are labeled TT and BB, and the interlayer interaction is repulsive. The LLL-projected density carries the Gaussian form factor e−q2ℓ2/4e^{-q^{2}\ell^{2}/4}, where ℓ\ell is the magnetic length. Thus each interaction term in Eq. (46) contains the Gaussian factor e−q2ℓ2/2e^{-q^{2}\ell^{2}/2}, which appears explicitly in the exchange integral. Since there is no interlayer tunneling, the relative charge is therefore conserved and the Hamiltonian has an exact U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry.

At total filling one, the coherent state fills one common pseudospinor at every guiding center,

|χϕ⟩=12​(|T⟩+ei​ϕ​|B⟩).|\chi_{\phi}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(|T\rangle+e^{i\phi}|B\rangle\right). (48)

Its density matrix is

ρm​α,m′​β=δm​m′​12​(1e−i​ϕei​ϕ1)α​β,ρ2=ρ.\rho_{m\alpha,m^{\prime}\beta}=\delta_{mm^{\prime}}\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1&e^{-i\phi}\\ e^{i\phi}&1\end{pmatrix}_{\alpha\beta},\qquad\rho^{2}=\rho. (49)

The direct Hartree term of the balanced uniform state cancels the neutralizing backgrounds. The Fock contraction generates the interlayer exchange field. This establishes a self-consistent uniform Hartree-Fock saddle, but it does not establish exactness of finite-dd Hartree-Fock. At T=0T=0, the coherent spinor of Eq. (48) forms the filled ++ band, while its orthogonal partner forms the empty −- band. For ϕ=0\phi=0, these are the symmetric and antisymmetric HF levels, respectively. Intraband +→++\!\rightarrow\!+ bubbles vanish, whereas interband +→−+\!\rightarrow\!- particle-hole excitations are allowed. The latter generate polarization, vertex, and multiparticle correlation corrections beyond Hartree-Fock.

Figure 14 makes the distinction explicit. The filled ++ band removes only same-band particle-hole insertions. It does not remove virtual transitions from the filled ++ band to the empty −- band. The LLL projection eliminates Landau-level mixing; it does not eliminate guiding-center or pseudospin correlation physics. The uniform HF calculation retains the first-order exchange field and omits the higher-order diagrams, e.g., Fig. 14(d). At d=0d=0, VT​T=VT​BV_{TT}=V_{TB} and the Hamiltonian is SU(2) pseudospin invariant; the fully polarized νT=1\nu_{T}=1 ferromagnet is then an exact LLL ground state. This special SU(2) statement does not extend to finite dd, where VT​T​(q)−VT​B​(q)≠0V_{TT}(q)-V_{TB}(q)\neq 0.

The finite-dd distinction can be displayed at the Hamiltonian level. Writing ρ=ρT+ρB\rho=\rho_{T}+\rho_{B} and Sz=(ρT−ρB)/2S^{z}=(\rho_{T}-\rho_{B})/2, one obtains

H=12​A∑𝒒[\displaystyle H=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\bm{q}}\bigl[ V+​(q):ρ⁡(−𝒒)​ρ​(𝒒):\displaystyle V_{+}(q):\rho(-\bm{q})\rho(\bm{q}): (50)
+4V−(q):Sz(−𝒒)Sz(𝒒):],\displaystyle+4V_{-}(q):S^{z}(-\bm{q})S^{z}(\bm{q}):\bigr],

where V±​(q)=[VT​T​(q)±VT​B​(q)]/2V_{\pm}(q)=[V_{TT}(q)\pm V_{TB}(q)]/2. The V−V_{-} term is identically zero only at d=0d=0. For d>0d>0, it creates and scatters pseudospin particle-hole pairs about an in-plane polarized Slater determinant. Figure 14(d) illustrates one correlation correction generated by the V−V_{-} term. It also makes clear why the total filling νT=1\nu_{T}=1 does not provide a finite-dd Pauli-blocking theorem: one pseudospin orbital is full, while its orthogonal pseudospin orbital remains available.

XI.2 Precise Hartree-Fock theorem

The theorem established below is deliberately narrow and exact within its stated approximation. For the spatially uniform HF variational manifold at T=0T=0,

ℳuHF={∏m[u​cm​T†+v​cm​B†]​|0⟩:|u|2+|v|2=1},\mathcal{M}_{\rm uHF}=\left\{\prod_{m}\left[uc^{\dagger}_{mT}+vc^{\dagger}_{mB}\right]|0\rangle:\ |u|^{2}+|v|^{2}=1\right\}, (51)

the interlayer Fock matrix element XD​(d)X_{D}(d) [defined in Eq. (54)] is strictly positive for every finite dd. The balanced uniform stationary state therefore has nonzero transverse pseudospin. Equivalently,

XD​(d)>0(0≤d<∞)⟹⟨S+⟩uHF≠0.X_{D}(d)>0\quad(0\leq d<\infty)\ \Longrightarrow\ \langle S^{+}\rangle_{\rm uHF}\neq 0. (52)

In terms of the self-consistency condition, Eq. (55) below, the content of the statement is that a solution with nonzero polarization exists below a temperature XD/4​kBX_{D}/4k_{B} that is positive at every finite dd, and that it has the positive HF gap XDX_{D}. Equation (52) excludes a finite-dd transition from the uniform HF coherent saddle to a uniform HF incoherent saddle. It does not rule out a transition driven by correlations generated by the V−V_{-} term in Eq. (50), since uniform HF neglects these effects. This statement is restricted to spatially uniform HF. It does not exclude a density-wave instability within unrestricted HF or a transition driven by correlations beyond HF.

XI.3 Analytic exchange field, gap, and transition temperature

Let P=2​|⟨cm​T†​cm​B⟩|P=2|\langle c_{mT}^{\dagger}c_{mB}\rangle|. The two uniform HF levels are

ϵS=−XD​P2,ϵA​S=+XD​P2,\epsilon_{S}=-\frac{X_{D}P}{2},\qquad\epsilon_{AS}=+\frac{X_{D}P}{2}, (53)

where

XD​(d)\displaystyle X_{D}(d) =∫d2​q(2​π)2VT​B(q)e−q2ℓ2/2\displaystyle=\int\frac{d^{2}q}{(2\pi)^{2}}V_{TB}(q)e^{-q^{2}\ell^{2}/2}
=EC∫0∞dxe−x2/2−(d/ℓ)x\displaystyle=E_{\rm C}\int_{0}^{\infty}dx\,e^{-x^{2}/2-(d/\ell)x}

with EC=e2/(ϵ​ℓ)E_{\rm C}=e^{2}/(\epsilon\ell). We denote the HF quasiparticle splitting between the antisymmetric and symmetric levels by Δ⁡(T)≡ϵA​S−ϵS=XD​(d)​P​(T)\Delta(T)\equiv\epsilon_{AS}-\epsilon_{S}=X_{D}(d)P(T). Since the integrand is positive, XD​(d)>0X_{D}(d)>0 for all finite dd. This is the q=0q=0 interlayer exchange kernel of the earlier HF literature [13, 15, 31]; the closed form appears as the interlayer exchange constant in Ref. [32].

At filling one, the occupation difference of the two levels gives

P=tanh⁡(XD​P4​kB​T).P=\tanh\!\left(\frac{X_{D}P}{4k_{B}T}\right). (55)

The uniform HF free energy per flux quantum is

ℱ⁡(P)=XD4​P2−2​kB​T​ln⁡[2​cosh⁡(XD​P4​kB​T)].{\cal F}(P)=\frac{X_{D}}{4}P^{2}-2k_{B}T\ln\left[2\cosh\left(\frac{X_{D}P}{4k_{B}T}\right)\right]. (56)

The uniform HF solution follows immediately:

P(T=0)=1,Δ(T=0)=XD,kB​TcHF=XD4.\begin{gathered}P(T=0)=1,\qquad\Delta(T=0)=X_{D},\\ k_{B}T_{c}^{\rm HF}=\frac{X_{D}}{4}.\end{gathered} (57)

There is no numerical self-consistency problem and no fitting parameter. The exchange gap and thermal scale are fixed by the same LLL integral. At d=0d=0 the thermal scale reduces to the HF transition temperature of the ν=1\nu=1 spin ferromagnet [65]. As there, TcHFT_{c}^{\rm HF} is a mean-field amplitude scale and not the temperature of the physical transition (Appendix H); it is shown in Fig. 15.

For δ=d/ℓ\delta=d/\ell, the two asymptotic limits are

XDEC\displaystyle\frac{X_{D}}{E_{\rm C}} =π2−δ+12​π2​δ2−δ33+O⁡(δ4),\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}-\delta+\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}\delta^{2}-\frac{\delta^{3}}{3}+O(\delta^{4}), δ≪1,\displaystyle\delta\ll 1, (58)
XDEC\displaystyle\frac{X_{D}}{E_{\rm C}} =1δ​(1−1δ2+3δ4−15δ6+⋯),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\delta}\left(1-\frac{1}{\delta^{2}}+\frac{3}{\delta^{4}}-\frac{15}{\delta^{6}}+\cdots\right), δ≫1.\displaystyle\delta\gg 1. (59)

Thus

Δ=4​kB​TcHF=e2ϵ​d​(1−ℓ2d2+3​ℓ4d4+⋯).\Delta=4k_{B}T_{c}^{\rm HF}=\frac{e^{2}}{\epsilon d}\left(1-\frac{\ell^{2}}{d^{2}}+3\frac{\ell^{4}}{d^{4}}+\cdots\right). (60)

The large-distance uniform-HF coherence scale is Coulombic. This is a property of the HF exchange integral, which omits the intralayer correlations that dominate at large dd. The true large-dd scale is not known (Sec. XII.3). Figure 16 compares the exact result with the two expansions.

XI.4 Goldstone mode and coherent density wave

The coherent state breaks relative U⁡(1)U(1) and has a Goldstone mode. The LLL time-dependent HF result [13, 14] is

ℏ​ω​(Q)=Bδ​(Q)​Kδ​(Q),Q=q​ℓ,\hbar\omega(Q)=\sqrt{B_{\delta}(Q)K_{\delta}(Q)},\qquad Q=q\ell, (61)

where

Bδ​(Q)EC\displaystyle\frac{B_{\delta}(Q)}{E_{\rm C}} =ΓD​(0)−ΓD​(Q)EC,\displaystyle=\frac{\Gamma_{D}(0)-\Gamma_{D}(Q)}{E_{\rm C}},
Kδ​(Q)EC\displaystyle\frac{K_{\delta}(Q)}{E_{\rm C}} =ΓD​(0)−ΓS​(Q)+Dδ​(Q)EC,\displaystyle=\frac{\Gamma_{D}(0)-\Gamma_{S}(Q)+D_{\delta}(Q)}{E_{\rm C}},
ΓD​(Q)EC\displaystyle\frac{\Gamma_{D}(Q)}{E_{\rm C}} =∫0∞dxe−x2/2−δxJ0(Qx),\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}dx\,e^{-x^{2}/2-\delta x}J_{0}(Qx),
ΓS​(Q)EC\displaystyle\frac{\Gamma_{S}(Q)}{E_{\rm C}} =π2e−Q2/4I0(Q2/4),\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}e^{-Q^{2}/4}I_{0}(Q^{2}/4),
Dδ​(Q)EC\displaystyle\frac{D_{\delta}(Q)}{E_{\rm C}} =e−Q2/21−e−δ​QQ.\displaystyle=e^{-Q^{2}/2}\frac{1-e^{-\delta Q}}{Q}. (62)

At long wavelength,

ℏ​ω​(q)=ℏ​v​q+O⁡(q2),\hbar\omega(q)=\hbar vq+O(q^{2}), (63)

with

ℏ​vEC​ℓ=12​[(1+δ2)​F​(δ)−δ]​[F⁡(δ)−π/2+δ],\frac{\hbar v}{E_{\rm C}\ell}=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{[(1+\delta^{2})F(\delta)-\delta][F(\delta)-\sqrt{\pi/2}+\delta]}, (64)

where F=XD/ECF=X_{D}/E_{\rm C}. At d=0d=0 the SU(2)-symmetric ferromagnet has the expected quadratic mode. The dispersion is shown in Fig. 17.

The finite-qq zero has a definite symmetry meaning. Define

Ψ=⟨S+​(𝟎)⟩,Φ𝑸=⟨Sz​(𝑸)⟩.\Psi=\langle S^{+}(\bm{0})\rangle,\qquad\Phi_{\bm{Q}}=\langle S^{z}(\bm{Q})\rangle. (65)

The uniform (111)(111) state has Ψ≠0\Psi\neq 0 and Φ𝑸=0\Phi_{\bm{Q}}=0. At the roton transition the |Φ𝑸0|2|\Phi_{\bm{Q}_{0}}|^{2} coefficient changes sign. The |Ψ|2|\Psi|^{2} coefficient remains negative because XDX_{D} remains positive. Layer interchange combined with a relative-phase rotation takes Sz→−SzS^{z}\to-S^{z} at fixed Ψ\Psi, so no term cubic in Φ\Phi is allowed and the transition can be continuous. The modulation is then small just beyond the instability, and the local transverse pseudospin 1−mz2\sqrt{1-m_{z}^{2}} stays close to its uniform value. The ordered state is therefore

Ψ≠0,δ​nT​(𝒓)=−δ​nB​(𝒓)∝cos⁡(𝒒0⋅𝒓+θ).\Psi\neq 0,\qquad\delta n_{T}(\bm{r})=-\delta n_{B}(\bm{r})\propto\cos(\bm{q}_{0}\cdot\bm{r}+\theta). (66)

Here 𝐪0=𝐐0/ℓ\mathbf{q}_{0}=\mathbf{Q}_{0}/\ell is the physical modulation wave vector. This is a coherent charge-density wave (CDW). In exciton language it is a supersolid. Unrestricted HF calculations confirm this structure [34]. The finite-qq instability is not, within HF, a transition to an incoherent state. It is a transition from a spatially uniform condensate to a spatially modulated condensate.

XI.5 Roton condensation as an excitonic supersolid

The finite-qq instability has an independent order parameter and an independent broken symmetry. A minimal long-wavelength free energy for the uniform coherence Ψ\Psi and the roton field Φ𝑸0\Phi_{\bm{Q}_{0}} is

ℰ=\displaystyle{\cal E}={} rΨ​|Ψ|2+uΨ​|Ψ|4+rQ​|Φ𝑸0|2\displaystyle r_{\Psi}|\Psi|^{2}+u_{\Psi}|\Psi|^{4}+r_{Q}|\Phi_{\bm{Q}_{0}}|^{2} (67)
+uQ​|Φ𝑸0|4+uΨ​Q​|Ψ|2​|Φ𝑸0|2+⋯.\displaystyle+u_{Q}|\Phi_{\bm{Q}_{0}}|^{4}+u_{\Psi Q}|\Psi|^{2}|\Phi_{\bm{Q}_{0}}|^{2}+\cdots.

Within the uniform-HF continuation, the coherent saddle has rΨ<0r_{\Psi}<0 and rQ>0r_{Q}>0. The roton transition is the point where rQr_{Q} changes sign. The positive uniform exchange integral keeps the uniform-HF transverse field nonzero at every finite separation; it does not determine the renormalized coefficient after the higher-order correlation diagrams [e.g., Fig. 14(d)] are included. The modulated HF phase has two independent broken symmetries: relative U⁡(1)U(1) from Ψ≠0\Psi\neq 0, and translation from Φ𝑸0≠0\Phi_{\bm{Q}_{0}}\neq 0.

The layer-density modulation in Eq. (66) is out of phase between the two layers. Consequently it is a pseudospin-density wave rather than a total-charge density wave. This is precisely the modulation favored by the bilayer Coulomb interaction: the large Hartree cost of total charge modulation is avoided, while exchange energy is retained through the nonzero transverse pseudospin component. The coherent CDW found in unrestricted HF calculations [30, 33] has this structure, as do the unidirectional coherent CDW of Brey and Fertig [34], which in the lowest Landau level gives way to a coherent Wigner crystal near d/ℓ≃1.65d/\ell\simeq 1.65, and the excitonic CDW found for electron-hole layers by Chen and Quinn [35]. That the HF ground state beyond the instability is a coherent pseudospin-density wave was noted explicitly by Joglekar and MacDonald [31].

The Hartree-Fock conclusion is straightforward. A vanishing roton energy establishes an instability of the uniform saddle, not the vanishing of its uniform exchange integral. The unrestricted-HF branch has nonzero Ψ\Psi together with Φ𝑸0\Phi_{\bm{Q}_{0}}: a uniform (111)(111) condensate becomes a modulated coherent condensate. In exciton language, it is an excitonic supersolid. This coexistence of phase coherence and crystalline order is the defining supersolid structure emphasized for electron-hole bilayers by Joglekar, Balatsky, and Das Sarma [53]; the present quantum-Hall problem supplies a microscopic pseudospin-density-wave realization.

The distinction resolves a simple apparent puzzle. The roton collapses near d/ℓ∼1d/\ell\sim 1, while the interlayer exchange integral remains positive and has a long 1/d1/d tail. There is no conflict because these are different channels. The roton is a finite-wave-vector density channel; XDX_{D} is the uniform transverse-coherence channel. The former determines the loss of translation invariance. The latter determines the existence of interlayer phase coherence.

One argument beyond HF has been offered for the conventional identification. A Gaussian fluctuation expansion about the uniform saddle finds the renormalized order parameter and stiffness driven toward zero as the roton softens [31]. Such an expansion necessarily diverges at the instability of the saddle about which it is performed. The divergence shows that the uniform saddle is the wrong starting point beyond the instability. It cannot by itself decide whether coherence survives in the modulated state.

XI.6 Relation to earlier theory and experiment

The original theory of the (111)(111) state and its pseudospin representation established the basic structure of the problem [36, 13, 14, 54, 15]. The Chern–Simons formulation [66], the theory of charged vortices and merons [15, 67], and the Hartree-Fock density-wave solutions [30, 33] give complementary descriptions of the same coherent quantum Hall state. The present account is more explicit. The projected filled-band structure makes the uniform HF equation analytic at arbitrary separation. The collective mode in Eq. (61) and its softening are those of Refs. [13, 14, 30]. The stiffness in Eq. (104) is that of Ref. [15] evaluated in closed form. The exchange gap is the q=0q=0 exchange kernel of the same literature, with the closed form given in Ref. [32]. The closed formula for the HF amplitude scale at d>0d>0, Eq. (106), has to our knowledge not been written down before; its d=0d=0 limit is the result of Ref. [65]. The closed formula in Eq. (106), the gap in Eq. (105), and the mode in Eq. (61) are determined by the same exchange integral. This produces a complete one-parameter solution of the uniform theory.

The experimental record is equally direct. The zero-bias tunneling anomaly measures the low-energy interlayer coherent response [56]. The in-plane-field experiment measures the dispersing neutral collective mode [57]. Hall drag demonstrates the charged quantum Hall response [58, 59], while counterflow identifies the neutral superfluid channel [60, 61]. Subsequent experiments demonstrated exciton transport and perfect Coulomb drag [63, 64]. These phenomena are naturally unified by the pseudospin-ferromagnet description rather than treated as separate effects.

The analytic 1/d1/d exchange field gives a useful perspective on the rapid disappearance of strong coherence signatures with increasing effective layer separation. Within uniform HF, an apparent boundary follows when TcHFT_{c}^{\rm HF} reaches the experimental temperature or disorder scale. This is distinct from the finite-qq instability of the uniform HF saddle. Neither observation licenses an exact finite-dd conclusion for the interacting LLL bilayer.

XI.7 Phase structure

The zero-tunneling uniform-HF problem consequently has a sharp theorem: its coherent saddle exists for every finite d/ℓd/\ell, because XD​(d)>0X_{D}(d)>0. An unrestricted-HF analysis adds a distinct finite-qq instability of that uniform saddle and produces a translation-breaking coherent density wave [34]. The d/ℓ→∞d/\ell\rightarrow\infty limit has XD→0X_{D}\rightarrow 0 and decoupled layers. This is the Hartree-Fock phase structure; it is not an exact phase diagram of the finite-dd LLL Hamiltonian.

The finite-temperature structure is equally clear within HF. The interaction-generated amplitude scale is TcHF​(d)T_{c}^{\rm HF}(d) in Eq. (106). At a fixed temperature this produces an apparent critical separation. The phase-mode stiffness and vortex dynamics determine the long-distance ordering behavior and the actual Kosterlitz-Thouless transition temperature, while the microscopic HF amplitude scale is set by the exchange integral. The HF amplitude scale and the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition temperature describe distinct aspects of coherence: exchange sets the local amplitude, while phase fluctuations determine long-distance order. Thus, they are not competing explanations.

XI.8 Analytic phase portrait

The solution of the projected problem may be summarized by one positive function, F⁡(δ)=XD/ECF(\delta)=X_{D}/E_{\rm C}. It decreases monotonically from F⁡(0)=π/2F(0)=\sqrt{\pi/2} to F⁡(δ≫1)=1/δ+O⁡(δ−3)F(\delta\gg 1)=1/\delta+O(\delta^{-3}). Every uniform thermodynamic quantity follows from this function. The exchange gap is Δ/EC=F\Delta/E_{\rm C}=F, the amplitude-transition temperature is kB​TcHF/EC=F/4k_{B}T_{c}^{\rm HF}/E_{\rm C}=F/4, the condensation energy is F/4F/4 per flux quantum, and the sound velocity follows from Eq. (64). The separation dependence of the coherent state is therefore analytic throughout the full range of d/ℓd/\ell.

This HF structure is qualitatively different from a weak-coupling Cooper instability. In BCS theory, a small gap is generated by a logarithmic instability and is exponentially sensitive to the interaction. Here the HF gap is a direct Coulomb exchange matrix element in a filled Landau level. The common phrase “excitonic pairing” is useful for identifying the broken relative-U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry, but it should not obscure this basic difference in scale. The uniform-HF exchange gap has no BCS exponential. Its large-dd behavior is fixed by electrostatics and by the LLL form factor. This is the strong-coupling mean-field description continued to all dd. Whether it survives at large dd, where each layer is separately correlated, is a question beyond HF (Sec. XII.3).

The full HF phase portrait contains a uniform coherent region, a coherent modulated region, and the asymptotic decoupled limit. In the uniform region, the only broken symmetry is relative U⁡(1)U(1). In the modulated region, both relative U⁡(1)U(1) and translation are broken. The two order parameters are experimentally distinguishable. Interlayer tunneling and counterflow detect the transverse pseudospin order Ψ\Psi. A density-sensitive probe detects the finite-QQ pseudospin component Φ𝑸\Phi_{\bm{Q}}. Within HF, a complete characterization of the roton-condensed state would therefore exhibit both a phase-coherent response and a density-wave Bragg component.

The same organization clarifies the meaning of the Hall response. Within HF, the total charge sector of the uniform state remains incompressible and carries the integer Hall conductance. The HF quasiparticle gap is XD≃0.60​ECX_{D}\simeq 0.60E_{\rm C} at the roton instability: the neutral mode softens, but the HF charge gap does not collapse. The neutral sector supports the pseudospin Goldstone mode. When the coherent density wave forms, the order parameter modulates the relative density, not the total charge, and near the onset, where the modulation is small, the HF gap remains close to XDX_{D}. To that extent the quantum Hall charge response and the neutral supersolid response coexist within HF, and the state near the onset is the bilayer analog of a supersolid built from a neutral condensate embedded in a charged topological fluid. The charge response of the fully developed modulated states, which have charged excitations of their own, is a separate question that this argument does not settle [34].

The analytic result gives a sharp diagnostic inside uniform HF. A finite-separation loss of the uniform-HF coherence amplitude would require a zero of XD​(d)X_{D}(d); Eq. (54) rules this out. A finite-qq zero instead diagnoses the loss of spatial uniformity. The unrestricted-HF density wave condenses in a coherent background [34]. These statements do not constrain a correlation-driven loss of coherence beyond HF.

At large separation the distinction between a small scale and a vanished scale is essential. The HF 1/d1/d tail can easily fall below an experimental base temperature, giving the visual appearance of a transition at a finite d/ℓd/\ell. The same tail remains finite in the T=0T=0 projected HF equation. The apparent boundary and the zero-temperature analytic continuation are therefore both expected features of the same exchange physics. One is controlled by a laboratory temperature; the other by the strict ground-state limit.

XII The two problems compared

Sections III–X and Sec. XI treat one phenomenon at the two ends of the range of magnetic field. This section compares them. It contains no new calculation. Its purpose is to state what the two problems have in common, where they differ, and what the results of one do and do not imply for the other. We return to the four questions posed in Sec. II D: (1) Does mean-field theory predict interlayer coherence at every separation? (2) How does the coherence scale depend on dd at large separation, and does the mean-field result survive corrections? (3) Is the evolution from small to large dd a phase transition or a crossover from strong to weak coupling? (4) What is the relation between interlayer coherence and states that break translation symmetry?

XII.1 Mean-field theory: one diagram, two kinds of scale

Mean-field theory answers the first question in the same way in both problems, and for the same reason. The bare interlayer interaction has one sign at every wave vector, so the exchange self-energy that it generates cannot vanish. At zero field the kernel of the gap equation is positive and the instability exists at every rsr_{s} and dd (Sec. V). At νT=1\nu_{T}=1 the exchange integral is positive at every finite dd [Eq. (52)]. In both, the scale falls off only algebraically with the separation,

kB​Tc(0)\displaystyle k_{B}T_{c}^{(0)} ∝ℏ​vFd\displaystyle\propto\frac{\hbar v_{F}}{d} (zero field, fixed ​rs),\displaystyle(\text{zero field, fixed }r_{s}),
kB​TcHF\displaystyle k_{B}T_{c}^{\rm HF} →e24​ϵ​d\displaystyle\to\frac{e^{2}}{4\epsilon d} (νT=1),\displaystyle(\nu_{T}=1), (68)

by Eqs. (21) and (60). The origin of the power is also common. The interlayer interaction transfers wave vectors q≲1/dq\lesssim 1/d, and nothing in mean-field theory screens it: at zero field this confines the pairing to within ℏ​vF/d\hbar v_{F}/d of the Fermi surface, and at νT=1\nu_{T}=1 it removes the form factor of the Landau level from the leading term of the exchange integral (Appendix J).

The two scales are nevertheless of different kinds. At zero field ℏ​vF/d\hbar v_{F}/d is the prefactor of an exponential, exp[−π3/2/(2α)]\exp[-\pi^{3/2}/(2\sqrt{\alpha})], which is produced by the Cooper logarithm together with the logarithm of the unscreened kernel. At νT=1\nu_{T}=1 the gap is a Coulomb exchange energy with no exponential (Sec. XI.8). In the language of the crossover, the mean-field theory at νT=1\nu_{T}=1 is a strong-coupling description continued to all dd, whereas at zero field the same approximation contains the weak-coupling instability of the Fermi surface at one end and the two-body bound state at the other (Appendix E.7).

The zero-field counterpart of the calculation of Sec. XI within mean-field theory is the Hartree-Fock theory of interlayer coherence in balanced electron-electron and electron-hole bilayers developed by Zhu and Das Sarma [11]. That work obtains the zero-temperature coherence phase diagram and the finite-temperature onset by solving the self-consistent HF gap equation. The common conclusion is structural: interlayer Coulomb exchange produces a spontaneous transverse pseudospin field and a finite HF coherence scale without interlayer tunneling. The LLL calculation of Sec. XI is the analytically soluble quantum-Hall specialization of this Hartree-Fock mechanism. The distinction in scope is equally clear. At zero field the kernel is set by the Fermi surface, whereas at νT=1\nu_{T}=1 it is fixed by the LLL form factor and guiding-center algebra. In both cases the result is a Hartree-Fock statement, not an assertion that the corresponding finite-coupling many-body problem is exhausted by HF. One difference is instructive. At zero field the HF coherence of the electron-electron bilayer, unlike that of the electron-hole bilayer of Secs. III–X, exists only for rsr_{s} above a critical value that depends on dd [11], whereas in the LLL the kinetic energy is quenched and the uniform-HF coherent saddle exists at every finite dd.

XII.2 The fate of the mean-field tail at zero field

At zero field the second question has an answer. The layers are compressible, and their response screens the interlayer interaction. Static screening reduces the coupling to λs∝rs​(aB/d)2\lambda_{s}\propto r_{s}(a_{B}/d)^{2} [Eq. (23)], and the transition temperature becomes exponentially small in d2d^{2} instead of algebraic in dd. Within the ladder approximation dynamical screening appears to undo most of this, through the plasmon-induced coupling λpl∝d−1/2\lambda_{\rm pl}\propto d^{-1/2}. But that coupling is cancelled at second order by the crossed rung, and what is left of it is known [Eqs. (40) and (41)]. The result is rigorous for the leading exponent as rs→0r_{s}\to 0 at fixed dd [Eq. (43)], and for d→∞d\to\infty at fixed rsr_{s} it holds under the assumptions stated with Eq. (45). In both limits the instability is present, and its scale decreases smoothly, as a Gaussian in dd for d≫aBd\gg a_{B}. A first-order transition to a different state is not excluded by the theory (Appendix E.8). Between the limits the existence of the instability at every dd is a property of the RPA ladder and is not established for the full problem (Sec. IX). The 1/d1/d law of mean-field theory is an artifact of leaving out the response of the layers.

XII.3 Beyond Hartree-Fock at νT=1\nu_{T}=1: expectations

Nothing in this problem is known in a controlled way beyond HF. The field-theoretic treatments are uncontrolled, and the finite-size numerics [68, 69, 70, 71] are limited by size and geometry. With that caveat we state our own expectation. It is a conjecture, not a result of this paper.

We expect HF to be qualitatively right in its main conclusion: there is no zero-temperature transition at a finite d/ℓd/\ell at which interlayer coherence is lost. The evolution from small to large separation is a crossover from strong to weak coupling, the analog of the crossover from Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) to BCS pairing. This is the picture suggested by experiments on graphene double layers [72] and by the description of the large-dd state as a paired state of composite fermions connected to the exciton condensate [73, 74, 75].

We expect HF to be quantitatively wrong at large d/ℓd/\ell. The 1/d1/d tail of Eq. (60) neglects intralayer correlations. At large separation each layer is a composite-fermion liquid, and interlayer coherence is a weak-coupling pairing instability of these liquids with a scale far below e2/(ϵ​d)e^{2}/(\epsilon d). We expect this scale to be exponentially small, so that the true coherence scale falls rapidly for d/ℓ≳1d/\ell\gtrsim 1 and mimics a transition. The large-dd law is not settled: gauge-fluctuation treatments give an algebraic gap, Δ∝1/d2\Delta\propto 1/d^{2} up to logarithms, strongly reduced by pair breaking [76, 77]. A crossover without a transition leaves no room for a phase of broken translation symmetry. In this scenario the density-wave states of HF, the supersolid included, do not survive as distinct phases; that they are likely preempted in the lowest Landau level was already noted in Ref. [34].

The crossover is not the only possibility. A sequence of distinct paired states separated by transitions was proposed in Ref. [78], with an intermediate (3,3,−1)(3,3,-1) state arising from px−i​pyp_{x}-ip_{y} interlayer pairing of composite fermions. That state has a Hall drag opposite in sign to that of the (111)(111) state. No such sign reversal has been reported: the measured Hall drag rises from zero to the quantized (111)(111) value [58, 59]. The px+i​pyp_{x}+ip_{y} channel favored in trial-wave-function studies [79] is the one connected to the exciton condensate [73, 75].

XII.4 What the zero-field results imply for νT=1\nu_{T}=1, and what they do not

The expectation of Sec. XII.3 resembles the zero-field result of Sec. XII.2 in its central element: a scale at large dd far below the mean-field one, with the instability still present. The zero-field theory is a case in which the failure of the mean-field tail is derived, rigorously for the leading exponent as rs→0r_{s}\to 0 and conditionally for d→∞d\to\infty, and it identifies the mechanism. The 1/d1/d tail is a property of the exchange integral with the bare interaction, and it does not survive once the carriers of each layer respond to the interlayer interaction. At νT=1\nu_{T}=1 the same ingredients are expected at large dd: each layer is then expected to be a compressible composite-fermion liquid (Sec. XII.3), and the interlayer interaction is confined to q≲1/d≪1/ℓq\lesssim 1/d\ll 1/\ell. The zero-field result is consistent with the expectation that the HF tail of Eq. (60) is not the true law at large dd. The other elements of the expectation, the absence of a transition and the crossover from strong coupling, are not derived at zero field either; there they rest on the estimates of Appendix E.7.

The zero-field result does not establish the expectation, and it does not determine the law that replaces the tail. Four differences prevent the argument from being carried over. First, neither controlled limit of the zero-field theory has an image in the lowest Landau level. By Eq. (1) the projection sets rs=2​κLLr_{s}=2\kappa_{\rm LL} to zero without making the interaction weak, and d/aB=κLL​d/ℓd/a_{B}=\kappa_{\rm LL}\,d/\ell then vanishes as well, whereas the Gaussian law, Tc∝exp⁡[−const​(d/aB)2]T_{c}\propto\exp[-\mathrm{const}\,(d/a_{B})^{2}] at leading exponential order [Eq. (45)], requires d≫aBd\gg a_{B}. Moreover the zero-field system at small rsr_{s} is weakly paired at every dd, while the νT=1\nu_{T}=1 state at small dd is strongly coupled. Second, the zero-field result at large dd rests on each layer being a Fermi liquid, whose static response is fixed by its compressibility and its quasiparticle parameters, and is itself conditional. The low-energy theory of the half-filled Landau level involves gauge fluctuations that have no counterpart at zero field, and the treatments that include them find an algebraic and not an exponential law [76, 77]. Third, on the weak-pairing side at zero field the normal state from which the instability develops is the same pair of Fermi liquids at every dd, whereas at νT=1\nu_{T}=1 the state at small dd is an incompressible quantum Hall state, whose HF description is exact at d=0d=0, and the compressible layers appear only at large dd. Fourth, the pairing at zero field is in the ss-wave channel, while in the composite-fermion description of Refs. [78, 79] the paired states discussed in Sec. XII.3 are pp-wave. The comparison is therefore a precedent and not a proof. It shows that one element of the scenario conjectured at νT=1\nu_{T}=1, the failure of the mean-field tail, occurs in the neighboring problem in the limits in which it can be checked. It is not evidence about the νT=1\nu_{T}=1 system itself.

XII.5 Broken translation symmetry and supersolids

In both problems states of broken translation symmetry appear, and in both they must be distinguished from the loss of coherence. At νT=1\nu_{T}=1 the statement is sharp within HF theory. The roton instability at d/ℓ≃1.175d/\ell\simeq 1.175 leads to a coherent pseudospin-density wave, which has both orders and is an excitonic supersolid (Sec. XI.5), and unrestricted HF theory finds a coherent Wigner crystal at larger separation [34]. Whether these phases exist beyond HF is not known; our expectation is that they do not (Sec. XII.3). At zero field the crystalline phases lie at large rsr_{s}: the Wigner crystal of an isolated layer, and the crystal of dipolar excitons, which requires rs≳10r_{s}\gtrsim 10 and d≳13​aBd\gtrsim 13\,a_{B} and gives way to the dilute superfluid at still lower density (Appendix E.7). The zero-field theory of this paper assumes a liquid and does not describe them (Sec. X). That a crystalline state of the electron-hole bilayer can retain the exciton coherence, and is then a supersolid, was proposed in Ref. [53].

The structural point is the same in both problems. Translation symmetry and the relative U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry are independent, their order parameters are independent [Eq. (67)], and an instability in the density channel is not by itself an instability of the coherence. At νT=1\nu_{T}=1 this is the content of result (vii) of the Introduction. At zero field the corresponding question, whether the crystalline phases of Fig. 21 retain the exciton coherence, is outside the theory of this paper.

XII.6 The separation as the tuning parameter

At zero field there are two crossovers between the condensation of tightly bound excitons and weak pairing, one as a function of rsr_{s} at fixed dd and one as a function of dd at fixed rsr_{s} (Appendix E.7 and Fig. 21). For rs<(2/g)1/2r_{s}<(2/g)^{1/2} the binding energy is below the Fermi energy at every dd and there is no crossover. At νT=1\nu_{T}=1 the density and the field are tied by the filling factor, and only the crossover in dd can exist: d/ℓ=kF​dd/\ell=k_{F}d is varied at fixed νT\nu_{T}. The small-dd end is the strong-coupling one, where HF theory is exact at d=0d=0. The large-dd end is the one at which we expect weak coupling (Sec. XII.3); a crossover of this kind has been reported in graphene double layers [72].

In both problems the physical transition at finite temperature is of Kosterlitz-Thouless type and is bounded by the phase stiffness, and the mean-field scale is a different quantity. At zero field the bound is kB​TKT≤g​EF/8k_{B}T_{\rm KT}\leq gE_{F}/8 [Eq. (84)], and the mean-field TcT_{c} approaches the transition temperature only on the weak-pairing side. At νT=1\nu_{T}=1 the phase stiffness bound is (π/2)​ρs(\pi/2)\rho_{s}, which is 0.0097​EC0.0097\,E_{\rm C} at d/ℓ=1d/\ell=1, a factor of 17 below kB​TcHFk_{B}T_{c}^{\rm HF}, and which falls off as 1/d31/d^{3} within HF theory (Appendix H), faster than the 1/d1/d decay of the zero-temperature exchange gap XDX_{D}. In a measurement at fixed temperature a scale that decreases smoothly with dd produces an apparent critical separation in either problem. This is a thermal effect and not a transition of the ground state.

XII.7 Experiment

The experimental situation is the reverse of the theoretical one. At νT=1\nu_{T}=1 interlayer coherence, the collective mode, quantized Hall drag, and counterflow transport have all been observed (Sec. XI.6), and the theory beyond mean field is uncontrolled. At zero field the theory has controlled limits, but in them the transition temperature is far too small to be observed (Sec. X). The interlayer coherence observed in the experiments is in the regime in which EBE_{B} is comparable to EFE_{F} or larger (Sec. X), where neither limit applies.

XII.8 Status of the results

Table 6 lists the main results of the paper with the kind of statement that each of them is. The entries for the two problems should not be read across: a controlled result at zero field does not raise the status of the corresponding conjecture at νT=1\nu_{T}=1.

XIII Conclusion

Exciton superfluidity in bilayers has been treated here at zero magnetic field and at νT=1\nu_{T}=1 as one problem in two settings. In both, mean-field theory gives interlayer coherence at every layer separation, with a scale that decays as 1/d1/d. The two parts of the paper establish what can be said beyond that statement in each case, and the answers are of different kinds because the problems differ in whether they have a small parameter.

Zero field. Replacing the single electron layer by an electron-hole bilayer changes the problem of pairing by the dynamically screened Coulomb interaction in three ways. Within the RPA the interaction in the pairing channel is attractive at all Matsubara frequencies, so in the ladder approximation the instability exists without any balance between attraction and repulsion. The finite range dd of the interlayer interaction limits the momentum transfer to 1/d1/d, which confines the pairing to energies within ℏ​vF/d\hbar v_{F}/d of the Fermi surface and makes the frequency sum converge, as 1/ωc1/\omega_{c} above the plasmon scale ℏ​Ω∗=2​g​EF​Ed\hbar\Omega_{*}=\sqrt{2gE_{F}E_{d}}, so no cutoff has to be chosen. And the leading vertex correction (e.g., the crossed-rung correction), which in the single layer is unknown and of order unity, can be computed at large separation, where it is still of order unity.

The ladder theory has a simple analytic core. The unscreened interaction gives a transition temperature that decays as 1/d1/d, static screening one that decays as exp⁡(−const​d2)\exp(-{\rm const}\,d^{2}), and dynamic screening one that decays as exp⁡(−const​d)\exp(-{\rm const}\sqrt{d}) through a plasmon-induced coupling λpl≃0.109​rs​(Ed/EF)1/2\lambda_{\rm pl}\simeq 0.109\,r_{s}(E_{d}/E_{F})^{1/2}, and the full numerical solution confirms these forms. The plasmon-induced coupling, however, comes entirely from the region of frequency and momentum in which the carriers are slow compared with the plasmons, where Migdal’s theorem fails and the adiabatic limit takes its place.

Beyond the ladder, the following is established. (i) At second order the crossed rung cancels the plasmon-induced coupling. The sum of the two diagrams is given by the identity of Eq. (35); it is less than 8% of λpl\lambda_{\rm pl} in the whole range computed and about one percent of it or less for kF​d>2k_{F}d>2. (ii) The remainder is known in both limits. It is C3​(d)​rs3C_{3}(d)\,r_{s}^{3} for rs→0r_{s}\to 0 at fixed dd, with C3C_{3} in closed form [Eq. (93)], and Jw​g​rs4​(aB/d)7/2J_{w}\sqrt{g}\,r_{s}^{4}(a_{B}/d)^{7/2} with Jw=3.441×10−4J_{w}=3.441\times 10^{-4} for d→∞d\to\infty at fixed rsr_{s}, and the numerical results converge to both. The second-order dynamical contribution to ln⁡Tc\ln T_{c}, which in the ladder is λpl/λs2\lambda_{\rm pl}/\lambda_{s}^{2}, independent of rsr_{s} and equal to 22.6​(d/aB)7/222.6\,(d/a_{B})^{7/2} at large dd, becomes R⁡(d)​rsR(d)\,r_{s} at small rsr_{s}, with R=1.56R=1.56 at d=aBd=a_{B} and R∝aB/dR\propto a_{B}/d at large dd. (iii) For linearized dispersion and Gaussian density fluctuations the cancellation is exact at every order. (iv) For rs→0r_{s}\to 0 at fixed dd the leading exponent is that of first-order perturbation theory in the statically screened interaction. The corrections to ln⁡Tc\ln T_{c} are of order ln⁡(1/rs)\ln(1/r_{s}) and come from the static crossed rung and the intralayer terms.

What is not established is the cancellation of the dynamical terms beyond second order when the dispersion has curvature. The result for d→∞d\to\infty at any rsr_{s} in the liquid phase, ln⁡Tc≃−(m∗/m)​(16​g3/2/π​rs)​(d/aB)2\ln T_{c}\simeq-(m^{*}/m)(16g^{3/2}/\pi r_{s})(d/a_{B})^{2}, with EB/EFE_{B}/E_{F} as the small parameter when rs≳1r_{s}\gtrsim 1, is conditional on it. It requires that the terms not contained in the static quasiparticle interaction be small compared with λs\lambda_{s}. At second order they are, by the factor λw/λs∝rs3​(aB/d)3/2\lambda_{w}/\lambda_{s}\propto r_{s}^{3}(a_{B}/d)^{3/2}, and beyond second order we assume it. We consider the assumption very likely to be correct, but an evaluation of the third-order terms, or a proof, is needed before the large-dd result can be called exact, and the present work does not resolve the problem at all orders. The prefactor of TcT_{c} has not been calculated in either limit. Between the limits, where the experiments are, the RPA ladder has an instability at every rsr_{s} and dd, but the enhancement of its scale by dynamical screening should not be relied upon.

High field. The zero-tunneling νT=1\nu_{T}=1 bilayer has an analytic uniform LLL Hartree-Fock solution. Its interlayer exchange field is nonzero at every finite separation. The resulting uniform-HF theorem is that its T=0T=0 saddle remains interlayer coherent, with ΔHF=XD\Delta_{\rm HF}=X_{D} and kB​TcHF=XD/4k_{B}T_{c}^{\rm HF}=X_{D}/4. The uniform-HF exchange scale is algebraic at large d/ℓd/\ell. The finite-wave-vector roton instability in unrestricted HF produces a coherent density wave and does not, by itself, set the uniform exchange field to zero. The identification of this instability with the loss of interlayer coherence is not supported by the HF theory on which it rests. Finite-dd LLL correlations are not eliminated by Pauli blocking; they are the physics omitted by HF and determine whether the Hartree-Fock phase structure survives beyond mean field. Our expectation is that the absence of a zero-temperature transition survives, as a crossover from strong to weak coupling, while the corresponding coherence energy scale is expected to decay faster than the uniform-HF 1/d1/d law at large separation.

The two together. The persistence of the coherent mean-field solution at every separation is the part of mean-field theory that survives where it can be tested. It follows from the sign of the bare interlayer interaction, it is exact within HF in both problems, and at zero field it survives for rs→0r_{s}\to 0 and, under the stated assumptions, for d→∞d\to\infty. At νT=1\nu_{T}=1 its survival beyond HF is a conjecture. The 1/d1/d law of mean-field theory is not robust at zero field. In the controlled limits, conditionally for d→∞d\to\infty, it is replaced by a Gaussian once the response of the layers is included, and the larger scale that dynamical screening seems to restore within the ladder is removed by the vertex correction of the same order. At νT=1\nu_{T}=1 we expect the HF tail to fail for the same physical reason, but no controlled calculation shows it, and the law that replaces it is not known. In each problem one common inference is not supported. At zero field it is that dynamical screening greatly enhances the pairing scale: the enhancement is cancelled at second order and is absent in the controlled limits. At νT=1\nu_{T}=1 it is that the softening of the collective mode marks the loss of coherence: within the HF theory on which that inference rests, it marks the onset of a coherent density wave. What is missing differs in kind. At zero field it is the dynamical terms of third and higher order with curvature, the prefactor of TcT_{c}, and a controlled treatment of the intermediate regime and of the crossover to the Bose side. At νT=1\nu_{T}=1 it is any controlled theory of the coherence at large d/ℓd/\ell, where each layer is separately correlated. The comparison made here suggests how the second problem might be approached, from the weak-pairing side. Whether the outcome there is a crossover and not a transition is our conjecture; the comparison does not test it.

Although not relevant to the current theoretical work where all impurity disorder effects are ignored focusing on the pristine bilayers, actual experimental systems invariably have disorder, which would suppress superfluidity in the same way as magnetic impurities suppress ordinary superconductivity since charge disorder in the two layers is unlikely to be identical. Disorder effects have been considered in Refs. [80, 81].
