Appendix D Numerical details

Angular average. For θ<π/2\theta<\pi/2 we substitute q=δ​cosh⁡tq=\delta\cosh t with δ=|k−p|\delta=|k-p|, which makes the integrand smooth for a 1/q1/q interaction, and use 40 Gauss-Legendre points in tt; for θ>π/2\theta>\pi/2 we use 16 points in θ\theta. The result agrees with adaptive quadrature to 10−1010^{-10}.

Momentum cells. The cells are geometric in |ξ||\xi| on each side of the Fermi surface. The kernel is averaged over each cell with four Gauss-Legendre points and over the diagonal cell, which contains the logarithmic singularity, with eight points on each half. The factor 1/(ω2+ξ2)1/(\omega^{2}+\xi^{2}) is integrated analytically, ∫𝑑ξ/(ω2+ξ2)=ω−1​arctan⁡(ξ/ω)\int d\xi/(\omega^{2}+\xi^{2})=\omega^{-1}\arctan(\xi/\omega). The error of the eigenvalue is proportional to the square of the logarithmic cell size. We use 40 and 56 cells per side above the Fermi surface and extrapolate; for the frequency-independent kernels we use 120 cells. With 40, 56, 80, 120, and 170 cells the unscreened eigenvalue at rs=d/aB=1r_{s}=d/a_{B}=1, T=10−2​EFT=10^{-2}E_{F} is 2.6603, 2.6937, 2.7119, 2.7219, and 2.7259, and the extrapolations from successive pairs are 2.7285, 2.7295, and 2.7298.

Frequency blocks. The first ten positive Matsubara frequencies are kept individually and the rest are grouped in blocks whose size grows by a factor 1.5, up to 105​EF10^{5}E_{F}. The kernel is tabulated at 197 values of ν\nu and averaged over each block with four points. The error is proportional to the square of the logarithm of the growth factor, and we extrapolate from growth factors 1.5 and 1.8. At rs=d/aB=1r_{s}=d/a_{B}=1 and T=10−2​EFT=10^{-2}E_{F} the extrapolations from the pairs of growth factors (1.5,1.8)(1.5,1.8) and (1.25,1.5)(1.25,1.5) are 0.76560.7656 and 0.76580.7658. A frequency cutoff ωc\omega_{c}, where one is used, retains exactly the Matsubara frequencies below ωc\omega_{c}.

Tests. For a constant attraction λ=0.25\lambda=0.25 within ±0.2​EF\pm 0.2\,E_{F} of the Fermi surface the code gives TcT_{c} within 0.2%0.2\% of the BCS value 1.134Ωe−1/λ1.134\,\Omega\,e^{-1/\lambda}. For a frequency-independent kernel the Matsubara solver and the direct solution with tanh⁡(ξ/2​T)/2​ξ\tanh(\xi/2T)/2\xi agree to 0.15%0.15\% in η\eta.

Crossed rung. Equations (37) and (39) are evaluated in the variables θ\theta, the angle between 𝐤\mathbf{k} and 𝐤′\mathbf{k}^{\prime}, the polar coordinates (q,φ)(q,\varphi) of 𝐪\mathbf{q}, and ν\nu. The integrand is symmetric under 𝐪→𝚫−𝐪\mathbf{q}\to\bm{\Delta}-\mathbf{q}, and we multiply it by 2​|𝚫−𝐪|2/(q2+|𝚫−𝐪|2)2|\bm{\Delta}-\mathbf{q}|^{2}/(q^{2}+|\bm{\Delta}-\mathbf{q}|^{2}), which leaves the integral unchanged and removes the singularity at 𝐪=𝚫\mathbf{q}=\bm{\Delta}. We use Gauss-Legendre nodes on geometric panels in θ\theta and qq, a geometric grid in ν\nu, and for φ\varphi panels that are refined geometrically toward the zeros of ξ1\xi_{1} and ξ2\xi_{2} and toward the direction of 𝚫\bm{\Delta}. The sum Blad+BcrB_{\rm lad}+B_{\rm cr} is evaluated from the closed form in Eq. (35), so the cancellation is not subject to rounding. Increasing the number of nodes in each variable by about 40% changes λlad\lambda_{\rm lad} by about 10−310^{-3} or less in relative terms, and λnet\lambda_{\rm net} by less than 0.1%0.1\% at kF​d>2k_{F}d>2 and by up to 3%3\% at kF​d<1k_{F}d<1.

Low temperatures. TcT_{c} is located by decreasing TT in decades from 3​EF3\,E_{F} until η>1\eta>1 and refining by the secant method in ln⁡T\ln T. The lowest temperature is about 10−12​EF10^{-12}E_{F}. If η<1\eta<1 there, TcT_{c} is obtained by extrapolation and is marked as such: for the statically screened kernel η\eta is linear in ln⁡T\ln T at low temperature, as in BCS theory, and it is extrapolated linearly from the last four temperatures. The slope of the numerical η⁡(T)\eta(T) agrees with the independently computed λs\lambda_{s} of Eq. (22) to within 0.08% at every point, and fits to the last three and the last six temperatures change ln⁡Tc\ln T_{c} by at most 0.01%, although the extrapolation extends over hundreds of decades. For the dynamically screened kernel the combination η2/(λs​η+λpl)\eta^{2}/(\lambda_{s}\eta+\lambda_{\rm pl}), which is linear in ln⁡T\ln T [Eq. (31) and Fig. 8(b)], is extrapolated linearly to its value at η=1\eta=1.

Appendix E Diagrams through second order, the controlled limits, the two crossovers, and the renormalization group

This appendix gives the complete set of pairing-channel diagrams through second order, both in the bare and in the screened interaction, and states for each one whether it is contained in our results and why. It then uses this classification to examine the two limits in which the theory is controlled: small rsr_{s}, where the leading exponent is that of leading-order perturbation theory, and large d/aBd/a_{B}, where the result follows from the large energy denominators of all processes that involve the plasmons, under assumptions that are stated. It finally discusses the two distinct crossovers between weak pairing and Bose condensation of excitons, as a function of dd at fixed rsr_{s} and as a function of rsr_{s} at fixed dd, and what a renormalization-group (RG) treatment of the Polchinski-Shankar type [83, 84] does and does not capture. The main conclusions are collected in Sec. E.9.

E.1 The object that is expanded

The transition temperature is determined by the linearized equation for the anomalous self-energy,

ϕ(k)=−T∑pI(k,p)𝒢e(p)𝒢h(−p)ϕ(p),\displaystyle\phi(k)=-T\sum_{p}I(k,p)\,\mathcal{G}_{e}(p)\,\mathcal{G}_{h}(-p)\,\phi(p), (71)

where k=(𝐤,i​ωn)k=(\mathbf{k},i\omega_{n}), II is the vertex that is irreducible in the electron-hole pair channel, and 𝒢e,h\mathcal{G}_{e,h} are the full normal propagators. A diagram of II has an incoming electron and hole and an outgoing electron and hole, and it cannot be separated into two parts by cutting one electron line and one hole line. Equation (71) is exact. Three things are expanded: the kernel II, the self-energy in 𝒢\mathcal{G}, and the polarization inside the interaction lines. Charge conservation ties them together through Ward identities, so a truncation is consistent only if the three are truncated together.

The rules are the following. A solid line is the bare propagator 𝒢0\mathcal{G}^{0}. The electron line is in layer 1 and the hole line in layer 2. There is no interlayer tunneling, so the two external lines never join, and there is no exchange between an electron and a hole. Every closed loop is summed over the two layers. A wavy line is the bare interaction, VqV_{q} between vertices in the same layer and −Uq-U_{q} between vertices in different layers; a double wavy line is the RPA interaction of Sec. IV, W11W_{11} or W12W_{12}. Diagrams that contain a tadpole are omitted: for the neutral balanced bilayer the Hartree terms add up to the capacitor shift 2​π​e2​n​d/ϵ2\pi e^{2}nd/\epsilon of the chemical potential and its iterations, which are absorbed at fixed density.

E.2 Expansion in the bare interaction

Figure 18 shows all diagrams through second order in the bare interaction.

First order. The kernel has one diagram, the interlayer rung B1, I(1)=−UqI^{(1)}=-U_{q}. Solving Eq. (71) with this kernel generates the ladder of all iterations, of which the first is shown in Fig. 18(a). With bare propagators this is the unscreened theory of Sec. VI, Eq. (21). The HF theory of Ref. [11] is the same ladder with the exchange self-energy included in the propagators.

Second order. The irreducible kernel has five diagrams, Fig. 18(b): the crossed rungs B2.1, the two vertex corrections B2.2 and B2.3, in which an intralayer line VV spans the interlayer vertex on the electron or on the hole line, and the two diagrams B2.4 and B2.5, in which the rung is interrupted by a bubble in the electron or in the hole layer, −Uq​Π​Vq−Vq​Π​Uq-U_{q}\Pi V_{q}-V_{q}\Pi U_{q}. At the same order the propagators acquire the exchange self-energy. There are no other diagrams: a second-order diagram has two interaction lines, and with at most one loop the possibilities are exhausted by these five and by the reducible iteration.

Why this is not a weak-coupling expansion. The bare series is not an expansion in a small parameter, for two reasons that both come from small momentum transfer.

First, the bubble diagrams are larger than the rung they correct. Their ratio to B1 at ν≪vF​q\nu\ll v_{F}q is

B2​.4+B2​.5B1=−2​N0​Vq=−2​𝒢q​d,𝒢=g​daB,\frac{{\rm B2.4}+{\rm B2.5}}{{\rm B1}}=-2N_{0}V_{q}=-\frac{2\mathcal{G}}{qd},\qquad\mathcal{G}=\frac{gd}{a_{B}}, (72)

and a rung with nn bubbles is of order (𝒢/q​d)n(\mathcal{G}/qd)^{n}. For q​d<𝒢qd<\mathcal{G} the series must be summed to all orders, which gives the RPA [85]. The parameter 𝒢\mathcal{G} is dd times the Thomas-Fermi wave vector g/aBg/a_{B}, which in two dimensions does not depend on the density. Screening of the interlayer interaction does not become weak when rs→0r_{s}\to 0. It is controlled by d/aBd/a_{B} alone.

Second, the first-order term itself does not define a coupling constant. The Fermi-surface average of B1 is (α/π)​∫d​y​e−y/y(\alpha/\pi)\int dy\,e^{-y}/y with y=q​dy=qd, which diverges logarithmically at small yy. In the gap equation the divergence is cut off by the energy difference of the two states, Eq. (19), and the result is the double logarithm of Eq. (20) and lnTc∝−1/α\ln T_{c}\propto-1/\sqrt{\alpha}. This is not the behavior of the system at small rsr_{s}. The forward divergence is removed by the bubbles of Eq. (72), after which the coupling constant is finite and lnTc∝−1/α\ln T_{c}\propto-1/\alpha (Sec. E.5).

The expansion must therefore be reorganized in terms of the screened interaction.

E.3 Expansion in the screened interaction

When the bubble chains are summed into WW, counting interaction lines is no longer a consistent ordering, because W​Π=O⁡(1)W\Pi=O(1): a closed loop compensates one screened line. The consistent count is

order=(number of ​W​ lines)−(number of closed loops),\text{order}=(\text{number of }W\text{ lines})-(\text{number of closed loops}), (73)

which is the formal expansion in 1/N1/N for NN fermion flavors, with W∝1/NW\propto 1/N and each loop ∝N\propto N. A bare bubble on a WW line is excluded, since it is already contained in WW.

First order. One diagram, the screened rung S1, I(1)=W12​(q,i​ν)I^{(1)}=W_{12}(q,i\nu) [Fig. 19(a)].

Second order. Twelve diagrams, shown in Fig. 19(b)–(d). We obtained them by exhaustive computer enumeration of all pair-irreducible diagrams with two, three, and four WW lines: there are 3 with two lines and no loop, 7 with three lines and one loop, and 2 with four lines and two loops. They fall into three groups.

(i) Two WW lines and no loop: the crossed rungs S2.1, with two interlayer lines, and the vertex corrections S2.2 and S2.3, in which an intralayer line W11W_{11} spans the interlayer vertex.

(ii) Corrections to the polarization inside the rung, W​Π(1)​WW\Pi^{(1)}W: the two self-energy insertions S2.4 and S2.5, the Maki-Thompson diagram S2.6, and the two Aslamazov-Larkin diagrams S2.7 and S2.8. The loop is in either layer.

(iii) The three-leg loops S2.9–S2.12, in which a closed loop is attached by two lines to one external line and by one line to the other, in both orientations.

The first group is what line counting also gives. The other two groups are required by Eq. (73) and are absent from a naive count of screened lines.

Ward identities. The vertex at which a WW line meets a fermion line is a density vertex, and charge conservation groups the diagrams into sets that are consistent only as a whole.

(a) S2.2 and S2.3 together with the self-energy Σ=−𝒢​W11\Sigma=-\mathcal{G}W_{11} of the propagators. At q=0q=0 and finite ν\nu the vertex is given by Eq. (18). Where the self-energy is linear in frequency it equals ZZ and cancels the factors Z−1Z^{-1} of the propagators (Sec. V.2). In the opposite limit, ν→0\nu\to 0 at fixed small qq, the product of vertex and quasiparticle weight is χ/N∗\chi/N^{*}, the ratio of the compressibility to the quasiparticle density of states [43].

(b) S2.4, S2.5, and S2.6. The polarization must vanish at q=0q=0 for ν≠0\nu\neq 0, and its high-frequency form n​q2/m​ν2nq^{2}/m\nu^{2} must be unchanged (ff-sum rule). The two self-energy insertions and the Maki-Thompson diagram satisfy this only as a sum.

(c) S2.7 and S2.8. The same identities. The two Aslamazov-Larkin diagrams cancel at q=0q=0 only as a pair.

(d) S2.9 with S2.10, and S2.11 with S2.12. The two orientations of a three-leg loop cancel when one leg carries q=0q=0 at ν≠0\nu\neq 0. When one leg carries ν=0\nu=0 and q→0q\to 0, their sum is the derivative of the two-leg loop with respect to the chemical potential, which is a part of the static density vertex of (a).

(e) S2.1 has no Ward partner. It is required by the order counting alone, and it is the only diagram with two interaction lines and no closed loop in which both lines are interlayer. With the loops summed over the layers, other topologies also have assignments with interlayer lines only, for example the Aslamazov-Larkin diagrams with their two loops in opposite layers.

E.4 What our results contain

Table 7 lists which diagrams enter each calculation.

The ladder calculations (Secs. VI and VII) contain S1 and all its iterations, with bare propagators. The statically screened version keeps S1 at ν=0\nu=0, the dynamically screened version keeps its full frequency dependence, and the unscreened version replaces it by B1. In each case the eigenvalue problem is solved exactly, with no cutoff.

The self-energy and the vertex corrections S2.2, S2.3 are left out together. The reason is the Ward identity (a): they form one set, and keeping the self-energy alone, as in Eliashberg theory, produces an error of order unity in the region ν≫vF​q\nu\gg v_{F}q from which the dynamical part of the ladder result comes (a factor as large as Z−4Z^{-4} in λpl\lambda_{\rm pl}, in the limit described in Sec. V.2). Their combined effect is small in neither limit of the identity. At large dd it is known in both: it cancels for ν≫vF​q\nu\gg v_{F}q at frequencies at which the self-energy is linear, and for ν≪vF​q\nu\ll v_{F}q it is expressed by Fermi-liquid parameters (Sec. E.6). At general rsr_{s} and dd it is not known, and leaving the set out is the statement that the calculation is of first order.

The crossed rungs S2.1 are evaluated in Sec. VIII, with the full dynamically screened interaction on both lines, between states at the Fermi surface. This is the quantity that enters the exponent of a weak-coupling TcT_{c}. The result is λcr≃−λpl\lambda_{\rm cr}\simeq-\lambda_{\rm pl} from the frequency-dependent part and λGMB\lambda_{\rm GMB} from the static part. We have not solved Eq. (71) with S2.1 in the kernel at all frequencies.

The polarization corrections S2.4–S2.8 and the three-leg loops S2.9–S2.12 are not evaluated. The RPA uses the bare bubble. These diagrams are first order in the intralayer coupling relative to S1. Their effect is subleading at small rsr_{s} and is absorbed in Fermi-liquid parameters at large dd, as discussed next.

Table 8 summarizes the size of each contribution in the two limits.

E.5 The small-rsr_{s} limit: leading-order perturbation theory

Statement. For rs→0r_{s}\to 0 at any fixed d/aB>0d/a_{B}>0,

limrs→0λs​ln⁡EFkB​Tc=1,λs=απ​s​(𝒢),s⁡(𝒢)=𝒮⁡(𝒢)𝒢,\lim_{r_{s}\to 0}\ \lambda_{s}\,\ln\frac{E_{F}}{k_{B}T_{c}}=1,\qquad\lambda_{s}=\frac{\alpha}{\pi}\,s(\mathcal{G}),\quad s(\mathcal{G})=\frac{\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{G})}{\mathcal{G}}, (74)

with α=g​rs/2\alpha=\sqrt{g}\,r_{s}/2 and 𝒢=g​d/aB\mathcal{G}=gd/a_{B}. The function ss depends on the separation only. It interpolates between

s⁡(𝒢)≃ln⁡12​𝒢−γ(𝒢≪1),s⁡(𝒢)≃π28​𝒢2(𝒢≫1),s(\mathcal{G})\simeq\ln\frac{1}{2\mathcal{G}}-\gamma\quad(\mathcal{G}\ll 1),\qquad s(\mathcal{G})\simeq\frac{\pi^{2}}{8\mathcal{G}^{2}}\quad(\mathcal{G}\gg 1), (75)

where γ\gamma is Euler’s constant; s⁡(1)=0.248s(1)=0.248. This is the result of leading-order perturbation theory in the statically screened interaction: the first-order kernel S1 at ν=0\nu=0, iterated. The statement concerns the leading exponent. The form λs=(α/π)​s​(𝒢)\lambda_{s}=(\alpha/\pi)s(\mathcal{G}) requires kF​d≫1k_{F}d\gg 1, which holds in the limit at any fixed positive dd.

Why the leading order is S1 at zero frequency. By Sec. E.2 the bubbles must be summed, so the leading kernel is S1 and not B1. Its frequency dependence does not enter the leading logarithm. The logarithm of Eq. (71) comes from states with |ξp||\xi_{p}| and |ωm||\omega_{m}| between TcT_{c} and the cutoff, while the momentum transfer between two such states is fixed by the angle between them and is of order 1/d1/d. For all but a vanishing fraction of the logarithmic range the frequency transfer is small compared with vF​qv_{F}q, and S1 can be evaluated at ν=0\nu=0. Its Fermi-surface average is λs\lambda_{s}.

Why the corrections do not change the limit. Every other term is of higher order in rsr_{s} (Table 8). A correction δ​λ\delta\lambda changes ln⁡Tc\ln T_{c} by δ​λ/λs2\delta\lambda/\lambda_{s}^{2}. The intralayer terms (the self-energy, S2.2, S2.3, S2.4–S2.12) are of relative order α​ln⁡(1/α)\alpha\ln(1/\alpha), the logarithm being the one that appears in the effective mass of the two-dimensional electron gas at high density [50]. Then δ​λ/λs2∼ln⁡(1/α)​π/s⁡(𝒢)\delta\lambda/\lambda_{s}^{2}\sim\ln(1/\alpha)\,\pi/s(\mathcal{G}), which grows logarithmically. The static crossed rung gives δ​λ/λs2=−[ln⁡kF​d+c]\delta\lambda/\lambda_{s}^{2}=-[\ln k_{F}d+c], which at fixed dd also grows as ln⁡(1/rs)\ln(1/r_{s}). Neither of these is bounded by a constant, but each is small compared with the leading term 1/λs∝1/rs1/\lambda_{s}\propto 1/r_{s}. The net dynamical term is C3​(d)​rs3C_{3}(d)\,r_{s}^{3} at fixed dd, with the coefficient of Eq. (93), and gives λnet/λs2=R⁡(d)​rs\lambda_{\rm net}/\lambda_{s}^{2}=R(d)\,r_{s} [Eq. (95)], which vanishes in the limit. Equation (74) follows. The remainder in ln⁡Tc\ln T_{c} is of order ln⁡(1/rs)\ln(1/r_{s}): the prefactor of TcT_{c} is a power of rsr_{s}.

Dependence on dd, and the role of the crossed rung. Two different statements must be kept apart.

At fixed dd, the dynamically screened ladder has the same leading exponent as Eq. (74), because λpl/λs∝rs→0\lambda_{\rm pl}/\lambda_{s}\propto r_{s}\to 0. The crossed rung is not needed for the limit at fixed separation. The ladder is nevertheless not uniformly valid. It reaches the limit only for rs≪0.64​(aB/d)3/2r_{s}\ll 0.64\,(a_{B}/d)^{3/2}, and where it does it overestimates TcT_{c} by exp⁡(λpl/λs2)\exp(\lambda_{\rm pl}/\lambda_{s}^{2}), a factor that does not depend on rsr_{s} and is exp⁡[22.6​(d/aB)7/2]\exp[22.6\,(d/a_{B})^{7/2}] at large dd for g=2g=2.

When dd is large as well, the ladder fails in the exponent: for d>d×d>d_{\times} [Eq. (29)] its second-order term λpl\lambda_{\rm pl} exceeds its first-order term λs\lambda_{s}, however small rsr_{s} is, and it gives lnTc∝−d/rs2\ln T_{c}\propto-\sqrt{d}/r_{s}^{2} where the first-order result is lnTc∝−d2/rs\ln T_{c}\propto-d^{2}/r_{s}. The crossed rung removes this: λnet/λs\lambda_{\rm net}/\lambda_{s}, which at large dd is the sum of terms proportional to rs3​(aB/d)3/2r_{s}^{3}(a_{B}/d)^{3/2} and rs2​(aB/d)3r_{s}^{2}(a_{B}/d)^{3} with the coefficients of Appendix F, and λs​ln⁡kF​d\lambda_{s}\ln k_{F}d both vanish for rs→0r_{s}\to 0 and for d→∞d\to\infty. With the crossed rung the first-order result holds along any path on which rs→0r_{s}\to 0 and kF​d≫1k_{F}d\gg 1, and in this sense the statement that at small rsr_{s} there is an exact result for every d/aBd/a_{B} is correct. It refers to the statically screened theory, not to the HF theory.

The limit is not uniform as d→0d\to 0 in the form written. For kF​d≲1k_{F}d\lesssim 1 the coupling is the full Fermi-surface average of the static interaction [the first equality of Eq. (22)], not (α/π)​s​(𝒢)(\alpha/\pi)s(\mathcal{G}). At d=0d=0 it is (α/π)​ln⁡(2/g​α)(\alpha/\pi)\ln(2/g\alpha), which behaves as rs​ln⁡(1/rs)r_{s}\ln(1/r_{s}), whereas s⁡(𝒢)s(\mathcal{G}) diverges as ln⁡(1/𝒢)\ln(1/\mathcal{G}). We expect Eq. (74) to hold there with the full average, but the expressions of this paper for the second-order terms assume small-angle scattering and do not cover that regime.

The unscreened theory is not the small-rsr_{s} limit. The unscreened ladder gives lnTc≃−π3/2/2α\ln T_{c}\simeq-\pi^{3/2}/2\sqrt{\alpha}, which is larger than −1/λs-1/\lambda_{s} by a factor that diverges as rs→0r_{s}\to 0. It would be correct only if the forward singularity of the interaction survived down to momentum transfers of order kB​Tc/ℏ​vFk_{B}T_{c}/\hbar v_{F}, and static screening removes it at q≲𝒢/dq\lesssim\mathcal{G}/d, whatever the density. Dynamic screening restores the singularity for ν\nu above the plasmon frequency, and the ladder converts this into λpl\lambda_{\rm pl}, which the crossed rung cancels.

The prefactor. Equation (74) fixes the exponent. The prefactor requires every term of Table 8, and we have computed two of them. One has a simple and exact structure. The static crossed rung is

λGMB=−λs2​[ln⁡kF​d+c],\lambda_{\rm GMB}=-\lambda_{s}^{2}\bigl[\ln k_{F}d+c\bigr], (76)

with a coefficient of the logarithm equal to unity. Our numerical results give a slope of 0.980.98 when kF​dk_{F}d is varied at fixed dd, and cc between 0.9 and 1.1 for 5≤d/aB≤205\leq d/a_{B}\leq 20. The logarithm has a direct interpretation. For scattering at small angle the crossed channel has the same logarithm as the Cooper channel, with the opposite sign, down to the energy at which the curvature of the Fermi surface distinguishes the two [Eq. (36)], which is

Ec=ℏ2m​d2=ℏ​vF/dkF​d.E_{c}=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{md^{2}}=\frac{\hbar v_{F}/d}{k_{F}d}. (77)

Between EcE_{c} and ℏ​vF/d\hbar v_{F}/d the two channels cancel, and the Cooper logarithm that determines TcT_{c} extends only up to EcE_{c}. Equation (76) expresses this: inserted in 1/(λs+λGMB)≃1/λs+ln⁡kF​d+c1/(\lambda_{s}+\lambda_{\rm GMB})\simeq 1/\lambda_{s}+\ln k_{F}d+c, it replaces the cutoff ℏ​vF/d\hbar v_{F}/d of the statically screened ladder by EcE_{c},

kB​Tc=C′​ℏ2m​d2​exp⁡[−1λs].k_{B}T_{c}=C^{\prime}\,\frac{\hbar^{2}}{md^{2}}\,\exp\Bigl[-\frac{1}{\lambda_{s}}\Bigr]. (78)

The crossed rung alone gives C′=Cs​e−c≈0.2C^{\prime}=C_{s}e^{-c}\approx 0.2 to 0.50.5, where Cs≈0.7C_{s}\approx 0.7 to 1.31.3 is the prefactor of the statically screened ladder in units of ℏ​vF/d\hbar v_{F}/d, obtained from the numerical solution. This is not the complete prefactor. The intralayer terms, which we have not evaluated, multiply C′C^{\prime} by a function of d/aBd/a_{B} and, through the logarithm mentioned above, by a power of rsr_{s}. In units of EFE_{F} the scale ℏ2/m​d2\hbar^{2}/md^{2} is itself 2​EF/(kF​d)2∝rs22E_{F}/(k_{F}d)^{2}\propto r_{s}^{2}.

E.6 The large-dd limit: large energy denominators

Statement. For d→∞d\to\infty at any fixed rsr_{s}, under the two assumptions listed below,

limd→∞(aBd)2​ln⁡EFkB​Tc=m∗m​16​g3/2π​rs,\lim_{d\to\infty}\Bigl(\frac{a_{B}}{d}\Bigr)^{2}\ln\frac{E_{F}}{k_{B}T_{c}}=\frac{m^{*}}{m}\,\frac{16\,g^{3/2}}{\pi\,r_{s}}, (79)

where m∗m^{*} is the quasiparticle effective mass of a single layer at the given rsr_{s}. The conditions are kF​d≫1k_{F}d\gg 1 and d≫aBd\gg a_{B}. No smallness of rsr_{s} is required. The assumptions are (A1) that each layer is a Fermi liquid, and (A2) that the cancellation between the Cooper channel and the crossed channel, which is exact at every order for linearized dispersion and which we have verified with curvature at second order, also holds for the curvature terms of third and higher order, in the precise sense that the sum δ​λ\delta\lambda of all contributions to the pair coupling beyond the static quasiparticle interaction satisfies δ​λ/[(m/m∗)​λs]→0\delta\lambda/[(m/m^{*})\lambda_{s}]\to 0 as d→∞d\to\infty. Statement (1) below needs only (A1). Statements (2) and (3) are proven at second order and rest on (A2) beyond it.

The scales. At large dd the problem has three energies below EFE_{F}, separated by the two large parameters,

ℏ​Ω∗:ℏ​vFd:Ec=𝒢​kF​d:kF​d:1,\hbar\Omega_{*}:\frac{\hbar v_{F}}{d}:E_{c}=\sqrt{\mathcal{G}}\,k_{F}d:k_{F}d:1, (80)

with ℏ​Ω∗/EF=(g2​rs2​aB/d)1/2\hbar\Omega_{*}/E_{F}=(g^{2}r_{s}^{2}a_{B}/d)^{1/2} and kB​Tck_{B}T_{c} far below all of them. The plasmon energy at q=1/dq=1/d is the largest, the range ℏ​vF/d\hbar v_{F}/d of the interlayer interaction in energy comes next, and the curvature energy EcE_{c} of Eq. (77) is the smallest. The exciton binding energy is Ed=α​ℏ​vF/dE_{d}=\alpha\,\hbar v_{F}/d. For rs=1r_{s}=1 and d=8​aBd=8a_{B}, in units of EFE_{F}, ℏ​Ω∗=0.71\hbar\Omega_{*}=0.71, ℏ​vF/d=0.18\hbar v_{F}/d=0.18, Ec=0.016E_{c}=0.016, and Ed=0.13E_{d}=0.13.

The argument. Three statements are needed.

(1) Below EcE_{c} the pairing is that of the statically screened interaction. For pair states within EcE_{c} of the Fermi surface the frequency transfer is at most EcE_{c}, which is smaller than ℏ​vF​q\hbar v_{F}q at the relevant q∼1/dq\sim 1/d by the factor 1/kF​d1/k_{F}d. The interaction is S1 at ν=0\nu=0, the crossed channel has no logarithm, and the Cooper channel gives ln⁡(Ec/kB​Tc)=1/λ\ln(E_{c}/k_{B}T_{c})=1/\lambda with λ\lambda the Fermi-surface average of the static quasiparticle interaction.

(2) Processes between EcE_{c} and ℏ​vF/d\hbar v_{F}/d do not renormalize λ\lambda. All interlayer momentum transfers are q≲1/d≪kFq\lesssim 1/d\ll k_{F}, so the scattering is at small angle. The electron of a pair and its hole move in opposite directions, so a small momentum transfer changes their energies by opposite amounts, and Eq. (35) then gives Bcr=−BladB_{\rm cr}=-B_{\rm lad} at every frequency, up to terms of relative order Ec2/(ν2+ξ2)E_{c}^{2}/(\nu^{2}+\xi^{2}). On these scales a patch of the Fermi surface and the opposite patch form a one-dimensional system of counterpropagating fermions with a density-density interaction, in which the Cooper logarithm is cancelled by the crossed channel at every order when the dispersion is linearized (Sec. VIII.3) [47, 48, 49]. Equation (76) is the second-order term of this cancellation with the curvature included, and it is the term we have verified explicitly, including the momentum integration: the logarithm is regulated by the curvature at EcE_{c} and its coefficient is unity. Beyond second order the statement rests on (A2).

(3) Processes at and above the plasmon energy do not renormalize λ\lambda. These are the processes of the wedge, Eq. (24), in which the pair is scattered into virtual states at frequencies ν≳ω+​(q)\nu\gtrsim\omega_{+}(q). Their energy denominators, ℏ​ν≳ℏ​ω+​(q)\hbar\nu\gtrsim\hbar\omega_{+}(q), are large compared with the energy ℏ​vF​q\hbar v_{F}q that the carriers can exchange at the same wave vector. The comparison is local in qq, since the plasmon is gapless: the ratio ω+​(q)/vF​q\omega_{+}(q)/v_{F}q is of order 𝒢\sqrt{\mathcal{G}} at q=1/dq=1/d and increases as q→0q\to 0, so the condition holds uniformly at large dd. On the time scale of such a process the carriers do not move, and for static carriers the dynamical part of the interaction changes the amplitude of the pair but not its energy, Eq. (42). In the ladder alone these processes give λpl\lambda_{\rm pl}; with the crossed diagrams they give λnet\lambda_{\rm net}, which at second order is smaller by a factor of order 1/[𝒢​(kF​d)2]1/[\mathcal{G}(k_{F}d)^{2}] (Fig. 20) and whose limit is given in Eq. (98).

The same conclusion can be reached from the interaction itself. For ν≪ω±​(q)\nu\ll\omega_{\pm}(q) both dielectric functions are large, ε±≃(Vq±Uq)​N0​P\varepsilon_{\pm}\simeq(V_{q}\pm U_{q})N_{0}P, and Eq. (8) becomes

W12​(q,i​ν)≃−1N02​P​(q,ν)2​UqVq2−Uq2=W12​(q,0)P​(q,ν)2.W_{12}(q,i\nu)\simeq-\frac{1}{N_{0}^{2}P(q,\nu)^{2}}\,\frac{U_{q}}{V_{q}^{2}-U_{q}^{2}}=\frac{W_{12}(q,0)}{P(q,\nu)^{2}}. (81)

The plasmon frequencies have dropped out. What remains is the capacitive interaction between the layers divided by the square of the polarization of the particle-hole continuum, which is unity for ν≪vF​q\nu\ll v_{F}q. The plasmons have been eliminated, and their only trace is the static screening they provide.

Statements (1)–(3) leave the static quasiparticle interaction as the only input. Because q≪kFq\ll k_{F} it is given by Fermi-liquid theory, Sec. IX: the self-energy and the vertex corrections S2.2 and S2.3 combine into the static density vertex χ/N∗\chi/N^{*}, the three-leg loops are part of the same vertex, the polarization corrections S2.4–S2.8 replace N0N_{0} by the exact compressibility χ\chi in the dielectric functions, and for (Vq±Uq)​|χ|≫1(V_{q}\pm U_{q})|\chi|\gg 1 the compressibility cancels between the vertices and the screening. The result is λ=(m/m∗)​λs\lambda=(m/m^{*})\lambda_{s} and Eq. (79). Including the prefactor from statement (1),

kB​Tc=C′′​ℏ2m​d2​exp⁡[−m∗m​16​g3/2π​rs​(daB)2​(1+δ)],k_{B}T_{c}=C^{\prime\prime}\,\frac{\hbar^{2}}{md^{2}}\,\exp\Bigl[-\frac{m^{*}}{m}\,\frac{16\,g^{3/2}}{\pi\,r_{s}}\Bigl(\frac{d}{a_{B}}\Bigr)^{2}\bigl(1+\delta\bigr)\Bigr], (82)

where δ→0\delta\to 0 as d→∞d\to\infty under assumption (A2); the corrections to 𝒮⁡(𝒢)≃π2/8​𝒢\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{G})\simeq\pi^{2}/8\mathcal{G} and to the Fermi-surface average contribute O⁡(aB/d)+O⁡(1/kF​d)O(a_{B}/d)+O(1/k_{F}d) to it. Since δ\delta multiplies a large exponent it is not a correction to the prefactor, and Eq. (79) is the precise form of the statement.

What is and is not established. The identity of Eq. (35), the numerical cancellation of λpl\lambda_{\rm pl} by the crossed rung, and the logarithm of Eq. (76) are results. The reduction of the intralayer terms to m∗m^{*}, with the compressibility cancelling, follows from (A1) and the Ward identities at q≪kFq\ll k_{F}. That the terms of third and higher order leave a contribution to the pair coupling that is small compared with λs∝d−2\lambda_{s}\propto d^{-2}, and not merely one that decays no more slowly, is (A2); a remainder proportional to d−2d^{-2} would change the coefficient in Eq. (79). It is supported by the exact solution for linearized dispersion and by the second-order results, and we know of no mechanism that would violate it, but we have not computed a third-order term. Equation (79) is exact if (A2) holds.

Relation to Migdal’s theorem. The large energy denominators are the reason the limit is controlled, and it is worth stating precisely which theorem they give. There are two ways in which the intermediate states of a vertex correction can be far off the energy shell.

In Migdal’s theorem the large denominator is electronic. The boson is slow, ω≪vF​q\omega\ll v_{F}q, the intermediate electron is off shell by ℏ​vF​q\hbar v_{F}q, and the vertex correction is small, of order ω/vF​q∼ωD/EF\omega/v_{F}q\sim\omega_{D}/E_{F} [21]. The interaction remains retarded, and Eliashberg theory, the ladder without vertex corrections, is the leading-order theory.

Here the large denominator is bosonic. The boson is fast, ω±≫vF​q\omega_{\pm}\gg v_{F}q by Eq. (33), and the intermediate states are off shell by the plasmon energy. A process with a large bosonic denominator is instantaneous on the time scale of the carriers. That makes the interaction static, which is the result. It does not make the vertex corrections small. In the expansion in the dynamically screened interaction they are of order unity, λcr=−λpl\lambda_{\rm cr}=-\lambda_{\rm pl}, and the large denominators are what allows them to be summed. The corresponding statement for phonons is the canonical transformation that eliminates a fast boson and leaves an instantaneous interaction [86], and the known breakdown of Migdal’s theorem at q<ω/vFq<\omega/v_{F} [87] is the same physics.

The two theorems are mirror images, and both are realized in bilayers: Migdal’s in the all-electron bilayer with a large ratio of layer masses [23], where the acoustic plasmon of the heavy layer is slow for the light carriers, and the present one in the equal-mass electron-hole bilayer, where both plasmons are fast. Both rest on a ratio of the boson frequency to vF​qv_{F}q, small in one and large in the other, and each fixes the leading exponent. They differ in the leading-order theory they select: Eliashberg theory for Migdal’s limit, and BCS theory with the statically screened interaction for the present one. The smallness of ℏ​Ω∗/EF\hbar\Omega_{*}/E_{F}, that is, of EB/EFE_{B}/E_{F}, is what places the whole problem inside the domain of Fermi-liquid theory and guarantees kF​d≫1k_{F}d\gg 1 and d≫aBd\gg a_{B} when rs≳1r_{s}\gtrsim 1. In that sense EB/EF≪1E_{B}/E_{F}\ll 1 is the condition for the controlled theory. It is not the condition ω≪vF​q\omega\ll v_{F}q of Migdal’s theorem, which is violated by the factor 𝒢\sqrt{\mathcal{G}}.

How fast the limit is approached. The cancellation of the dynamical terms is complete to within about one percent of λpl\lambda_{\rm pl} already at kF​d=2k_{F}d=2 (Table 4). The static coupling reaches its asymptotic form more slowly: 𝒮⁡(𝒢)​𝒢\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{G})\mathcal{G} is within 10%10\% of π2/8\pi^{2}/8 only for 𝒢≳35\mathcal{G}\gtrsim 35, that is, d≳17​aBd\gtrsim 17\,a_{B} for g=2g=2, and within 27%27\% at 𝒢=10\mathcal{G}=10. The effective mass in Eq. (79) is a property of the single layer and is close to unity for rs≲2r_{s}\lesssim 2.

E.7 The two crossovers between weak pairing and Bose condensation

The linearized zero-field theory of this paper applies when the pairs are large and weakly bound. In the opposite regime the electron and the hole form an exciton, and the system is a gas of dipolar bosons. The two regimes are connected without a symmetry change [3, 88, 89, 39], and in the (rs,d/aB)(r_{s},d/a_{B}) plane the connection can be made along two different axes. The two crossovers are physically distinct, and we discuss them in turn.

E.7.1 Two-body scales and many-body parameters

An isolated pair has three properties that matter (Sec. III and Appendix B). Its binding energy EB​(d)E_{B}(d) falls from 2​Ry2\,{\rm Ry} at d=0d=0 to Ed=e2/ϵ​dE_{d}=e^{2}/\epsilon d at large dd. Its in-plane size aX=⟨r2⟩1/2a_{X}=\langle r^{2}\rangle^{1/2}, which we obtain from the same numerical solution, grows from 1.22​aB1.22\,a_{B} at d=0d=0 to (2​aB​d3)1/4(2a_{B}d^{3})^{1/4} at large dd, where the relative motion is harmonic with level spacing ℏ​ω0=2​2​Ry​(aB/d)3/2\hbar\omega_{0}=2\sqrt{2}\,{\rm Ry}\,(a_{B}/d)^{3/2}. And it carries a dipole moment e​ded, so two excitons repel at large distance as e2​d2/ϵ​r3e^{2}d^{2}/\epsilon r^{3}, with a dipolar length r0=2​d2/aBr_{0}=2d^{2}/a_{B} for bosons of mass 2​m2m.

At density nn these combine into three dimensionless parameters,

EBEF=g​rs24​EBRy,π​n​aX2=aX2rs2​aB2,n​r02=4​d4π​rs2​aB4.\frac{E_{B}}{E_{F}}=\frac{g\,r_{s}^{2}}{4}\,\frac{E_{B}}{\rm Ry},\qquad\pi na_{X}^{2}=\frac{a_{X}^{2}}{r_{s}^{2}a_{B}^{2}},\qquad nr_{0}^{2}=\frac{4d^{4}}{\pi r_{s}^{2}a_{B}^{4}}. (83)

The first compares the binding of a pair with the kinetic energy that Pauli exclusion imposes on its constituents. The second measures the overlap of neighboring pairs. In the harmonic regime π​n​aX2=g​EF/ℏ​ω0\pi na_{X}^{2}=g\,E_{F}/\hbar\omega_{0}, so it also compares the Fermi energy with the internal excitation energy of an exciton. The third is the strength of the interaction between excitons.

Figure 21(a) shows the lines on which these parameters are of order unity. They define three regimes.

(I) Weak pairing, EB≪EFE_{B}\ll E_{F}. The Fermi surfaces exist, the pairs are much larger than their spacing, and the zero-field theory of this paper applies. At large dd the boundary EB=EFE_{B}=E_{F} is d=(g/2)​rs2​aBd=(g/2)\,r_{s}^{2}\,a_{B}.

(II) Overlapping pairs, EB≳EFE_{B}\gtrsim E_{F} but π​n​aX2≳1\pi na_{X}^{2}\gtrsim 1. The binding energy exceeds the Fermi energy, yet the pairs overlap and their internal level spacing is below the Fermi energy. Neither description is quantitative. At large dd this regime lies between d≃0.8​rs4/3​aBd\simeq 0.8\,r_{s}^{4/3}a_{B} and d=(g/2)​rs2​aBd=(g/2)r_{s}^{2}a_{B}, and it widens with increasing rsr_{s}.

(III) Dipolar bosons, π​n​aX2≪1\pi na_{X}^{2}\ll 1. The excitons are rigid, and the system is a two-dimensional Bose gas with dipolar repulsion. For n​r02≳290nr_{0}^{2}\gtrsim 290 the bosons crystallize [52]; within regime III this requires rs≳10r_{s}\gtrsim 10 and d≳13​aBd\gtrsim 13\,a_{B}, and the crystal then lies between the line d/aB=3.9​rsd/a_{B}=3.9\sqrt{r_{s}} and the boundary of regime III [Fig. 21(a)]. For dd below about 0.9​aB0.9\,a_{B} for equal masses the repulsion is too weak to prevent the formation of biexcitons [90], and the dilute phase is then a gas of biexcitons.

For a short-range attraction in two dimensions the mean-field crossover is governed by EB/EFE_{B}/E_{F} alone, with the chemical potential μ=EF−EB/2\mu=E_{F}-E_{B}/2 changing sign at EB=2​EFE_{B}=2E_{F} [91, 38]. For the long-range interaction considered here the size of the pair is an independent length, and the intermediate regime II has no counterpart in the short-range problem.

E.7.2 What is known at the two ends

Weak-pairing end. TcT_{c} is given by Eq. (78) at small rsr_{s} and by Eq. (82) at large dd. The mean-field and Kosterlitz-Thouless temperatures coincide up to corrections of relative order kB​Tc/EFk_{B}T_{c}/E_{F}.

Bose end. The mean-field temperature at which pairs form is of order EBE_{B} and has nothing to do with the transition. Superfluidity is lost by the unbinding of vortices, at

kB​TKT=π2​ℏ2​ns2​m≤g8​EF,k_{B}T_{\rm KT}=\frac{\pi}{2}\,\frac{\hbar^{2}n_{s}}{2m}\leq\frac{g}{8}\,E_{F}, (84)

where ns≤nn_{s}\leq n is the superfluid density of excitons of mass 2​m2m at the transition [94]. Equation (84) is an upper bound and not an estimate. For a weakly interacting Bose gas kB​TKT=(2​π​ℏ2​n/M)/ln⁡(ξ/g~)k_{B}T_{\rm KT}=(2\pi\hbar^{2}n/M)/\ln(\xi/\tilde{g}) with ξ≃380\xi\simeq 380 and g~\tilde{g} the dimensionless coupling [95], so the ratio of TKTT_{\rm KT} to the bound is 4/ln⁡(ξ/g~)4/\ln(\xi/\tilde{g}). In the dilute limit g~\tilde{g} itself vanishes logarithmically with the density, and the ratio tends to zero as the inverse of a double logarithm [96]. At g~=1\tilde{g}=1 it is about 0.70.7, and it approaches unity for stronger interaction, where the weak-coupling formula no longer applies. The bound refers to the phase of the pair field; the larger order-parameter manifold that exists for g>1g>1 can only lower the transition.

The interaction itself crosses over. In regime III the excitons are neutral and there are no free carriers, so the interlayer attraction that binds a pair is unscreened. The unscreened ladder is then the Schrödinger equation of the pair, and HF theory gives the exact two-body binding energy. This does not make HF theory a controlled calculation of the transition temperature of the exciton gas, which is governed by Eq. (84) and by the interaction between excitons. In regime I the attraction is screened, and by Secs. E.5 and E.6 the screening is static. Between the two limits the appropriate interaction changes from one to the other, because the polarization of the layers is suppressed at energies below the gap once a gap opens [51, 29]. This is the origin of the sensitivity of the energetics to the treatment of screening found in Ref. [27]. The unscreened HF theory and the statically screened theory are therefore not competing approximations to one problem. Each describes the pairing interaction correctly at one end, the unscreened one for the formation of pairs on the Bose side and the statically screened one on the weak-pairing side. The dynamically screened ladder interpolates too (Fig. 7), but for a reason, λpl\lambda_{\rm pl}, that the crossed rung removes on the weak-pairing side.

E.7.3 Crossover as a function of dd at fixed rsr_{s}

Here the density is fixed and the two-body problem changes: EBE_{B}, aXa_{X}, and r0r_{0} all depend on dd, while EFE_{F} and the bound of Eq. (84) do not.

For rs<(2/g)1/2r_{s}<(2/g)^{1/2} there is no crossover. Even at d=0d=0 the binding energy 2​Ry2\,{\rm Ry} is below EF=4​Ry/g​rs2E_{F}=4\,{\rm Ry}/gr_{s}^{2}, and the system is in the weak-pairing regime for every dd. As dd decreases the coupling grows only logarithmically, Eq. (75), and saturates when kF​d∼1k_{F}d\sim 1.

For rs>(2/g)1/2r_{s}>(2/g)^{1/2} the binding energy exceeds EFE_{F} at small dd, and regimes II and I are traversed with increasing dd. Regime III is reached at small dd only if in addition the pairs do not overlap there, π​n​aX2<1\pi na_{X}^{2}<1, which at d=0d=0 requires rs>1.22r_{s}>1.22; for g=2g=2 and 1<rs<1.221<r_{s}<1.22 the sequence is II, I. For larger rsr_{s} the order is III, II, I [vertical arrow in Fig. 21(a)]. On the Bose side, where the exciton gas is a superfluid, TcT_{c} is bounded by g​EF/8gE_{F}/8, is a sizable fraction of it, and depends on dd only through the interaction between excitons. On the weak-pairing side it is given by Eq. (82) and falls as a Gaussian in dd. The fall sets in when EBE_{B} drops below EFE_{F}, at d≃(g/2)​rs2​aBd\simeq(g/2)r_{s}^{2}a_{B}, and it is very steep: at rs=3r_{s}=3 the weak-coupling exponent 1/λeff1/\lambda_{\rm eff} is already 355355 at d=8​aBd=8a_{B} (Table 4), where EB/EF=0.72E_{B}/E_{F}=0.72. Figure 21(b) shows the scales. As a function of dd at fixed density we therefore expect the transition temperature to have a plateau followed by a collapse over a narrow range of dd. This is a physical estimate. Neither the height of the plateau nor the form of the collapse through regime II is calculated here, and the picture assumes that no other phase intervenes. In an experiment at finite temperature and with finite disorder such a collapse is indistinguishable from a transition at a critical separation, although within the present theory it is a crossover and the ground state is paired on both sides.

Two features are specific to this crossover. The weak-pairing end is controlled for every rsr_{s} in the liquid phase, by the large energy denominators of Sec. E.6, and not only for small rsr_{s}. And the Bose end is not a simple limit. For d≲0.9​aBd\lesssim 0.9\,a_{B} the dipolar repulsion is too weak, the excitons attract and form biexcitons [90], and at d=0d=0 the model is a single electron-hole plasma. For rs≳10r_{s}\gtrsim 10 the path also crosses the region of the dipole crystal, between d/aB≃3.9​rsd/a_{B}\simeq 3.9\sqrt{r_{s}} and the boundary of regime III.

E.7.4 Crossover as a function of rsr_{s} at fixed dd

Here the two-body problem is fixed, EBE_{B}, aXa_{X}, and r0r_{0} are constants, and the density changes [horizontal arrow in Fig. 21(a)]. This is the crossover familiar from cold atomic gases, with EB/EF∝rs2E_{B}/E_{F}\propto r_{s}^{2} as the tuning parameter.

Both ends are controlled, for dd above the biexciton threshold of about 0.9​aB0.9\,a_{B}. For rs→0r_{s}\to 0 the result is Eq. (78), with an essential singularity lnTc∝−1/rs\ln T_{c}\propto-1/r_{s}. For rs→∞r_{s}\to\infty all three parameters of Eq. (83) behave as required for a dilute Bose gas, π​n​aX2→0\pi na_{X}^{2}\to 0 and n​r02→0nr_{0}^{2}\to 0, and TcT_{c} lies below the bound of Eq. (84), which is Ry/2​rs2{\rm Ry}/2r_{s}^{2} for any gg, by the slowly varying factor given there. In units of the Rydberg the transition temperature thus rises as exp(−const/rs)\exp(-{\rm const}/r_{s}) at high density and falls as rs−2r_{s}^{-2}, up to the double logarithm, at low density. It must therefore have a maximum in between, and we expect it where EB∼EFE_{B}\sim E_{F} [Fig. 21(c)]. Since it is bounded by (g/8)​EF(g/8)E_{F}, our estimate for the maximum is a fraction of the exciton binding energy, of order 0.1​EB​(d)0.1\,E_{B}(d), which at large dd is of order 0.1​e2/ϵ​d0.1\,e^{2}/\epsilon d near rs≈(2​d/g​aB)1/2r_{s}\approx(2d/ga_{B})^{1/2}. Neither the position nor the height of the maximum is determined by the calculations of this paper.

The path is not free of other phases at every dd. By Eq. (83) the dipolar bosons are on the crystalline side of n​r02=290nr_{0}^{2}=290 for rs<2​(d/aB)2/290​π=0.066​(d/aB)2r_{s}<2(d/a_{B})^{2}/\sqrt{290\pi}=0.066\,(d/a_{B})^{2}. For d≳13​aBd\gtrsim 13\,a_{B} this exceeds the value of rsr_{s} at which regime III begins, and the path at fixed dd then passes through the crystal before it reaches the dilute superfluid at larger rsr_{s}. For example, at d=100​aBd=100\,a_{B} and rs=500r_{s}=500 one has π​n​aX2≃0.006\pi na_{X}^{2}\simeq 0.006 and n​r02≃510nr_{0}^{2}\simeq 510. For d≲13​aBd\lesssim 13\,a_{B} no crystal of excitons intervenes.

Three features are specific to this crossover. The screening parameter 𝒢=g​d/aB\mathcal{G}=gd/a_{B} does not change along it, so on the weak-pairing side the interaction does not become unscreened as the density increases; only the coupling α\alpha decreases. The dimensionless separation kF​d∝1/rsk_{F}d\propto 1/r_{s} does change, so the weak-pairing end is always in the regime of small-angle scattering. And on the Bose side the exciton gas becomes more dilute and more weakly interacting as rsr_{s} increases, so that the limit rs→∞r_{s}\to\infty is a superfluid, although a crystal can intervene on the way, as just described.

E.7.5 Comparison

The two crossovers differ in what is tuned, in which ends are controlled, and in the functional form of the weak-pairing side:

d​at fixed​rs:ln⁡kB​TcEF≃−m∗m​16​g3/2π​rs​(daB)2,\displaystyle d\ \text{at fixed}\ r_{s}:\quad\ln\frac{k_{B}T_{c}}{E_{F}}\simeq-\frac{m^{*}}{m}\frac{16g^{3/2}}{\pi r_{s}}\Bigl(\frac{d}{a_{B}}\Bigr)^{2},
rs​at fixed​d:ln⁡kB​TcEF≃−2​πg​s​(𝒢)​1rs.\displaystyle r_{s}\ \text{at fixed}\ d:\quad\ln\frac{k_{B}T_{c}}{E_{F}}\simeq-\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{g}\,s(\mathcal{G})}\,\frac{1}{r_{s}}. (85)

In both, TcT_{c} in the controlled weak-pairing regime is many orders of magnitude below EFE_{F}. Where in the crossover it becomes observable is not determined by our calculation; the numbers of Table 4 suggest that this requires EBE_{B} comparable to EFE_{F} or larger. This is consistent with the conclusion of quantum Monte Carlo calculations that the condensate is appreciable only at low density and small separation [28, 29]. The present theory does not describe the crossover region itself, where the suppression of screening by the gap must be treated self-consistently [51]; what it provides is the asymptotic form of the weak-pairing side of both crossovers.

E.8 What a renormalization-group treatment captures

The RG of Polchinski and Shankar [83, 84] is the natural framework for the statement that an attractive interaction guarantees pairing, and it is useful to say precisely which parts of the present problem it covers.

E.8.1 The framework and what it captures

The RG is formulated for fermions within a shell of width Λ≪EF\Lambda\ll E_{F} around the Fermi surface, and it follows the couplings as Λ\Lambda is reduced. For the bilayer the fermions are the electrons of layer 1 and the holes of layer 2, with identical Fermi surfaces. At tree level the only interactions that are not irrelevant are those between particles whose momenta are constrained to the Fermi surface in one of two ways: forward scattering, within a layer and between the layers, and the scattering of an electron-hole pair of zero total momentum into another such pair. The latter defines the pair couplings

λl=−N∗g∫02​πd​θ2​πW12qp(2kFsinθ2)coslθ,\lambda_{l}=-\frac{N^{*}}{g}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\!\frac{d\theta}{2\pi}\,W^{\rm qp}_{12}\Bigl(2k_{F}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\Bigr)\cos l\theta, (86)

one for each angular momentum ll. At one loop the forward-scattering functions do not flow, and

d​λld​t=λl2,t=ln⁡Λ0Λ,\frac{d\lambda_{l}}{dt}=\lambda_{l}^{2},\qquad t=\ln\frac{\Lambda_{0}}{\Lambda}, (87)

so that an attractive coupling, λl>0\lambda_{l}>0 in our convention, grows and diverges at kBTc≃Λ0exp[−1/λl(Λ0)]k_{B}T_{c}\simeq\Lambda_{0}\exp[-1/\lambda_{l}(\Lambda_{0})], while a repulsive one flows to zero. All other one-loop contributions to the flow, including the crossed channel, are suppressed by Λ/EF\Lambda/E_{F}.

The framework captures the following.

(a) The inevitability of pairing at weak coupling. If the pair coupling at the scale Λ0\Lambda_{0} is attractive in any channel, the normal state is unstable, however small the coupling. This is the rigorous content of the argument that an attractive electron-hole interaction guarantees superfluidity. It requires the two Fermi surfaces to coincide. A mismatch δ​μ\delta\mu stops the flow at Λ∼δ​μ\Lambda\sim\delta\mu.

(b) The form of TcT_{c}. The exponent −1/λ(Λ0)-1/\lambda(\Lambda_{0}) and the fact that only the Fermi-surface average of the interaction in the given channel enters it.

(c) The asymptotic irrelevance of everything else. Below a sufficiently small Λ\Lambda the flow is that of Eq. (87) exactly. Vertex corrections, crossed diagrams, and the frequency dependence of the couplings affect only the initial condition.

(d) The contrast with the single layer. For a repulsive bare interaction all λl​(Λ0)\lambda_{l}(\Lambda_{0}) are negative at leading order and flow to zero. Pairing can then come only from terms of second order in the interaction in the initial condition, as in the mechanism of Kohn and Luttinger [97], or from the dynamics of screening, as in the plasmon mechanism, and neither is part of the leading-order RG. In the bilayer the attraction is present at leading order.

E.8.2 What it does not capture

(a) The initial condition. The flow of Eq. (87) begins at a scale Λ0\Lambda_{0} at which the couplings must be supplied. They are the result of eliminating all modes between EFE_{F} and Λ0\Lambda_{0}, and this elimination is the entire content of the zero-field part of this paper: the screening, the plasmons, the crossed rung, the Fermi-liquid renormalizations. The RG does not perform it. In particular, the sign of λ⁡(Λ0)\lambda(\Lambda_{0}) at general rsr_{s} is not determined by the sign of the bare interaction; it is determined by the bare interaction only when the elimination is controlled. It is controlled, and the result is attractive, at small rsr_{s}, where λ⁡(Λ0)=λs\lambda(\Lambda_{0})=\lambda_{s} to leading order. At large dd for any rsr_{s} we have argued that λ⁡(Λ0)=(m/m∗)​λs\lambda(\Lambda_{0})=(m/m^{*})\lambda_{s}, under the assumptions stated in Sec. E.6; this result does not depend on the sign of the compressibility of the layers.

(b) The long range of the Coulomb interaction. The tree-level analysis assumes coupling functions that are smooth on the Fermi surface. The bare interlayer interaction is singular in the forward direction, and the first-order pair coupling does not exist (Sec. E.2). If the singular interaction is kept unscreened, the flow equation acquires a source term,

d​λd​t=λ2+A,A=απ,\frac{d\lambda}{dt}=\lambda^{2}+A,\qquad A=\frac{\alpha}{\pi}, (88)

as for the color-magnetic interaction in quark matter [45]. Its solution λ=A​tan⁡(A​t)\lambda=\sqrt{A}\tan(\sqrt{A}\,t) diverges at A​t=π/2\sqrt{A}\,t=\pi/2, which is the unscreened result of Eq. (21). Screening must be included before the RG is set up, and the plasmons, which are collective modes of the same fermions at energies well above the shell, are not among its degrees of freedom.

(c) The scale at which the flow begins. The suppression of the crossed channel by Λ/EF\Lambda/E_{F} presupposes couplings that vary on the scale of kFk_{F}. At large dd the pair coupling varies over the angle 1/kF​d1/k_{F}d, and the suppression factor is Λ/Ec\Lambda/E_{c} with Ec=ℏ2/m​d2E_{c}=\hbar^{2}/md^{2}. For Ec<Λ<ℏ​vF/dE_{c}<\Lambda<\hbar v_{F}/d the crossed channel is not suppressed and cancels the Cooper channel, so the coupling does not flow [statement (2) of Sec. E.6]. The flow of Eq. (87) begins at Λ0∼Ec\Lambda_{0}\sim E_{c} and not at ℏ​vF/d\hbar v_{F}/d. An RG that starts the Cooper flow at ℏ​vF/d\hbar v_{F}/d overestimates TcT_{c} by a factor of order kF​dk_{F}d.

(d) Retardation by a fast boson. For phonons the RG reproduces Eliashberg theory, because the coupling becomes marginal only below the Debye energy and Migdal’s theorem controls the elimination above it [83, 98]. A one-loop flow in the Cooper channel alone, with the frequency-dependent coupling W12​(q,i​ν)W_{12}(q,i\nu) and started at EFE_{F}, is the RG form of the dynamically screened ladder. It generates λpl\lambda_{\rm pl} as Λ\Lambda passes through the plasmon energy [upper curve in Fig. 20(b)]. At those scales the crossed channel is of the same size, and the flow of the two together generates nothing [lower curve]. The correct elimination of the plasmons is the one described in Sec. E.6.

(e) The Bose regime and the crossovers. The RG is an expansion around the Fermi-surface fixed point. When EB≳EFE_{B}\gtrsim E_{F} the coupling is of order unity at the scale EFE_{F}, there is no range of scales in which Eq. (87) applies, and the composite bosons, their dipolar interaction, and the crossover of Sec. E.7 are outside the framework.

(f) Fluctuations of the order parameter and first-order transitions. The divergence of the coupling gives the mean-field instability. The Kosterlitz-Thouless physics is beyond it, although at weak coupling this is a small correction. A first-order transition to a different state, such as crystallization, is not signaled by the flow, and its absence is an assumption.

E.8.3 The sequence of scales at large dd

The elimination of modes at large dd can be summarized as a sequence, which Fig. 20 illustrates.

From EFE_{F} to ℏ​Ω∗\hbar\Omega_{*}: the carriers of each layer become Landau quasiparticles with mass m∗m^{*}; the interlayer pair coupling is the bare one in the wedge and the screened one outside it.

Through ℏ​Ω∗\hbar\Omega_{*}: the plasmons are eliminated. The Cooper channel and the crossed channel each generate a coupling of magnitude λpl\lambda_{\rm pl}, with opposite signs. The interaction between the quasiparticles becomes Eq. (81).

From ℏ​vF/d\hbar v_{F}/d to EcE_{c}: the interaction is static, the scattering is at small angle, and the pair coupling does not flow.

Below EcE_{c}: Eq. (87), with λ⁡(Ec)=(m/m∗)​λs\lambda(E_{c})=(m/m^{*})\lambda_{s}, up to kBTc=C′′Ecexp[−1/λ(Ec)]k_{B}T_{c}=C^{\prime\prime}E_{c}\exp[-1/\lambda(E_{c})].

E.8.4 Bearing on the existence of superfluidity at all rsr_{s} and dd

The physical argument that the bilayer is superfluid at zero temperature for every rsr_{s} and dd, because the bare electron-hole interaction is attractive at every wave vector, can now be placed. The RG shows that it is sufficient for the renormalized pair coupling at low energy to be attractive. We find it attractive in every regime in which it can be computed: at small rsr_{s} at fixed dd; at large dd for all rsr_{s} in the liquid phase, under the assumptions of Sec. E.6, where the result holds whatever the compressibility; and on the Bose side, where the pairs are bound. Within the RPA the first-order kernel is attractive at all rsr_{s} and dd, by Eq. (12), which is a statement about that kernel and not about the complete irreducible vertex. No mechanism that would reverse the sign at intermediate parameters has appeared, but its absence is not proven. The argument is therefore supported at every point where it can be tested, with three qualifications that the analysis makes explicit. It does not exclude a first-order transition to a state of different symmetry. The scale of the superfluidity on the weak-pairing side is set by the statically screened interaction, which makes it unobservably small once EBE_{B} is well below EFE_{F}. And because that scale falls as a Gaussian in dd, at sufficiently large dd it drops below the scale of any instability that a single layer has on its own, such as pairing of the Kohn-Luttinger type [97], which does not depend on dd; in the ideal model the two would then have to be compared, at energies far below anything accessible.

E.9 Summary of this appendix

(1) Through second order the irreducible pairing vertex has one plus five diagrams in the bare interaction and one plus twelve in the screened interaction (Figs. 18 and 19). The bare series is not a weak-coupling expansion, because screening is governed by g​d/aBgd/a_{B} and not by rsr_{s}.

(2) Our numerical results contain the first-order screened rung and all its iterations. The crossed rung is evaluated at the Fermi surface. The remaining eleven second-order diagrams and the self-energy are not evaluated, and Tables 7 and 8 state what they do in each limit.

(3) At small rsr_{s} and fixed d>0d>0 the leading exponent is that of first-order perturbation theory in the statically screened interaction: λs​ln⁡(EF/kB​Tc)→1\lambda_{s}\ln(E_{F}/k_{B}T_{c})\to 1 with λs=(α/π)​s​(g​d/aB)\lambda_{s}=(\alpha/\pi)\,s(gd/a_{B}). The static crossed rung and the intralayer terms of second order change ln⁡Tc\ln T_{c} by amounts of order ln⁡(1/rs)\ln(1/r_{s}), and the energy scale of the prefactor is ℏ2/m​d2\hbar^{2}/md^{2}; the net dynamical interlayer term changes ln⁡Tc\ln T_{c} by R⁡(d)​rsR(d)\,r_{s}, which vanishes in the limit (Appendix F). The dynamically screened ladder has the same limit at fixed dd but not when dd is large as well; the crossed rung removes that defect.

(4) At large dd, for every rsr_{s} in the liquid phase, every process that involves the plasmons has a large energy denominator, and the result is ln⁡Tc→−(m∗/m)​(16​g3/2/π​rs)​(d/aB)2\ln T_{c}\to-(m^{*}/m)(16g^{3/2}/\pi r_{s})(d/a_{B})^{2}. This is the fast-boson counterpart of Migdal’s theorem and selects the statically screened interaction. The cancellation on which it rests is established at second order, where the remainder is Jw​g​rs4​(aB/d)7/2J_{w}\sqrt{g}\,r_{s}^{4}(a_{B}/d)^{7/2} and is smaller than λs\lambda_{s} by a factor proportional to rs3​(aB/d)3/2r_{s}^{3}(a_{B}/d)^{3/2} (Appendix F), and at every order for linearized dispersion; that the remaining terms are small compared with λs\lambda_{s} is an assumption that we consider very likely to hold, and the result is conditional on it.

(5) Weak pairing and Bose condensation of excitons are connected by two distinct crossovers. As a function of rsr_{s} at fixed d≳0.9​aBd\gtrsim 0.9\,a_{B} both ends are controlled, and we estimate a maximum of TcT_{c} of order 0.1​EB​(d)0.1\,E_{B}(d); for d≳13​aBd\gtrsim 13\,a_{B} a crystal of excitons intervenes. As a function of dd at fixed rsr_{s} large enough for dilute excitons to exist at small dd we expect a plateau bounded by g​EF/8gE_{F}/8 followed by a collapse that is Gaussian in dd. The pairing interaction is unscreened on the Bose side and statically screened on the weak-pairing side. The crossover region itself is not calculated.

(6) An RG of the Polchinski-Shankar type captures the inevitability of pairing for an attractive low-energy coupling and the form of TcT_{c}. It does not supply the coupling or the scale at which the flow begins, and these are what the diagrams determine.

The two results are tests of the four-dimensional quadrature of Sec. VIII, and conversely. Figure 22(a) shows λnet/C3​rs3\lambda_{\rm net}/C_{3}r_{s}^{3} from the full RPA calculation for rsr_{s} down to 1/321/32. It tends to 1 linearly in rsr_{s} for every dd examined: at rs=1/32r_{s}=1/32 it is between 1.06 and 1.12 for d≤20​aBd\leq 20a_{B}, and the linear extrapolation to rs=0r_{s}=0 from the two smallest values of rsr_{s} differs from 1 by at most 1.3%. Figure 22(b) shows the remainder, λnet−C3​rs3\lambda_{\rm net}-C_{3}r_{s}^{3}, divided by λw\lambda_{w} of Eq. (98). For d≥5​aBd\geq 5a_{B} this ratio depends on dd and only weakly on rsr_{s}: it varies by at most 12% over 0.25≤rs≤30.25\leq r_{s}\leq 3. For rs=1r_{s}=1 it is 1.114, 1.050, 1.023, and 1.012 at d/aB=40d/a_{B}=40, 80, 160, and 320, and a fit quadratic in aB/da_{B}/d to these four values extrapolates to 1.001 at d=∞d=\infty. For d≥5​aBd\geq 5a_{B} the computed values are therefore described by

λnet≃C3​(d)​rs3+C4​(d)​rs4,C4→Jw​g​(aBd)7/2,\lambda_{\rm net}\simeq C_{3}(d)\,r_{s}^{3}+C_{4}(d)\,r_{s}^{4},\qquad C_{4}\to J_{w}\sqrt{g}\,\Bigl(\frac{a_{B}}{d}\Bigr)^{7/2}, (100)

with C3C_{3} given by Eq. (93) and C4/[Jw​g​(aB/d)7/2]≈1+3.3​aB/dC_{4}/[J_{w}\sqrt{g}(a_{B}/d)^{7/2}]\approx 1+3.3\,a_{B}/d at large dd for g=2g=2. We have not derived C4​(d)C_{4}(d) at finite dd. It is the coefficient of the region |ν|∼vF​q|\nu|\sim v_{F}q, of which the wedge is the part that survives at large dd, and its integral, taken alone, diverges at low frequency, where it joins the region of Eq. (93). The leading divergence is the term of order rs3r_{s}^{3}; a subleading logarithmic one would give a term of order rs4​ln⁡(1/rs)r_{s}^{4}\ln(1/r_{s}), which is therefore possible. The numerical values of the remainder for d≤2​aBd\leq 2a_{B} increase slowly as rsr_{s} decreases from 1/41/4 to 1/321/32, which is consistent with such a term, and this is the reason for the form of the correction in Eq. (93).

F.4 Consequence for the transition temperature

A weak addition δ​λ\delta\lambda to the coupling changes ln⁡Tc\ln T_{c} by δ​λ/λs2\delta\lambda/\lambda_{s}^{2}. For the dynamical terms of second order this is now known in both limits. For rs→0r_{s}\to 0 at fixed dd, by Eq. (95),

δ​ln⁡Tc|net=R⁡(d)​rs→ 0,\delta\ln T_{c}\big|_{\rm net}=R(d)\,r_{s}\ \to\ 0, (101)

with RR of order one at d∼aBd\sim a_{B} and decreasing as aB/da_{B}/d (Table 9). The dynamical part of the interlayer interaction therefore does not contribute to the prefactor of TcT_{c} in this limit at second order; the terms that do are λGMB\lambda_{\rm GMB} and the intralayer corrections. In the ladder approximation the corresponding quantity is λpl/λs2\lambda_{\rm pl}/\lambda_{s}^{2}, which does not vanish with rsr_{s} and is 22.6​(d/aB)7/222.6\,(d/a_{B})^{7/2} at large dd. For d→∞d\to\infty at fixed rsr_{s}, by Eqs. (98) and (23),

δ​ln⁡Tc|net=256​Jwπ2​g7/2​rs2​(daB)1/2=0.101​rs2​(daB)1/2\delta\ln T_{c}\big|_{\rm net}=\frac{256\,J_{w}}{\pi^{2}}\,g^{7/2}\,r_{s}^{2}\Bigl(\frac{d}{a_{B}}\Bigr)^{1/2}=0.101\,r_{s}^{2}\Bigl(\frac{d}{a_{B}}\Bigr)^{1/2} (102)

for g=2g=2. This increases with dd, but as d\sqrt{d}, while the leading term 1/λs1/\lambda_{s} increases as d2d^{2}: the ratio is λnet/λs∝rs3​(aB/d)3/2\lambda_{\rm net}/\lambda_{s}\propto r_{s}^{3}(a_{B}/d)^{3/2}. At second order the condition δ​λ/λs→0\delta\lambda/\lambda_{s}\to 0 of Sec. IX is thus satisfied with a known coefficient. These statements concern the second-order term only. The dynamical terms of third and higher order with curvature have not been evaluated, and the assumption about them stated in Sec. IX remains an assumption.

Appendix G Stiffness and response functions at νT=1\nu_{T}=1

The two factors in Eq. (61) are the phase and density sectors of the coherent state. A phase twist changes the exchange energy by Bδ​(Q)B_{\delta}(Q), and a relative-density fluctuation costs Kδ​(Q)K_{\delta}(Q). The projected equations of motion are

ℏ​∂tSy​(𝒒)\displaystyle\hbar\partial_{t}S^{y}(\bm{q}) =Kδ​(q​ℓ)​Sz​(𝒒),\displaystyle=K_{\delta}(q\ell)S^{z}(\bm{q}),
ℏ​∂tSz​(𝒒)\displaystyle\hbar\partial_{t}S^{z}(\bm{q}) =−Bδ​(q​ℓ)​Sy​(𝒒),\displaystyle=-B_{\delta}(q\ell)S^{y}(\bm{q}), (103)

for a condensate along xx, with SyS^{y} the phase variable. They give Eq. (61) without any long-wavelength approximation. In particular, Bδ​(0)=0B_{\delta}(0)=0 is the microscopic statement of the Goldstone theorem: a uniform change of the spontaneously chosen interlayer phase costs no energy.

The phase stiffness follows by expanding the first factor at small QQ,

Bδ​(Q)\displaystyle B_{\delta}(Q) =4​π​ρs​Q2+O⁡(Q4),\displaystyle=4\pi\rho_{s}Q^{2}+O(Q^{4}), (104)
ρsEC\displaystyle\frac{\rho_{s}}{E_{\rm C}} =116​π​[(1+δ2)​F​(δ)−δ],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{16\pi}\left[(1+\delta^{2})F(\delta)-\delta\right],

where F⁡(δ)=XD/ECF(\delta)=X_{D}/E_{\rm C}. Here ρs\rho_{s} is the conventional stiffness, defined by the energy density ρs​(∇ϕ)2/2\rho_{s}(\nabla\phi)^{2}/2. It is the interlayer stiffness ρE\rho_{E} of Ref. [15] in closed form and equals EC/(16​2​π)E_{\rm C}/(16\sqrt{2\pi}) at d=0d=0. The second factor at Q=0Q=0 is the inverse relative-density susceptibility. The sound velocity is the geometric mean of these two microscopic quantities. This result identifies the charged and neutral responses of the (111)(111) state. Symmetric electric fields couple to the total density and produce the integer quantum Hall response. Antisymmetric fields couple to the neutral phase-density variables in Eq. (103). A quantized Hall plateau and a gapless neutral mode are therefore simultaneous and complementary signatures of the same state.

The stiffness also makes the connection with counterflow immediate. A counterflow current is a gradient of the interlayer phase. The energy density of a long wavelength twist is ρs​(∇ϕ)2/2\rho_{s}(\nabla\phi)^{2}/2. The same ρs\rho_{s} sets the in-plane-field tunneling response and the long-distance phase dynamics. In the present problem the stiffness is not an independent phenomenological parameter: it is an explicit analytic function of d/ℓd/\ell through Eq. (104).

The exchange gap has an equally direct response interpretation. The symmetric and antisymmetric bands in Eq. (53) are split by XD​PX_{D}P. The coherent state therefore has a neutral collective mode together with a finite quasiparticle splitting,

Δ⁡(T)=XD​P​(T).\Delta(T)=X_{D}P(T). (105)

The gap is maximal at T=0T=0, where P=1P=1. It vanishes at the thermal HF transition together with the coherence amplitude. The ratio Δ⁡(0)/(kB​TcHF)=4\Delta(0)/(k_{B}T_{c}^{\rm HF})=4 is universal in the projected uniform theory.

Appendix H Finite temperature and the separation-dependent coherence scale at νT=1\nu_{T}=1

The finite-temperature solution is contained in one equation, Eq. (55). It has the usual bifurcation from P=0P=0 at

kB​TcHF​(d)=e24​ϵ​ℓ​π2​ed2/(2​ℓ2)​erfc⁡(d2​ℓ).k_{B}T_{c}^{\rm HF}(d)=\frac{e^{2}}{4\epsilon\ell}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}e^{d^{2}/(2\ell^{2})}\operatorname{erfc}\!\left(\frac{d}{\sqrt{2}\ell}\right). (106)

Near the transition, writing t=T/TcHFt=T/T_{c}^{\rm HF}, one obtains

P2=3​(1−t)−125​(1−t)2+O⁡[(1−t)3].P^{2}=3(1-t)-\frac{12}{5}(1-t)^{2}+O[(1-t)^{3}]. (107)

Thus the gap closes as Δ⁡(T)=XD​3​(1−T/TcHF)+⋯\Delta(T)=X_{D}\sqrt{3(1-T/T_{c}^{\rm HF})}+\cdots. At low temperature PP is saturated and the condensation energy per flux quantum is XD/4X_{D}/4.

The experimental implication must be stated with care. TcHFT_{c}^{\rm HF} is the mean-field amplitude scale at which the HF gap closes. It is not the temperature of the physical transition, which in two dimensions is of Kosterlitz-Thouless type and bounded by the stiffness, kB​TKT≤(π/2)​ρsk_{B}T_{\rm KT}\leq(\pi/2)\rho_{s} [37, 15]. From Eq. (104) this bound is 0.0097​EC0.0097E_{\rm C} at d/ℓ=1d/\ell=1, a factor of 1717 below TcHFT_{c}^{\rm HF}. The same overestimate is well known for the ν=1\nu=1 spin ferromagnet [65]. The qualitative point survives. At a fixed laboratory temperature a coherence scale that decreases smoothly with d/ℓd/\ell produces an apparent separation boundary. Since TcHFT_{c}^{\rm HF} falls as e2/(4​ϵ​d)e^{2}/(4\epsilon d), and the stiffness bound falls faster, as 1/d31/d^{3}, increasing d/ℓd/\ell eventually drives the sample above its coherence scale. This is a thermal loss of observable coherence. It does not imply that the T=0T=0 exchange field has vanished at that separation. The distinction is particularly important at large d/ℓd/\ell, where the uniform-HF scale is small but nonzero.

The no-tunneling limit is also the cleanest setting for the Goldstone mode. A small symmetric–antisymmetric splitting adds

Ht=−ΔSAS∑mSmx,H_{t}=-\Delta_{\rm SAS}\sum_{m}S_{m}^{x}, (108)

after choosing the condensate along xx. It pins the phase and produces a Josephson gap in the collective mode. It does not generate the exchange field. In the interaction-dominated regime ΔSAS≪XD\Delta_{\rm SAS}\ll X_{D}, tunneling probes a spontaneously coherent state already present in the zero-tunneling Hamiltonian.

An in-plane field is an especially direct probe. It supplies the tunneling wave vector

qB=e​d​B∥ℏ,e​Vres=ℏ​ω​(qB​ℓ).q_{B}=\frac{edB_{\parallel}}{\hbar},\qquad eV_{\rm res}=\hbar\omega(q_{B}\ell). (109)

The experimentally measured dispersing tunneling resonance is therefore a direct measurement of Eq. (61) [57]. Its low-QQ slope measures Eq. (64); its finite-QQ evolution measures the approach to the roton instability.

Appendix I Quantitative scales and controlled perturbations at νT=1\nu_{T}=1

The numbers in Table 10 display the full strength of the analytic result. At d/ℓ=1d/\ell=1, the zero-temperature exchange gap is 0.656​EC0.656E_{\rm C} and the HF transition scale is 0.164​EC0.164E_{\rm C}. Even at d/ℓ=4d/\ell=4, where the coherent scale is small in comparison with the d=0d=0 value, the analytic exchange field remains 0.237​EC0.237E_{\rm C}. The decrease is rapid but smooth. No fitting form, numerical interpolation, or finite-size extrapolation is involved.

For GaAs, the conversion to Kelvin is immediate after specifying B⟂B_{\perp} and the dielectric constant. The Coulomb unit scales as EC∝B⟂/ϵE_{\rm C}\propto\sqrt{B_{\perp}}/\epsilon, while d/ℓ∝d​B⟂d/\ell\propto d\sqrt{B_{\perp}}. Changing density or field therefore changes both the absolute exchange scale and the dimensionless separation. This is the microscopic origin of the strong field dependence of interlayer-coherence phenomena. The formula in Eq. (106) gives the entire HF dependence without introducing a material-specific coherence parameter.

Layer imbalance provides another controlled test. A voltage bias couples to SzS^{z},

HV=−eV∑mSmz.H_{V}=-eV\sum_{m}S_{m}^{z}. (110)

It tilts the pseudospin out of the easy plane. If mzm_{z} denotes the resulting normalized layer polarization, the transverse coherent component is P⟂=1−mz2P_{\perp}=\sqrt{1-m_{z}^{2}}. The transverse exchange field becomes XD​P⟂X_{D}P_{\perp}, while the HF quasiparticle splitting, which is the magnitude of the self-consistent field along the tilted pseudospin, remains XDX_{D} at T=0T=0. Thus imbalance suppresses tunneling coherence by geometrically reducing the transverse pseudospin component while retaining the same interaction-generated exchange field. This is a direct pseudospin-ferromagnet consequence and is distinct from a loss of coherence induced by increasing d/ℓd/\ell.

Finite layer width modifies the interaction form factors in Eq. (47). The calculation proceeds identically after replacing the strict-2D Coulomb kernels by the appropriate subband form factors. The analytic structure remains the same: the interlayer exchange integral determines the gap, amplitude scale, and the collective kernels. The zero-width result is therefore the universal reference curve against which finite-width samples may be compared.

Disorder and density inhomogeneity broaden experimental crossovers but do not alter the basic organizing principle. The coherent phase is controlled microscopically by the positive interlayer exchange field. The roton transition is controlled by the finite-QQ stiffness. These two quantities are different functions of the same projected interaction, and they lead to different physical boundaries. The analytic separation of these mechanisms is useful precisely because experimental phase diagrams often show a single apparent boundary while the microscopic theory contains distinct thermal and translational phenomena.

Appendix J Exchange integral at νT=1\nu_{T}=1

The exchange integral is

XDEC=∫0∞dxe−x2/2−δx=eδ2/2∫δ∞due−u2/2.\frac{X_{D}}{E_{\rm C}}=\int_{0}^{\infty}dx\,e^{-x^{2}/2-\delta x}=e^{\delta^{2}/2}\int_{\delta}^{\infty}du\,e^{-u^{2}/2}. (111)

Completing the square gives the last expression. The short-distance series follows by expanding the complementary error function. The large-distance expansion follows more transparently by observing that the integral is dominated by x∼1/δx\sim 1/\delta:

XDEC\displaystyle\frac{X_{D}}{E_{\rm C}} =∫0∞d​x​e−δ​x​(1−x22+x48−⋯)\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}dx\,e^{-\delta x}\left(1-\frac{x^{2}}{2}+\frac{x^{4}}{8}-\cdots\right)
=1δ−1δ3+3δ5−15δ7+⋯.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\delta}-\frac{1}{\delta^{3}}+\frac{3}{\delta^{5}}-\frac{15}{\delta^{7}}+\cdots. (112)

The LLL form factor has disappeared from the leading term because the exchange process is carried by q∼1/dq\sim 1/d. This gives a simple physical explanation for the e2/(ϵ​d)e^{2}/(\epsilon d) scale. At large separation the HF exchange field is long ranged.

Appendix K Uniform density matrix and the exchange self-energy

The uniform density matrix can be written in pseudospin form as

ρm=12​[1+P⁡(cos⁡ϕ​σx+sin⁡ϕ​σy)].\rho_{m}=\frac{1}{2}\left[1+P(\cos\phi\,\sigma_{x}+\sin\phi\,\sigma_{y})\right]. (113)

The exchange self-energy is obtained by contracting one density operator in Eq. (46),

Σα​β=−∫d2​q(2​π)2Vα​β(q)e−q2ℓ2/2ρα​β.\Sigma_{\alpha\beta}=-\int\frac{d^{2}q}{(2\pi)^{2}}V_{\alpha\beta}(q)e^{-q^{2}\ell^{2}/2}\rho_{\alpha\beta}. (114)

For a balanced state the diagonal intralayer terms shift both HF bands equally. The off-diagonal interlayer term is

ΣT​B=−XD​⟨cm​T†​cm​B⟩,\Sigma_{TB}=-X_{D}\langle c_{mT}^{\dagger}c_{mB}\rangle, (115)

which immediately gives Eq. (53). The resulting Green function is a 2×22\times 2 matrix with poles at ϵS\epsilon_{S} and ϵA​S\epsilon_{AS}. Taking the difference of their Fermi functions yields Eq. (55).

The diagrammatic content of the approximation is most transparent in the {+,−}\{+,-\} basis defined by Eq. (48). The HF Green functions are

Gs(iωn)=1i​ωn−ϵs,s=+,−,G_{s}(i\omega_{n})=\frac{1}{i\omega_{n}-\epsilon_{s}},\qquad s=+,-, (116)

with n+=1n_{+}=1 and n−=0n_{-}=0 at T=0T=0. The same-band bubble is Pauli blocked,

Π+⁣+​(i​Ωn)∝n+−n+i​Ωn=0.\Pi_{++}(i\Omega_{n})\propto\frac{n_{+}-n_{+}}{i\Omega_{n}}=0. (117)

The interband bubble is instead nonzero,

Π+⁣−​(𝒒,i​Ωn)=n+−n−i​Ωn+ϵ+−ϵ−​ℱ+⁣−​(𝒒),\Pi_{+-}(\bm{q},i\Omega_{n})=\frac{n_{+}-n_{-}}{i\Omega_{n}+\epsilon_{+}-\epsilon_{-}}\,\mathcal{F}_{+-}(\bm{q}), (118)

where ℱ+⁣−​(𝒒)\mathcal{F}_{+-}(\bm{q}) is the LLL guiding-center form factor. Equation (118) is the microscopic particle-hole propagator of the pseudospin mode. It enters the TDHF ladder that produces Eq. (61), and it also enters self-energy and vertex corrections omitted by static HF. A zero external momentum does not set the internal momentum in Eq. (118) to zero.

Consequently, ρ2=ρ\rho^{2}=\rho establishes only that the one-body HF density matrix is a projector. It is not an identity eliminating the connected two-particle correlator. The finite-dd interaction contains the anisotropy

V−​(q)=VT​T​(q)−VT​B​(q)2>0,V_{-}(q)=\frac{V_{TT}(q)-V_{TB}(q)}{2}>0, (119)

which couples pseudospin-density fluctuations and has nonzero matrix elements from the coherent Slater determinant to states containing +→−+\!\rightarrow\!- particle-hole pairs. The first-order Fock self-energy is therefore the uniform HF self-energy, not the full finite-dd projected self-energy. The unique exact point of this argument is d=0d=0, where V−​(q)=0V_{-}(q)=0 and global pseudospin rotations map the state to a completely filled one-component LLL.

At finite temperature the same equation has a transparent physical interpretation. The exchange field is XD​PX_{D}P, while thermal occupation of the upper pseudospin band reduces PP. The self-consistency condition is exactly the magnetization equation of a pseudospin-1/21/2 ferromagnet in its self-generated in-plane field. The ordered solution is selected for T<TcHFT<T_{c}^{\rm HF}; its phase remains arbitrary because tunneling is absent.

Appendix L Derivation of the collective-mode kernels

Introduce the projected pseudospin densities

Sa(𝒒)=12∑m​m′⟨m|e−i𝒒⋅𝑹|m′⟩cm​α†σα​βacm′​β.S^{a}(\bm{q})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{mm^{\prime}}\langle m|e^{-i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{R}}|m^{\prime}\rangle c_{m\alpha}^{\dagger}\sigma^{a}_{\alpha\beta}c_{m^{\prime}\beta}. (120)

Here 𝐪\mathbf{q} is the physical wave vector, and Q=|𝐪|​ℓQ=|\mathbf{q}|\ell is its dimensionless magnitude, with ℓ\ell the magnetic length. Their LLL commutator algebra contains the magnetic-translation phase sin⁡[(𝒒×𝒌)​ℓ2/2]\sin[(\bm{q}\times\bm{k})\ell^{2}/2]. Linearization about the state in Eq. (48) couples Sy​(𝒒)S^{y}(\bm{q}) and Sz​(𝒒)S^{z}(\bm{q}) and produces the two equations in Eq. (103). The interlayer exchange kernel is the Bessel transform ΓD​(Q)\Gamma_{D}(Q) in Eq. (62); the intralayer exchange kernel is ΓS​(Q)\Gamma_{S}(Q); and Dδ​(Q)D_{\delta}(Q) is the direct capacitive contribution.

The long-wave expansion is obtained from J0​(Q​x)=1−Q2​x2/4+O⁡(Q4)J_{0}(Qx)=1-Q^{2}x^{2}/4+O(Q^{4}). It gives the phase-stiffness factor in Eq. (104). The direct term has a finite Q→0Q\rightarrow 0 limit because

limQ→01−e−δ​QQ=δ.\lim_{Q\rightarrow 0}\frac{1-e^{-\delta Q}}{Q}=\delta. (121)

This is the capacitive energy of a uniform relative-density fluctuation. Combining the two terms gives the sound velocity in Eq. (64). The complete formula, rather than only the gradient expansion, is needed to follow the dispersion to the roton wave vector.

The roton minimum is an exchange effect. At momenta of order 1/ℓ1/\ell, the LLL form factor and the noncommutative guiding-center algebra make the phase and density kernels strongly momentum dependent. The direct term stabilizes the long-wavelength density sector, whereas exchange produces the finite-QQ competition. At the instability, the collective mode vanishes at Q0=q0​ℓ≃1.317Q_{0}=q_{0}\ell\simeq 1.317, identifying the physical wave number q0q_{0} of the emergent coherent density wave.

Appendix M Finite-sphere data at νT=1\nu_{T}=1

The N=8N=8, Nϕ=7N_{\phi}=7 finite-sphere spectrum is summarized in Table 11 and Fig. 23. The neutral L=1L=1 spacing and charged curvature are finite-size spectral diagnostics, whereas XDX_{D} is the thermodynamic uniform-HF one-particle splitting. They are not the same observable and should not be identified.

The comparison is useful in a limited and concrete sense. At d/ℓ=0.5d/\ell=0.5, the finite-size charged curvature is positive and the spectrum is consistent with a robust coherent incompressible regime. By d/ℓ=1d/\ell=1, both finite-size diagnostics have fallen sharply. At d/ℓ=4d/\ell=4, the neutral spacing is nearly zero and the charged curvature is negative for this geometry. This entry requires a caveat. At Nϕ=7N_{\phi}=7 each layer holds four electrons, and the composite fermions of a decoupled layer see an effective flux 2​Q∗=Nϕ−2​(N/2−1)=12Q^{*}=N_{\phi}-2(N/2-1)=1, which leaves the second composite-fermion shell half filled. The vanishing L=1L=1 spacing and the negative curvature at large dd therefore reflect the open-shell degeneracy imposed by the (111)(111) shift, and are not evidence about the thermodynamic state. Thus the N=8N=8 spectrum does not support extrapolating the uniform-HF gap to an exact many-body charge gap at large d/ℓd/\ell; it is consistent with strong finite-dd correlation physics absent from HF, but at this size it cannot establish it. Conversely, it cannot locate a thermodynamic transition by itself. This is the appropriate division of labor: HF supplies the analytic uniform saddle and its exchange scale, while finite-size diagonalization provides a nonperturbative but size-limited test of competing correlations. Larger-scale numerical studies find nontrivial evolution away from the small-dd coherent regime [68, 69, 70, 71].
